Fix a named positively oriented inertial laboratory chart with coordinates
$(x,y,z,t)$, spatial domain $\mathbb R^3$, and time domain $\mathbb R$. Adopt SI
units, a vacuum speed $c>0$, an angular frequency $\omega>0$, and
$k_0:=\omega/c$ (so $[k_0]=\mathrm{m}^{-1}$). Let
$\mathbf x_\perp:=(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2$. Use the unitary two-dimensional
Fourier transform $\mathcal F_2$ whose Schwartz-space convention is
$$\widehat f(\boldsymbol\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}f(\mathbf x_\perp) e^{-2\pi i\mathbf x_\perp\cdot\boldsymbol\xi}\,d^2\mathbf x_\perp,$$
and whose inverse is its unitary $L^2$ extension. The variable
$\boldsymbol\xi$ is in cycles per metre; its associated angular spatial
wavevector is $\mathbf q:=2\pi\boldsymbol\xi$ in $\mathrm{m}^{-1}$, with
$|\mathbf q|^2:=q_x^2+q_y^2$.

Choose $0<\delta<1$ and $u_0\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ with
$\mathcal F_2u_0$ supported, up to null sets, in
$D_\delta:=\{\boldsymbol\xi:|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|\le\delta k_0\}$.
For $\boldsymbol\xi\in D_\delta$ put
$$k_z(\boldsymbol\xi):=\sqrt{k_0^2-|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|^2},$$
which is real and strictly positive there. For each $z\in\mathbb R$, define the
exact multiplier on all of $\mathbb R^2$ by
$$m_{\mathrm{exact}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi):=\begin{cases}e^{izk_z(\boldsymbol\xi)},&\boldsymbol\xi\in D_\delta,\\0,&\boldsymbol\xi\notin D_\delta,\end{cases}$$
and define the paraxial multiplier on all of $\mathbb R^2$ by
$$m_{\mathrm{par}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi):=e^{ik_0z}e^{-iz|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|^2/(2k_0)}.$$
The exact scalar and paraxial scalar propagators are the $L^2$ equivalence
classes
$$u_{\mathrm{exact}}(z):=\mathcal F_2^{-1}\!\left[m_{\mathrm{exact}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi)\,\mathcal F_2u_0(\boldsymbol\xi)\right],\qquad u_{\mathrm{par}}(z):=\mathcal F_2^{-1}\!\left[m_{\mathrm{par}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi)\,\mathcal F_2u_0(\boldsymbol\xi)\right].$$
The associated real scalar fields are the real parts of these phasors multiplied
by $e^{-i\omega t}$. If $u_0$ carries $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, both propagated
fields carry the same unit. “Exact” here names the exact positive axial
dispersion multiplier inside this scalar model; it does not assert exact
Maxwell validity. Forward propagation is $z\ge0$; the formulas also define the
mathematical continuation to negative $z$.

At a fixed $\boldsymbol\xi\in D_\delta$, write
$\mathbf K(\boldsymbol\xi):=(2\pi\xi_x,2\pi\xi_y,k_z(\boldsymbol\xi))$.
A candidate monochromatic vector plane-wave mode at frequency $\omega$ has
complex amplitudes $\mathbf e,\mathbf b\in\mathbb C^3$ in the real-field
encoding $e^{i(\mathbf K\cdot(x,y,z)-\omega t)}$. It is called an exact
source-free vacuum mode only when its associated real fields satisfy the
adopted source-free vacuum Maxwell equations. The longitudinal electric
coefficient is $e_z$, and
$\mathbf e_\perp:=(e_x,e_y)$ has norm
$|\mathbf e_\perp|^2:=|e_x|^2+|e_y|^2$. No scalar/vector polarization
factorization is part of this definition.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. For $n\ge1$, these are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of The derivative and the Riemann integral of a vector-valued function: an intrinsic derivative and a componentwise integral.

For $n=0$, use the zero-space case directly, without invoking that supplier's positive-codomain standing hypothesis. The space $\mathbb R^0$ has only its zero vector and carries the zero Euclidean norm and its induced metric (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5, The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms). Whenever the line map is defined near $0$, every difference quotient for real $t\ne0$ is this zero vector; define $D_vf(a)=0$. This is the unique possible derivative value, and its normwise difference-quotient error is exactly zero for all such $t$, so the real parameter still approaches an actual limit point. Every existing coordinate direction therefore has $\partial_jf(a)=0$; these zero-valued partial maps are continuous in the induced norm metrics. If the source dimension is zero, there are no partial indices and the sole direction is $v=0$; its constant line map is defined near $0$.

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: For $r>0$, [F4] identifies the angular vector field $-y\partial_x+x\partial_y$ with $\partial_\phi$. By [F2]–[F3], differentiating the integer winding factor gives $L_z^{\mathrm{sc}}u_z=-i\partial_\phi(fe^{i\ell\phi}) =\ell fe^{i\ell\phi}=\ell u_z$. The required axis form makes $u_z$ smooth at the origin: for $\ell\ge0$ its angular factor is $(x+iy)^\ell$, and for $\ell<0$ it is $(x-iy)^{|\ell|}$, each multiplied by the smooth radial factor $g(x^2+y^2)$. The rotation vector field vanishes at the origin, so the same identity holds there as well.

Step 1.1 gives $L_z^{\mathrm{sc}}u_z=\ell u_z$ everywhere, hence $L_z^{\mathrm{sc}}u_z\in L^2$ because $u_z\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$. Therefore $\langle L_z^{\mathrm{sc}}u_z,u_z\rangle_2 =\int_{\mathbb R^2}\ell|u_z|^2\,d^2x =\ell\langle u_z,u_z\rangle_2$; the denominator is positive since $u_z$ is nonzero. Division proves the claimed identity.

Step 1.1 includes ell=0, for which the axis factor is g(x^2+y^2).
Step 1.1 covers ell=1 and ell=-1 through the coordinate factors x+iy and x-iy.
Step 1.1 treats r=0 using the smooth extension and the vanishing rotation vector field.
Step 2.1 is pointwise and performs no radial integration by parts or boundary limit.

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

Work in a material rest frame: an inertial frame in whose coordinates each modelled material element has fixed spatial position $x$ and history $t\mapsto(ct,x)$, as defined by the framework's earlier material-closure formulation. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be the material region in that frame and $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ a nonempty open time interval. The electric field $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, polarization fields $P_\ell:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, and magnetic fields $B,H:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial-vector fields in that frame. At every fixed $x\in\Omega$, require $E(x,\cdot)\in C^0(I;\mathbb R^3)$ and $P_\ell(x,\cdot)\in C^2(I;\mathbb R^3)$ for each $1\le\ell\le N$, so the displayed time derivatives are classical. These are time-regularity conditions only; this postulate imposes no spatial regularity, which must be stated separately wherever a consuming field-equation result requires it. In SI, $E$ is in V m$^{-1}$, $P_\ell$ in C m$^{-2}$, $B$ in T and $H$ in A m$^{-1}$.

For a fixed finite integer $N\ge1$, adopt at every material point $x$ the constitutive equations

$$D(x,t)=\varepsilon_\infty E(x,t)+\sum_{\ell=1}^{N}P_\ell(x,t),\qquad B(x,t)=\mu H(x,t),$$

$$\partial_t^2P_\ell(x,t)+\gamma_\ell\partial_tP_\ell(x,t)+\omega_\ell^2P_\ell(x,t)=a_\ell E(x,t)\qquad (1\le\ell\le N).$$

Here $\varepsilon_\infty>0$ is a constant scalar with units F m$^{-1}$, $\mu>0$ is a constant scalar with units H m$^{-1}$, $a_\ell>0$ are constant parameters with units F m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, $\omega_\ell>0$ are constant angular frequencies with units s$^{-1}$, and $\gamma_\ell\ge0$ are constant damping rates with units s$^{-1}$. The parameters are independent of position and time; this is the meaning of homogeneous in this model. The model is linear because all displayed field and oscillator relations are linear with fixed coefficients, and spatially local because the oscillator equation at $x$ uses only the field and oscillator state at that same $x$. The magnetic law has only the constant scalar coefficient $\mu$ and no independent magnetic polarization variable; this is the nonmagnetic oscillator model adopted here.

The word nonmagnetic here means that the oscillator sector has no dynamic magnetic response; the fixed scalar coefficient $\mu$ can still encode a separate static constitutive response. To identify the displayed quantities with the framework's macroscopic definitions, stipulate $P_{\mathrm{tot}}=(\varepsilon_\infty-\varepsilon_0)E+\sum_{\ell=1}^N P_\ell$ and $M_{\mathrm{tot}}=(\mu_0^{-1}-\mu^{-1})B$. Then $D=\varepsilon_0E+P_{\mathrm{tot}}=\varepsilon_\infty E+\sum P_\ell$ and $H=\mu_0^{-1}B-M_{\mathrm{tot}}=\mu^{-1}B$. This is a constitutive identification in the model, not a microscopic decomposition.

At an initial time $t_0\in I$, the oscillator state consists of $P_\ell(x,t_0)$ and $\partial_tP_\ell(x,t_0)$. For a selected causal zero-past branch, choose an onset $\tau\in I$ and require $E(x,t)=0$ and $P_\ell(x,t)=\partial_tP_\ell(x,t)=0$ for every $t\in I$ with $t\le\tau$. Continuity gives $E(x,\tau)=0$, and the equation gives $\partial_t^2P_\ell(x,\tau)=0$, consistent with the $C^2$ zero extension through onset. For $t\ge\tau$ this branch is the retarded initial-value equation with those data, so its value at time $t$ uses the applied field only on $[\tau,t]$. If $\gamma_\ell=0$, no decaying stationary impulse response is assumed; in particular, this is not an absolutely integrable convolution for arbitrary bounded histories. This postulate does not assert that any actual material realizes the equations.

Use a material rest frame: an inertial frame in whose coordinates each modelled material element has fixed spatial position $x$ and history $t\mapsto(ct,x)$, as defined by the framework's earlier material-closure formulation. In that frame, let $E,P:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be the electric field and polarization, and let $V:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a free-carrier current density. At every fixed $x\in\Omega$, require $E(x,\cdot)\in C^0(I;\mathbb R^3)$ and $P(x,\cdot),V(x,\cdot)\in C^1(I;\mathbb R^3)$, so the displayed time derivatives are classical. These are time-regularity conditions only; this postulate imposes no spatial regularity, which must be stated separately wherever a consuming field-equation result requires it. In SI, $E$ is V m$^{-1}$, $P$ is C m$^{-2}$, and $V$ is A m$^{-2}$. Adopt

$$\partial_tP(x,t)=V(x,t),\qquad \partial_tV(x,t)+\gamma V(x,t)=aE(x,t),$$

$$D(x,t)=\varepsilon_\infty E(x,t)+P(x,t),\qquad B(x,t)=\mu H(x,t).$$

The constant scalar parameters satisfy $\varepsilon_\infty>0$, $\mu>0$, $a>0$ and $\gamma\ge0$. Their units are respectively F m$^{-1}$, H m$^{-1}$, F m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$ and s$^{-1}$. The fields $V$ and $P$ have units A m$^{-2}$ and C m$^{-2}$. All coefficients are independent of $x$ and $t$, and the equation at $x$ depends only on the state and electric field at $x$; these clauses define the homogeneous, linear, spatially local closure used here. To identify these constitutive quantities with the framework's macroscopic definitions, stipulate $P_{\mathrm{tot}}=(\varepsilon_\infty-\varepsilon_0)E+P$ and $M_{\mathrm{tot}}=(\mu_0^{-1}-\mu^{-1})B$. Then $D=\varepsilon_0E+P_{\mathrm{tot}}=\varepsilon_\infty E+P$ and $H=\mu_0^{-1}B-M_{\mathrm{tot}}=\mu^{-1}B$. This is a constitutive identification within the model, not a microscopic decomposition.

At an initial time $t_0\in I$, $P(x,t_0)$ and $V(x,t_0)$ are state data. A constant polarization offset is fixed with the Gauss-law data and is not determined by the current equation alone. The branch $\gamma=0$ is the collisionless model; it has no decaying stationary impulse kernel, and its zero-frequency response is not part of this postulate. This is a phenomenological closure, not a derivation of carrier mass, density, collision statistics or any actual material response.

Assume the smooth branch of the vacuum Maxwell postulate [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]: fields $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ jointly of class $C^1$ with the additional derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and continuous source densities $\rho,J$ of [[def-em-sources]]. Let $P,M$ and the derived objects $\rho_b,J_b,\rho_f,J_f,D,H$ be those of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]], with $P,M$ of class $C^2$, and use the operators of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Then:

**(a) [Bound-source conservation]** $\partial_t\rho_b+\operatorname{div}J_b=0$ on $\Omega\times I$. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the regular-distribution and classical-compatibility interfaces below. Identify continuous sources with their regular distributions using [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]] and [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]. Then

$$\partial_t\rho_f+\operatorname{div}J_f=\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J$$

as distributions on $U$, with derivatives as in [[def-distributional-derivative]]: the free pair is distributionally conserved exactly when the total pair is. Under the adopted four vacuum equations both sides are zero distributions, by [[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]]. These statements do not require classical derivatives of $\rho,J$. Where the partial derivatives $\partial_t\rho$ and $\partial_{x_i}J_i$ exist, the same identity holds pointwise by differentiating the free/bound decomposition; in particular, if these derivatives are continuous on $U$, both pairs satisfy the classical pointwise continuity equation. The bound-source conservation equation remains classical and uses only $P,M\in C^2$.

**(b) [Macroscopic equations]** On $\Omega\times I$,

$$\operatorname{div}D=\rho_f,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD.$$

**(c) [Interpretation and scope]** Equations (b) are an exact rewriting of the adopted vacuum equations under the decomposition of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]]: the two equations written in $E$ and $B$ are unchanged, and the $D$ and $H$ equations hold for every $C^2$ pair $(P,M)$, independently of any constitutive law. The classical bound identity of (a) uses the exchange of $\partial_t$ with $\operatorname{div}$ for $C^2$ data; the free/total identity is distributional in the stated continuous-source class, with its classical interpretation only under the additional derivatives stated in (a). The distributional conservation conclusion embeds the adopted smooth solution only; no macroscopic field-equation claim is made for the weak branch of the Maxwell postulate, for singular or sheet sources or for discontinuous $(P,M)$; no constitutive relation and no empirical statement is made.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F,G:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$. Then $F\times G$ is $C^1$ on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{div}(F\times G)=\langle\operatorname{curl}F,G\rangle-\langle F,\operatorname{curl}G\rangle,$$

$$\operatorname{curl}(F\times G)=(\operatorname{div}G)F-(\operatorname{div}F)G+DF\,G-DG\,F.$$

Here $DF\,G$ denotes the map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ whose $i$th coordinate at $p$ is $\sum_{j<3}\partial_jF_i(p)\,G_j(p)$, that is, the Jacobian matrix of $F$ at $p$ applied to the vector $G(p)$, and $DG\,F$ is defined the same way with the roles of $F$ and $G$ exchanged. The operators are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], the cross product is that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], the inner product that of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and the Jacobian matrix that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann),
On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of The vector space $F^{X}$ of all functions $X \to F$ with pointwise operations, and $F^{n}$ as the case $X = n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
(Vector space over a field). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4 and
Squares of nonzero elements are positive, the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
Integer powers $a^m$) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root (Square roots exist: a unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with $(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$; the positives are $\{x^2 : x \neq 0\}$).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
$\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and Conventions of this page, the standing $n \ge 1$ hypothesis, and what is taken up elsewhere in the reading order lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   (Squares of nonzero elements are positive), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms
is proved in Cauchy-Schwarz $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \le \lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ with its equality case, the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, the parallelogram law and polarisation, where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Fix a real angular frequency $\omega>0$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and use the $e^{-i\omega t}$ convention and SI field units of the fixed-frequency reciprocal-phasor model. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded device region with $C^1$ boundary in one stationary material-rest frame. Its continuous phasor coefficient maps are $\varepsilon,\mu:\overline\Omega\to\mathbb C^{3\times3}$ in $\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}$, respectively. derivations.claim: In the Lorentz branch set $J_{\mathrm{tot}}=J_f+\sum_{\ell=1}^M\partial_tP_\ell$, and in the Drude branch set $J_{\mathrm{tot}}=J_f+V$. From [L1] and [A1] or [A2], respectively, the field and constitutive equations give $\varepsilon_\infty\partial_tE=\operatorname{curl}H-J_{\mathrm{tot}}$ and $\mu\partial_tH=-\operatorname{curl}E$.

In the Lorentz branch, dot the $\ell$th oscillator equation [A1] with $\partial_tP_\ell/a_\ell$. Since $a_\ell>0$, the division is valid; the product rule in [F2] gives $E\cdot\partial_tP_\ell=\partial_t\!\left((|\partial_tP_\ell|^2+\omega_\ell^2|P_\ell|^2)/(2a_\ell)\right)+(\gamma_\ell/a_\ell)|\partial_tP_\ell|^2$. The last term is nonnegative because $\gamma_\ell\ge0$.

In the Drude branch, dot $\partial_tV+\gamma V=aE$ from [A2] with $V/a$. The product rule and $a>0$ give $E\cdot V=\partial_t(|V|^2/(2a))+(\gamma/a)|V|^2$, whose last term is nonnegative because $\gamma\ge0$.

Define the field energy density $u_f:\overline\Omega\times\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$ by $u_f=(\varepsilon_\infty|E|^2+\mu|H|^2)/2$. Differentiate it componentwise using [F2] and the field equations of step 1.1. This gives $\partial_tu_f=E\cdot\operatorname{curl}H-E\cdot J_{\mathrm{tot}}-H\cdot\operatorname{curl}E$. Applying [F1] yields $-\operatorname{div}(E\times H)-E\cdot J_f-\sum E\cdot\partial_tP_\ell$ in the Lorentz branch and $-\operatorname{div}(E\times H)-E\cdot J_f-E\cdot V$ in the Drude branch.

Define the total field-plus-material energy density $u:\overline\Omega\times\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$ branchwise: in the Lorentz branch, $u:=u_f+\sum_{\ell=1}^M\bigl(|\partial_tP_\ell|^2+\omega_\ell^2|P_\ell|^2\bigr)/(2a_\ell)$; in the Drude branch, $u:=u_f+|V|^2/(2a)$. All terms are nonnegative, have SI units $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, and are jointly smooth and $T$-periodic under the Statement's hypotheses. Substituting step 1.2 into the Lorentz field balance of step 2.1 cancels every $E\cdot\partial_tP_\ell$ term; substituting step 1.3 into its Drude balance cancels $E\cdot V$. Since the given source-free condition has $J_f=0$, each branch therefore satisfies $\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}(E\times H)=-\ell$ with exactly the loss density $\ell$ in the Statement.

Integrate the local identity of step 3.1 over $\Omega$ at each time and apply [F3] to $E\times H$. Then integrate in time from $0$ to $T$. The integrand $\partial_tu$ is continuous and integrable on the finite product domain, so [F4] permits integration first in time: $\int_\Omega\int_0^T\partial_tu\,dt\,dV=\int_\Omega(u(x,T)-u(x,0))\,dV=0$ by periodicity. Hence the time-integrated outward boundary flux equals $-T P_{\mathrm{mat}}$.

Divide step 4.1 by $T$ and use the total boundary-flux decomposition [F5]. The port term is $\|b\|_2^2-\|a\|_2^2$, the wall term is $P_\partial\ge0$ by [A3], and the remaining outgoing term is $P_{\mathrm{other}}\ge0$. Rearrangement gives the power balance in the Statement.

Since each of $P_{\mathrm{mat}},P_\partial,P_{\mathrm{other}}$ is nonnegative, step 5.1 gives $\|Sa\|_2^2\le\|a\|_2^2$ for every $a$; taking nonnegative square roots proves contractivity. If all three powers vanish for every $a$, set $K:=I_N-S^\dagger S$. Then $K^\dagger=K$ because $(S^\dagger S)^\dagger=S^\dagger S$, and the power balance gives $a^\dagger Ka=\|a\|_2^2-\|Sa\|_2^2=0$ for every $a$. Let $e_j$ denote the $j$th coordinate vector of $\mathbb C^N$. Testing $a=e_j$ gives $K_{jj}=0$; for $j<k$, testing $a=e_j+e_k$ gives $2\operatorname{Re}K_{jk}=0$, while testing $a=e_j+i e_k$ gives $-2\operatorname{Im}K_{jk}=0$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F,G:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$. Then $F\times G$ is $C^1$ on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{div}(F\times G)=\langle\operatorname{curl}F,G\rangle-\langle F,\operatorname{curl}G\rangle,$$

$$\operatorname{curl}(F\times G)=(\operatorname{div}G)F-(\operatorname{div}F)G+DF\,G-DG\,F.$$

Here $DF\,G$ denotes the map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ whose $i$th coordinate at $p$ is $\sum_{j<3}\partial_jF_i(p)\,G_j(p)$, that is, the Jacobian matrix of $F$ at $p$ applied to the vector $G(p)$, and $DG\,F$ is defined the same way with the roles of $F$ and $G$ exchanged. The operators are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], the cross product is that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], the inner product that of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and the Jacobian matrix that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

Use a material rest frame: an inertial frame in whose coordinates each modelled material element has fixed spatial position $x$ and history $t\mapsto(ct,x)$, as defined by the framework's earlier material-closure formulation. In that frame, let $E,P:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be the electric field and polarization, and let $V:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a free-carrier current density. In SI, $E$ is V m$^{-1}$, $P$ is C m$^{-2}$, and $V$ is A m$^{-2}$. Adopt

$$\partial_tP(x,t)=V(x,t),\qquad \partial_tV(x,t)+\gamma V(x,t)=aE(x,t),$$

$$D(x,t)=\varepsilon_\infty E(x,t)+P(x,t),\qquad B(x,t)=\mu H(x,t).$$

The constant scalar parameters satisfy $\varepsilon_\infty>0$, $\mu>0$, $a>0$ and $\gamma\ge0$. Their units are respectively F m$^{-1}$, H m$^{-1}$, F m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$ and s$^{-1}$. The fields $V$ and $P$ have units A m$^{-2}$ and C m$^{-2}$. All coefficients are independent of $x$ and $t$, and the equation at $x$ depends only on the state and electric field at $x$; these clauses define the homogeneous, linear, spatially local closure used here. To identify these constitutive quantities with the framework's macroscopic definitions, stipulate $P_{\mathrm{tot}}=(\varepsilon_\infty-\varepsilon_0)E+P$ and $M_{\mathrm{tot}}=(\mu_0^{-1}-\mu^{-1})B$. Then $D=\varepsilon_0E+P_{\mathrm{tot}}=\varepsilon_\infty E+P$ and $H=\mu_0^{-1}B-M_{\mathrm{tot}}=\mu^{-1}B$. This is a constitutive identification within the model, not a microscopic decomposition.

At an initial time $t_0$, $P(x,t_0)$ and $V(x,t_0)$ are state data. A constant polarization offset is fixed with the Gauss-law data and is not determined by the current equation alone. The branch $\gamma=0$ is the collisionless model; it has no decaying stationary impulse kernel, and its zero-frequency response is not part of this postulate. This is a phenomenological closure, not a derivation of carrier mass, density, collision statistics or any actual material response.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Work in a material rest frame: an inertial frame in whose coordinates each modelled material element has fixed spatial position $x$ and history $t\mapsto(ct,x)$, as defined by the framework's earlier material-closure formulation. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be the material region in that frame and $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ a nonempty open time interval. The electric field $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, polarization fields $P_\ell:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, and magnetic fields $B,H:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial-vector fields in that frame. In SI, $E$ is in V m$^{-1}$, $P_\ell$ in C m$^{-2}$, $B$ in T and $H$ in A m$^{-1}$.

For a fixed finite integer $N\ge1$, adopt at every material point $x$ the constitutive equations

$$D(x,t)=\varepsilon_\infty E(x,t)+\sum_{\ell=1}^{N}P_\ell(x,t),\qquad B(x,t)=\mu H(x,t),$$

$$\partial_t^2P_\ell(x,t)+\gamma_\ell\partial_tP_\ell(x,t)+\omega_\ell^2P_\ell(x,t)=a_\ell E(x,t)\qquad (1\le\ell\le N).$$

Here $\varepsilon_\infty>0$ is a constant scalar with units F m$^{-1}$, $\mu>0$ is a constant scalar with units H m$^{-1}$, $a_\ell>0$ are constant parameters with units F m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, $\omega_\ell>0$ are constant angular frequencies with units s$^{-1}$, and $\gamma_\ell\ge0$ are constant damping rates with units s$^{-1}$. The parameters are independent of position and time; this is the meaning of homogeneous in this model. The model is linear because all displayed field and oscillator relations are linear with fixed coefficients, and spatially local because the oscillator equation at $x$ uses only the field and oscillator state at that same $x$. The magnetic law has only the constant scalar coefficient $\mu$ and no independent magnetic polarization variable; this is the nonmagnetic oscillator model adopted here.

The word nonmagnetic here means that the oscillator sector has no dynamic magnetic response; the fixed scalar coefficient $\mu$ can still encode a separate static constitutive response. To identify the displayed quantities with the framework's macroscopic definitions, stipulate $P_{\mathrm{tot}}=(\varepsilon_\infty-\varepsilon_0)E+\sum_{\ell=1}^N P_\ell$ and $M_{\mathrm{tot}}=(\mu_0^{-1}-\mu^{-1})B$. Then $D=\varepsilon_0E+P_{\mathrm{tot}}=\varepsilon_\infty E+\sum P_\ell$ and $H=\mu_0^{-1}B-M_{\mathrm{tot}}=\mu^{-1}B$. This is a constitutive identification in the model, not a microscopic decomposition.

The oscillator state at a time $t_0\in I$ includes both $P_\ell(x,t_0)$ and $\partial_tP_\ell(x,t_0)$. For a causal zero-past response, the oscillator state vanishes before the declared onset of the applied field and the solution at $t$ depends only on that past field history. If $\gamma_\ell=0$, no decaying stationary impulse response is assumed; the zero-past branch is the retarded solution of the initial-value equation, not an absolutely integrable convolution for arbitrary bounded histories. This postulate does not assert that any actual material realizes the equations.

Then:

**(a) [Bound-source conservation]** $\partial_t\rho_b+\operatorname{div}J_b=0$ on $\Omega\times I$. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the regular-distribution and classical-compatibility interfaces below. Identify continuous sources with their regular distributions using [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]] and [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]. Then

$$\partial_t\rho_f+\operatorname{div}J_f=\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J$$

as distributions on $U$, with derivatives as in [[def-distributional-derivative]]: the free pair is distributionally conserved exactly when the total pair is. Under the adopted four vacuum equations both sides are zero distributions, by [[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]]. These statements do not require classical derivatives of $\rho,J$. Where the partial derivatives $\partial_t\rho$ and $\partial_{x_i}J_i$ exist, the same identity holds pointwise by differentiating the free/bound decomposition; in particular, if these derivatives are continuous on $U$, both pairs satisfy the classical pointwise continuity equation. The bound-source conservation equation remains classical and uses only $P,M\in C^2$.

**(b) [Macroscopic equations]** On $\Omega\times I$,

$$\operatorname{div}D=\rho_f,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD.$$

**(c) [Interpretation and scope]** Equations (b) are an exact rewriting of the adopted vacuum equations under the decomposition of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]]: the two equations written in $E$ and $B$ are unchanged, and the $D$ and $H$ equations hold for every $C^2$ pair $(P,M)$, independently of any constitutive law. The classical bound identity of (a) uses the exchange of $\partial_t$ with $\operatorname{div}$ for $C^2$ data; the free/total identity is distributional in the stated continuous-source class, with its classical interpretation only under the additional derivatives stated in (a). supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $N\ge1$, $I:=[0,T)$ with $0<T\le\infty$, and let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $I$. Let $U,S\in C^\infty(J\times\mathbb R,\mathbb R^N)$. Write $\operatorname{Sym}_N(\mathbb R)$ for the real symmetric $N\times N$ matrices and use the Euclidean dot product and norm on $\mathbb R^N$. Let $V\in C^\infty(\mathbb R,\operatorname{Sym}_N(\mathbb R))$ be bounded, independent of $t$, and positive semidefinite at every $x$, meaning $z^{\mathsf T}V(x)z\ge0$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^N$. Assume $U$ and all its mixed derivatives of total order at most two, and $S$, are Schwartz in $x$ locally uniformly for $t\in J$: for every compact $K\subset J$, every such derivative $D$ and every integer $m\ge0$, $\sup_{t\in K,x\in\mathbb R}(1+|x|)^m|DU(t,x)|<\infty$, and the analogous bounds hold for $S$. If
$$U_{tt}-U_{xx}+V(x)U=S,$$
define
$$E(t):=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R}\bigl(|U_t|^2+|U_x|^2+U^{\mathsf T}V(x)U\bigr)\,dx,$$
where $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm and $\|v(t,\cdot)\|_2^2:=\int_{\mathbb R}|v(t,x)|^2\,dx$ for any vector-valued function $v$. Then $E(t)\ge0$,
$$E'(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}U_t\cdot S\,dx,\qquad\sqrt{E(t)}\le\sqrt{E(0)}+\frac1{\sqrt2}\int_0^t\|S(\tau,\cdot)\|_2\,d\tau\quad(t\in I).$$
In particular $E$ is constant when $S=0$. If $t,x$ have length units and $U$ has unit $[U]$, then $V$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-2}$, $S$ has unit $[U]\mathrm m^{-2}$, $E$ has unit $[U]^2\mathrm m^{-1}$, and both sides of the square-root estimate have unit $[U]\mathrm m^{-1/2}$. This abstract estimate supplies neither pointwise decay nor a reconstruction of coupled Einstein–Maxwell perturbations.

derivations.claim: Let $\cosh x:=(e^x+e^{-x})/2$, $w(x):=1/\cosh x$, and $V(x):=-2w(x)^2$. These are smooth real functions. Put $\tau(x):=(e^x-e^{-x})/(e^x+e^{-x})$; direct differentiation gives $w'=-w\tau$, $\tau'=1-\tau^2=w^2$, and $w^2=1-\tau^2$. Therefore $w''=w(2\tau^2-1)=w-2w^3$. Inductively each derivative $w^{(k)}$ is $w$ times a polynomial $P_k(\tau)$; since $|\tau|\le1$ and $\cosh x\ge\tfrac12 e^{|x|}$, there is a finite constant $C_k$ with $|w^{(k)}(x)|\le C_ke^{-|x|}$ for all $x$. In particular, the integrals $\int_{\mathbb R}|w|^2\,dx$ and $\int_{\mathbb R}(|w|^2+|w'|^2)\,dx$ are finite, so the stated $L^2$ and $H^1$ norms are finite. Consequently the differential expression $A:=-\partial_x^2+V(x)$ satisfies $Aw=-w$.

Define $U(t,x)=e^t w(x)$. Then $U_{tt}=e^tw$ and $-U_{xx}+VU=e^t(-w''-2w^3)=-e^tw$ by step 1.1. For every compact $K\subset\mathbb R$, $e^t$ is bounded on $K$; for every integer $m\ge0$, $(1+|x|)^m e^{-|x|}$ is bounded on $\mathbb R$. The derivative bounds from step 1.1 therefore give the exact local-uniform decay condition in the refuted Statement for every spatial derivative of $U$. Thus $U$ is an admissible solution of that assertion. Therefore $U_{tt}-U_{xx}+VU=0$, while
$$\|U(t)\|_{H^1}+\|U_t(t)\|_2=e^t\bigl(\|w\|_{H^1}+\|w\|_2\bigr)\longrightarrow\infty.$$
The initial norm is finite and nonzero, so no time-uniform constant $C(V,N)$ as asserted exists. The example refutes only the claim that symmetry alone suffices; its potential violates the positive-semidefinite hypothesis of the supplied theorem and is not asserted to be an Einstein–Maxwell master potential.

Fix nonnegative integers $n_0,n_1,n_2,n_3$ and ordered coordinate bases, and put $C^k:=\mathbb R^{n_k}$ for $k=0,1,2,3$. The dual space $(C^k)^*$ is the vector space of linear functionals $C^k\to\mathbb R$, with the dual basis to the chosen coordinate basis. Let $D_0\in\mathbb R^{n_1\times n_0}$, $D_1\in\mathbb R^{n_2\times n_1}$, and $D_2\in\mathbb R^{n_3\times n_2}$ be linear maps satisfying $D_1D_0=0$ and $D_2D_1=0$. This data is a finite cochain complex. The transpose $D_k^{\mathsf T}$ denotes the representing matrix of the dual linear map in the dual bases. Let $M_1\in\mathbb R^{n_1\times n_1}$ and $M_2\in\mathbb R^{n_2\times n_2}$ be symmetric positive-definite matrices: $v^{\mathsf T}M_kv>0$ for each nonzero $v\in C^k$. They represent linear maps $M_1:C^1\to(C^1)^*$ and $M_2:C^2\to(C^2)^*$ in the chosen bases; in positive dimensions their inverses exist by the finite-dimensional positive-matrix result cited below, and the unique map on a zero-dimensional space is its own inverse.

The finite state space is $\mathcal X:=C^2\oplus(C^1)^*$, with state $(b,d)$, where $b$ is a column of $C^2$ coordinates and $d$ is a column in the dual basis of $(C^1)^*$. In this item, “phase space” means this finite-dimensional state space only; no symplectic form is asserted. On an open interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$, a semidiscrete trajectory is a continuously differentiable map $t\mapsto(b(t),d(t))\in\mathcal X$ satisfying

$$\dot b(t)=-D_1M_1^{-1}d(t),\qquad \dot d(t)=D_1^{\mathsf T}M_2b(t).$$

Its two discrete constraints are $D_2b(t)=0$ in $C^3$ and $D_0^{\mathsf T}d(t)=0$ in $(C^0)^*$. The associated quadratic energy is

$$\mathcal E(b,d):=\tfrac12\left(b^{\mathsf T}M_2b+d^{\mathsf T}M_1^{-1}d\right).$$

All objects here are finite-dimensional real linear-algebra data. The term “Maxwell” names this algebraic model and does not identify it with a continuum Maxwell or Einstein–Maxwell solution.

Use the finite cochain data fixed by the preceding definition item, namely finite real coordinate spaces $C^0,C^1,C^2,C^3$, maps $D_0,D_1,D_2$ with $D_1D_0=D_2D_1=0$, and symmetric positive-definite mass maps $M_1,M_2$. Inputs are rational matrices $D_0,D_1,D_2,M_1,M_2$, rational initial coordinates $b_0\in C^2$ and $d_{1/2}\in(C^1)^*$, a positive rational step size $\tau$, and an integer $N\geq0$. derivations.claim: The matrices in [A1] are the signed boundary-incidence maps of one oriented tetrahedron, with edges ordered $01,02,03,12,13,23$, faces ordered $012,013,023,123$, and cell orientation $0123$. Matrix multiplication gives $D_1D_0=0_{4\times4}$ and $D_2D_1=0_{1\times6}$. Also $D_2x=-1+1=0$ and $D_0^{\mathsf T}d_{1/2}=0_{4\times1}$, so the initial state satisfies both constraints.

Put $c:=(-1,1,-1,1)^{\mathsf T}$, so $D_2=c^{\mathsf T}$. Direct multiplication gives
$$D_1D_1^{\mathsf T}=\begin{pmatrix}3&1&-1&1\\1&3&1&-1\\-1&1&3&1\\1&-1&1&3\end{pmatrix}=4I_4-cc^{\mathsf T}.$$
For every $z\in\mathbb R^4$, this gives $\lVert D_1^{\mathsf T}z\rVert_2^2=4\lVert z\rVert_2^2-(c^{\mathsf T}z)^2\leq4\lVert z\rVert_2^2$. Hence, by Cauchy–Schwarz, $\lVert D_1v\rVert_2=\max_{\lVert z\rVert_2=1}|z^{\mathsf T}D_1v|\leq2\lVert v\rVert_2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^6$. Since $c^{\mathsf T}x=0$, $e:=x/\sqrt2$ is unit and $D_1D_1^{\mathsf T}e=4e$; consequently $f:=D_1^{\mathsf T}e/2$ is unit and $D_1f=2e$. Thus the operator norm of $D_1$ is exactly $2$, attained at $f$. Here $M_1=M_2=I$, so the $\sigma$ defined in [F3] is $2$. For a state $b=ue$, $d=vf$, the update in [F2] with $\tau=2$ gives $u^+=u-4v$ and $v^+=v+4u^+=4u-15v$, hence the invariant two-dimensional subspace has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&-4\\4&-15\end{pmatrix}$. The initial state has modal coordinates $(u,v)=(\sqrt2,0)$.

The matrix in step 2.1 has trace $-14$, determinant $1$, and eigenvalues $\lambda_-=-7-4\sqrt3$ and $\lambda_+=-7+4\sqrt3$, found by solving $\lambda^2+14\lambda+1=0$. Since $6<4\sqrt3<7$, $\lambda_-<-1$ and $-1<\lambda_+<0$. Direct substitution gives eigenvectors $v_-=(1,2+\sqrt3)^{\mathsf T}$ and $v_+=(1,2-\sqrt3)^{\mathsf T}$; their determinant is $-2\sqrt3\neq0$, so write the initial modal vector as $(\sqrt2,0)^{\mathsf T}=a v_-+b v_+$. The coefficient $a$ is nonzero, since otherwise $(\sqrt2,0)^{\mathsf T}$ would be a multiple of $v_+$, whose second coordinate $2-\sqrt3$ is nonzero. The first modal coordinate after $n$ steps is therefore $u_n=a\lambda_-^n+b\lambda_+^n$. If $u_n$ were bounded, then $b\lambda_+^n$ would be bounded because $|\lambda_+|<1$, so their difference $a\lambda_-^n$ would be bounded, contradicting $a\neq0$ and $|\lambda_-|>1$. Since $\lVert b_n\rVert_2\geq|u_n|$, the state orbit is unbounded.

By [F3], each update preserves both constraints, and step 1.1 sets them to zero initially. Explicitly, $D_2b^+=D_2b-\tau D_2D_1M_1^{-1}d=D_2b$ and $D_0^{\mathsf T}d^+=D_0^{\mathsf T}d+\tau(D_1D_0)^{\mathsf T}M_2b^+=D_0^{\mathsf T}d$, so induction gives zero constraints at every iterate. Thus exact constraint preservation holds at every step although this rational finite-complex algorithm has an unbounded orbit for $\tau\sigma=4>2$. This refutes the stated bounded-orbit claim.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix nonnegative integers $n_0,n_1,n_2,n_3$ and ordered coordinate bases, and put $C^k:=\mathbb R^{n_k}$ for $k=0,1,2,3$. The dual space $(C^k)^*$ is the vector space of linear functionals $C^k\to\mathbb R$, with the dual basis to the chosen coordinate basis. Let $D_0\in\mathbb R^{n_1\times n_0}$, $D_1\in\mathbb R^{n_2\times n_1}$, and $D_2\in\mathbb R^{n_3\times n_2}$ be linear maps satisfying $D_1D_0=0$ and $D_2D_1=0$. This data is a finite cochain complex. The transpose $D_k^{\mathsf T}$ denotes the representing matrix of the dual linear map in the dual bases. Let $M_1\in\mathbb R^{n_1\times n_1}$ and $M_2\in\mathbb R^{n_2\times n_2}$ be symmetric positive-definite matrices: $v^{\mathsf T}M_kv>0$ for each nonzero $v\in C^k$. They represent linear maps $M_1:C^1\to(C^1)^*$ and $M_2:C^2\to(C^2)^*$ in the chosen bases; in positive dimensions their inverses exist by the finite-dimensional positive-matrix result cited below, and the unique map on a zero-dimensional space is its own inverse.

The finite state space is $\mathcal X:=C^2\oplus(C^1)^*$, with state $(b,d)$, where $b$ is a column of $C^2$ coordinates and $d$ is a column in the dual basis of $(C^1)^*$. In this item, “phase space” means this finite-dimensional state space only; no symplectic form is asserted. On an open interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$, a semidiscrete trajectory is a continuously differentiable map $t\mapsto(b(t),d(t))\in\mathcal X$ satisfying

$$\dot b(t)=-D_1M_1^{-1}d(t),\qquad \dot d(t)=D_1^{\mathsf T}M_2b(t).$$

Its two discrete constraints are $D_2b(t)=0$ in $C^3$ and $D_0^{\mathsf T}d(t)=0$ in $(C^0)^*$. The associated quadratic energy is

$$\mathcal E(b,d):=\tfrac12\left(b^{\mathsf T}M_2b+d^{\mathsf T}M_1^{-1}d\right).$$

All objects here are finite-dimensional real linear-algebra data. The term “Maxwell” names this algebraic model and does not identify it with a continuum Maxwell or Einstein–Maxwell solution.

Assume Countable Choice for the smooth Lorentzian tangent-bundle conventions of the suppliers. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, $r_0>0$, and $\mathcal E=I\times(r_0,\infty)\times S^2$, where $S^2=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|=1\}$ has its unit round metric $q_{AB}$ and area form $d\Omega$. Let $D_A$ be the Levi-Civita covariant derivative of $q$, and raise angular indices with $q^{AB}$. A **Bondi-Sachs end** is a smooth Lorentzian metric on $\mathcal E$ written in coordinates $(u,r,x^A)$, $A,B=1,2$, as

$$g=-\left(e^{2\beta}\frac Vr-r^2\gamma_{AB}U^AU^B\right)du^2-2e^{2\beta}du\,dr-2r^2\gamma_{AB}U^Bdu\,dx^A+r^2\gamma_{AB}dx^A dx^B,$$

where $\beta,V,U^A,\gamma_{AB}$ are smooth, $\gamma_{AB}$ is positive definite, $\gamma^{AC}\gamma_{CB}=\delta^A_B$, and $\det(\gamma_{AB})=\det(q_{AB})$. Thus $u=\mathrm{constant}$ are outgoing null hypersurfaces, $r$ is the area radius, and $x^A$ are constant along their null generators. This Bondi gauge has $g_{rr}=g_{rA}=0$.

A **smooth Bondi expansion** is such an end with the differentiated uniform expansions

$$\gamma_{AB}=q_{AB}+\frac{C_{AB}(u,x)}r+\frac{P_{AB}(u,x)}{r^2}+O(r^{-3}),\qquad \beta=O(r^{-2}),\qquad U^A=\frac{U^A_{(2)}(u,x)}{r^2}+\frac{U^A_{(3)}(u,x)}{r^3}+O(r^{-4}),\qquad V=r-2m(u,x)+\frac{V_{(1)}(u,x)}r+O(r^{-2}).$$

Here $C_{AB}$, $P_{AB}$ and the displayed coefficients are smooth sphere fields on $I$; the determinant gauge imposes $q^{AB}C_{AB}=0$ and $q^{AB}P_{AB}=\tfrac12 C_{AB}C^{AB}$. For every compact $I'\subset I$, angular chart compact set, and derivative multi-index $\alpha$ of total order at most two, the partial derivatives of each $O(r^{-k})$ remainder obey $\partial_u^{\alpha_u}D^{\alpha_x}\partial_r^{\alpha_r}O(r^{-k})=O(r^{-k-\alpha_r})$ uniformly as $r\to\infty$. Define the **mass aspect** $m$ by the $r^{-1}$ coefficient in $V$, the **Bondi shear** by $C_{AB}=\lim_{r\to\infty}r(\gamma_{AB}-q_{AB})$, the **Bondi news** by $N_{AB}:=\partial_u C_{AB}$, and the **geometric Bondi mass** by $m_B(u):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{S^2}m(u,x)\,d\Omega$. The future null boundary used here is the formal $r\to\infty$ boundary $\mathcal I^+=I\times S^2$ with coordinates $(u,x^A)$; no conformal completion is included in this definition. A **vacuum Bondi expansion** means, in addition, that the Ricci tensor $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$ defined by the curvature convention of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]] vanishes to the asymptotic coefficient orders under discussion, with no cosmological term.

Assume Countable Choice for the smooth Lorentzian boundary conventions inherited from [[def-gr-fx-bondi-expansion]]. On its formal boundary $\mathcal I^+=I\times S^2$, let $\ell_{\mathcal I}=\partial_u$ be the null-generator direction and let $q_{AB}$ be the unit round metric on the cuts; the degenerate boundary metric is $q_{AB}dx^A dx^B$ with kernel $\mathbb R\ell_{\mathcal I}$. A **fixed Bondi frame** here means the chosen Bondi-Sachs chart and gauge $(u,r,x^A)$ of [[def-gr-fx-bondi-expansion]], including $g_{rr}=g_{rA}=0$ and $\det\gamma=\det q$, with the round cut metric $q_{AB}$ held fixed. It is a chart/gauge choice, not an observer congruence or tetrad. An **infinitesimal supertranslation** is the asymptotic vector field parametrized by a smooth real function $f:S^2\to\mathbb R$ whose leading boundary action is $\delta_fu=f(x)$ and whose leading bulk generator is

$$\xi_f=f\,\partial_u-\frac1rD^Af\,\partial_A+\frac12D^AD_Af\,\partial_r+O(r^{-1})\partial_u+O(r^{-2})\partial_A+O(r^{-1})\partial_r.$$

The displayed leading terms preserve Bondi gauge and the fixed round cut metric to the asymptotic orders used here; the omitted terms are not part of this definition. We use the active convention $\delta_f=\mathcal L_{\xi_f}$. Its action on the shear and news of [[def-gr-fx-bondi-expansion]] is

$$\delta_f C_{AB}=fN_{AB}-2D_AD_Bf+q_{AB}D^CD_Cf,\qquad \delta_f N_{AB}=f\,\partial_uN_{AB}.$$

The **finite active boundary supertranslation** with parameter $f$ is the map $\Phi_f(u,x)=(u+f(x),x)$ on
$$\mathcal D_f:=\{(u,x)\in I\times S^2:u+f(x)\in I\}.$$
It is a diffeomorphism from $\mathcal D_f$ onto $\mathcal D_{-f}$, with inverse $\Phi_{-f}$. If $I=\mathbb R$, it is a diffeomorphism of all of $\mathcal I^+$; for a shorter retarded-time interval the action is defined on this overlap only. In the same active convention, its induced action on the boundary shear and news is

$$C^{(f)}_{AB}(u,x)=C_{AB}(u+f(x),x)-2D_AD_Bf(x)+q_{AB}D^CD_Cf(x),\qquad N^{(f)}_{AB}(u,x)=N_{AB}(u+f(x),x),\quad (u,x)\in\mathcal D_f.$$

Differentiating these formulas for the parameter $tf$ at $t=0$ recovers the infinitesimal formulas above. This definition gives only the boundary action and induced shear/news; it does not specify the full finite bulk coordinate transformation.

The function $f$ carries length units when the retarded coordinate $u$ is read in SI geometric coordinates; the sphere derivatives and angular coordinates are dimensionless. The Hessian term is trace-free because $q^{AB}q_{AB}=2$. When $N_{AB}=0$, an infinitesimal supertranslation therefore changes a time-independent shear by the sphere trace-free Hessian while leaving the news zero.

Assume Countable Choice for the smooth Lorentzian bundle conventions of the suppliers. Let a vacuum Bondi expansion be as in [[def-gr-fx-bondi-expansion]], with $R_{ab}=0$ in the curvature convention of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]. Then, for the mass aspect $m$, shear $C_{AB}$, news $N_{AB}=\partial_uC_{AB}$, unit sphere metric $q_{AB}$ and its Levi-Civita derivative $D_A$ specified there,

$$\partial_um=\frac14D_AD_BN^{AB}-\frac18N_{AB}N^{AB}.$$

The identity is the leading supplementary vacuum Einstein coefficient at future null infinity; it is not an exact finite-radius equation.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The restriction $Y=\tfrac12(3x_3^2-1)$ is smooth on the sphere because it is the restriction of a polynomial. Put $T_{AB}:=D_AD_BY-\tfrac12q_{AB}D^2Y$. Its trace is zero. At $\theta=\pi/2$, $D_\theta D_\theta Y=3$, $D_\phi D_\phi Y=0$ and $D^2Y=3$, so $T_{\theta\theta}=3/2$; hence $T$ is nonzero.

With $t=u+r$, the metric $g_0=-du^2-2du\,dr+r^2q$ becomes $-dt^2+dr^2+r^2q$, the Minkowski metric in spherical spatial coordinates. Thus its Bondi data are exactly $C_{AB}=N_{AB}=m=0$. Since $f=aY$ is independent of $u$, [F2] gives $C^{(f)}_{AB}= -2aD_AD_BY+a q_{AB}D^2Y=-2aT_{AB}$ and $N^{(f)}_{AB}=0$. We use only these as formal boundary data; we do not assert that they are the coefficients of a finite transformed vacuum metric.

Set $m(u,x)=0$ for the formal data. With $N_{AB}=0$, [F3] is satisfied and $m_B(u)=\tfrac1{4\pi}\int_{S^2}m\,d\Omega=0$, so $dm_B/du=0$. The shear $C^{(f)}_{AB}=-2aT_{AB}$ is independent of $u$, hence $\Delta C_{AB}=0$ on every interval. These conclusions follow directly from the stipulated data and constraint; neither vacuum mass-loss nor the memory proposition is invoked.
