supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
For a smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, and $k\ge0$, define
$$I_M^k:\Omega^k(M)\longrightarrow C_\infty^k(M;\mathbb R),\qquad I_M^k(\omega)(\sigma)=\int_\sigma\omega.$$
On $c=\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\sigma$ this means $I_M^k(\omega)(c)=\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\int_\sigma\omega$, a finite sum. In negative degrees $I_M^k$ is the zero map. Forms and the de Rham complex at a boundary use [[lem-the-de-rham-complex-and-pullback-extend-to-manifolds-with-boundary]]. No orientation of $M$ is required: the domain simplex has the specified orientation. The name integration cochain map is justified by [[thm-de-rham-integration-is-a-cochain-map]].

derivations.claim:
Choose a finite coordinate-chart cover of the compact surface $\Sigma$ and a smooth partition $\{\phi_j\}_{j=1}^N$ subordinate to it by [F3]. In each chart, every matrix entry of $\phi_jP$ is a $C^2$ function supported compactly inside the coordinate domain; extend it by zero to $\mathbb R^2$. Start with $\rho(y)=c\exp(-1/(1-|y|^2))$ for $|y|<1$ and $\rho(y)=0$ otherwise, where $c>0$ normalizes its integral to one. The extension is smooth because every derivative at the boundary is a finite sum of terms bounded by $t^{-m}e^{-1/t}$ as $t\downarrow0$, and these tend to zero. Put $\rho_\epsilon(y)=\epsilon^{-2}\rho(y/\epsilon)$ and convolve each real and imaginary entry with it. For every multi-index $\alpha$ with $|\alpha|\leq2$, $\partial^\alpha(\rho_\epsilon*f)=\rho_\epsilon*(\partial^\alpha f)$ and
$$\|\rho_\epsilon*(\partial^\alpha f)-\partial^\alpha f\|_\infty\leq\sup_{|y|\leq\epsilon}\|\partial^\alpha f(\,\cdot-y)-\partial^\alpha f\|_\infty\longrightarrow0,$$
because each compactly supported derivative is uniformly continuous. For sufficiently small $\epsilon$, the convolved supports remain inside their charts. Summing the finitely many pulled-back approximants gives a smooth matrix field $Q_\epsilon\to P$ in $C^2$; replacing it by $(Q_\epsilon+Q_\epsilon^*)/2$ keeps it smooth Hermitian and preserves this convergence.

Fix $\epsilon$ so $\delta:=\sup_\Sigma\|Q_\epsilon-P\|<1/4$. For each $x\in\Sigma$, define
$$R_\epsilon(x)=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_{|z-1|=1/2}(zI-Q_\epsilon(x))^{-1}\,dz.$$
On this contour $\|(zI-P(x))^{-1}\|=2$, so the Neumann series shows $zI-Q_\epsilon(x)$ is invertible and its inverse has norm at most $4$. The finite-dimensional spectral theorem [F4] diagonalizes $Q_\epsilon(x)$. For an eigenvalue $\lambda$ inside the circle, the Cauchy integral formula [F4] gives $\oint_\Gamma(z-\lambda)^{-1}\,dz=2\pi i$. For an exterior eigenvalue put $c=1$, $R=1/2$, and $q=R/|\lambda-c|<1$. On $\Gamma$, the geometric expansion
$$\frac1{z-\lambda}=-\sum_{k=0}^N\frac{(z-c)^k}{(\lambda-c)^{k+1}}+r_N(z),\qquad \sup_\Gamma|r_N|\leq\frac{q^{N+1}}{|\lambda-c|(1-q)}$$
has a remainder whose contour integral tends to zero, since the circle has length $2\pi R$. Each polynomial term integrates to zero, as the parametrization $z=c+Re^{it}$ gives $\oint_\Gamma(z-c)^k\,dz=iR^{k+1}\int_0^{2\pi}e^{i(k+1)t}\,dt=0$. Thus the exterior eigenvalue contributes zero. Applying these two scalar calculations to the diagonalization shows that $R_\epsilon(x)$ is the orthogonal spectral projection onto eigenvalues inside the circle. The same contour is valid for $Q_t=P+t(Q_\epsilon-P)$ for every $t\in[0,1]$, so these projections vary continuously with $t$; their integer-valued ranks are constant and equal the rank one of $P$. The resolvent identity gives
$$\|R_\epsilon-P\|_\infty\leq\frac{1}{2\pi}\,\pi\,(4)\delta(2)=4\delta<1.$$
The contour integral also shows $R_\epsilon$ is smooth in $x$.

The restriction $R_\epsilon(x)|_{\operatorname{ran}P(x)}$ is injective: if $R_\epsilon v=0$ and $P v=v$, then $\|v\|=\|(P-R_\epsilon)v\|\leq\|P-R_\epsilon\|\,\|v\|$, which forces $v=0$. Both ranges are one-dimensional, so these restrictions form a continuous complex line-bundle isomorphism $E_P\cong E_{R_\epsilon}$ and [F6] gives $c_1(E_P)=c_1(E_{R_\epsilon})$. The compact surface has finitely many components by [F6]; apply the disconnected line-class convention of [F5] on each component and sum the pairings using the fundamental-class direct sum. In a local unit frame $u$ for $E_{R_\epsilon}$, its connection form is $A=u^*du$ and its scalar curvature is $dA$. The rank-one curvature matrix is $F_{R_\epsilon}=u(dA)u^*$, hence $\operatorname{tr}F_{R_\epsilon}=dA=\Omega_{\nabla_\epsilon}$. Applying [F5] to the smooth Hermitian line bundle $E_{R_\epsilon}$ and its projected Hermitian connection, then evaluating on $[\Sigma]$ using [F6] and [F7], gives
$$\frac{i}{2\pi}\int_\Sigma\operatorname{tr}F_{R_\epsilon}=\langle c_1(E_{R_\epsilon}),[\Sigma]\rangle=\langle c_1(E_P),[\Sigma]\rangle\in\mathbb Z.$$

The contour formula for $R_\epsilon$ and its first two coordinate derivatives show $R_\epsilon\to P$ in $C^2$: differentiating $(zI-Q_\epsilon)^{-1}$ once gives $(zI-Q_\epsilon)^{-1}(\partial_jQ_\epsilon)(zI-Q_\epsilon)^{-1}$, and differentiating twice gives a finite sum of products of uniformly bounded resolvents with first and second derivatives of $Q_\epsilon$. Thus in each chart of the fixed finite partition, $R_\epsilon$ and its first derivatives converge uniformly to $P$ and its first derivatives. On the compact supports of that partition, let $\delta_0$ and $\delta_1$ be the largest of the zeroth- and first-coordinate-derivative errors, and choose $M\ge1$ bounding all first derivatives of $P$ and $R_\epsilon$ for sufficiently small $\epsilon$. For the coordinate coefficient $F_{12}(P)=P(\partial_1P\,\partial_2P-\partial_2P\,\partial_1P)P$, submultiplicativity and $\|P\|=\|R_\epsilon\|=1$ give $\|F_{12}(R_\epsilon)-F_{12}(P)\|\le4M^2\delta_0+4M\delta_1$; the trace difference is at most $d$ times this bound. Hence the continuous coefficients in the fixed finite chart-partition formula [F11] converge uniformly. Put each compact chart support in the interior of a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q_j$. By [F12], both real and imaginary parts of each continuous zero-extended coefficient and its difference are Riemann integrable there. For a real continuous $h$ on $Q_j$, put $c=\sup_{Q_j}|h|$. Every Darboux sum of the constant functions $\pm c$ is $\pm c\operatorname{vol}(Q_j)$, since the cell volumes sum to the rectangle volume. Monotonicity in [F9] applied to $-c\le h\le c$ therefore gives $|\int_{Q_j}h|\le c\operatorname{vol}(Q_j)$. Applying this separately to the real and imaginary parts of a complex coefficient $g$ and using $|\operatorname{Re}g|,|\operatorname{Im}g|\le|g|$ gives $|\int_{Q_j}g|\le2\operatorname{vol}(Q_j)\sup_{Q_j}|g|$. Finite linearity then gives $\left|\int_\Sigma\operatorname{tr}F_{R_\epsilon}-\int_\Sigma\operatorname{tr}F_P\right|\leq2\sum_j\operatorname{vol}(Q_j)\sup_{Q_j}|\widetilde f_j^\epsilon-\widetilde f_j|\longrightarrow0$. The continuous-integral convention [F11] and this estimate show that the limit is the integral in the Statement. Step 2.1 gives the same integer for every sufficiently small $\epsilon$, so taking the limit proves the stated equality for $P$.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$

derivations.claim: Put $\theta=mv\cdot a/\hbar$. The loop identity in [F1] gives the scalar operator $e^{i\theta}I$ on the system Hilbert space, so it multiplies every vector in an isolated component by the same scalar and leaves squared moduli of inner products unchanged there.

Let $\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^d,dx;\mathbb C)$. On the path space $\mathbb C^2$ set $|0\rangle=(1,0)^T$, $|1\rangle=(0,1)^T$, and $\langle j|:=|j\rangle^*$. Its orthogonal projectors are $|0\rangle\langle0|=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ and $|1\rangle\langle1|=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$, so they are self-adjoint, square to themselves, have zero product and sum to $I_2$. Interpret the finite path-system product as $\mathcal H\oplus\mathcal H$ with $|0\rangle\otimes f=(f,0)$, $|1\rangle\otimes f=(0,f)$ and squared norm $\|(f,g)\|^2=\|f\|^2+\|g\|^2$; completeness follows componentwise from that of $\mathcal H$. In this explicit product model define the controlled loop $C=|0\rangle\langle0|\otimes L+|1\rangle\langle1|\otimes I$, where $L=B_m(v)T(a)B_m(v)^*T(a)^*$. By step 1.1, $C=U_\theta\otimes I$ with $U_\theta=\operatorname{diag}(e^{i\theta},1)$. Equip the path space with inner product $u^*w$ and put $u_+=(1,1)^T/\sqrt2$. The recombining path overlap is $u_+^*U_\theta u_+=(1+e^{i\theta})/2$. The addition law [F3] and Euler formula with parity [F4, F6] give $(1+e^{i\theta})/2=e^{i\theta/2}(e^{-i\theta/2}+e^{i\theta/2})/2=e^{i\theta/2}\cos(\theta/2)$. By [F4, F5], $|e^{i\theta/2}|=e^0=1$, and modulus is multiplicative by [F7], so the squared modulus of this overlap is $\cos^2(\theta/2)$. If the same scalar is applied to both arms, the path gate is $e^{i\theta}I_2$, whose matrix coefficient has squared modulus $1$ by [F4, F5].

citations.quote: For the separately selected qubit GKSL model, let $H=\hbar\omega|1\rangle\langle1|$ with $\omega\in\mathbb R$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ and $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, and let $L=\sqrt{\gamma}|0\rangle\langle1|$ with $\gamma\geq0$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, so $L$ has units $\mathrm{s}^{-1/2}$. For any initial density matrix $\rho(0)$ in the ordered basis $(|0\rangle,|1\rangle)$, the solution $\rho(t)=e^{t\mathcal L}\rho(0)$ for $t\geq0$ satisfies $\rho_{11}(t)=e^{-\gamma t}\rho_{11}(0)$, $\rho_{00}(t)=\rho_{00}(0)+(1-e^{-\gamma t})\rho_{11}(0)$, $\rho_{01}(t)=e^{(i\omega-\gamma/2)t}\rho_{01}(0)$, and $\rho_{10}(t)=e^{(-i\omega-\gamma/2)t}\rho_{10}(0)$.

Let $d\geq1$, let $r\geq0$ be an integer, let $H=H^*\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ have units joules, let $\hbar>0$ have units joule-seconds, and let $L_1,\ldots,L_r\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ have units $\mathrm{s}^{-1/2}$, with the finite GKSL convention of [[def-qsm-dt-gksl-definition]]. Put $K=-iH/\hbar-\frac12\sum_{a=1}^rL_a^*L_a$ and $R(u)=e^{uK}$ for $u\geq0$, with the exponential defined by its norm-convergent power series. For a density matrix $\rho\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, meaning $\rho=\rho^*\geq0$ and $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, define the no-jump branch at time $t\geq0$ by $W_{\varnothing,\varnothing}(t)=R(t)$ and its branch state by $W_{\varnothing,\varnothing}(t)\rho W_{\varnothing,\varnothing}(t)^*$.

All time variables $u,t,s_1,\ldots,s_n$ are measured in seconds. For $n\geq1$, a jump-history label is $\mathbf a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in\{1,\ldots,r\}^n$ and its jump times are seconds $0<s_1<\cdots<s_n<t$. Define the corresponding branch operator by $W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)=R(t-s_n)L_{a_n}R(s_n-s_{n-1})\cdots L_{a_2}R(s_2-s_1)L_{a_1}R(s_1)$ and the unnormalized branch state by $W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)\rho W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)^*$. Its branch-weight density is the real-valued scalar function $w_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)=\operatorname{Tr}(W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)\rho W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)^*)$. For $n\geq1$, let $\overline{\Delta}_n(t)=\{(s_1,\ldots,s_n)\in\mathbb R^n:0\leq s_1\leq\cdots\leq s_n\leq t\}$ and $\Delta_n(t)=\{(s_1,\ldots,s_n)\in\mathbb R^n:0<s_1<\cdots<s_n<t\}$. Use the same formula for $W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)$ on $\overline{\Delta}_n(t)$; it is continuous there because $R(u)=e^{uK}$ is continuous for $u\geq0$. If $V$ is a finite-dimensional real or complex vector space and $F:\overline{\Delta}_n(t)\to V$ has continuous coordinates in a basis, define $\int_{\Delta_n(t)}F(\mathbf s)\,d\mathbf s$ as exactly the repeated one-variable Riemann integral over the closed limits shown here $\int_0^t ds_n\int_0^{s_n}ds_{n-1}\cdots\int_0^{s_2}F(s_1,\ldots,s_n)\,ds_1$, integrating each real coordinate; for complex coordinates, integrate their real and imaginary parts separately. This value is independent of the basis because a change of basis is a finite linear combination and scalar Riemann integration is linear. For $V=\mathbb R$ this defines the scalar integral of the density $w_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)$; the same convention applies to branch-state integrands with values in $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and to integrands with values in the finite-dimensional complex vector space of complex-linear maps $M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_d(\mathbb C)$. The full recursion is well-defined for these arbitrary continuous integrands by [[lem-nrqmx-continuous-simplex-integrals]]: every inner integral is continuous in all remaining ordered parameters, so the next integral exists. That lemma also proves basis independence, linear-map commutation, the norm bound by the supremum times $t^n/n!$, and positivity for nonnegative real scalar integrands. Set $\int_a^a f(s)\,ds=0$ for a degenerate interval; hence every $n\geq1$ ordered-simplex integral at $t=0$ is zero. Let $\Delta_0(t)=\{()\}$ and define $\int_{\Delta_0(t)}F=F(())$; in the expansion, the $n=0$ contribution is the no-jump branch already defined above. For $n\geq1$, $W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}$ has units $\mathrm{s}^{-n/2}$ and $w_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}$ has units $\mathrm{s}^{-n}$; integrating over the $n$ time variables gives a dimensionless weight. If $r=0$, there are no branches with $n\geq1$. This definition alone does not assert that the branch weights sum to one.

Let $d\geq1$, let $H=H^*\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ have units joules, let $\hbar>0$ have units joule-seconds, and let $L_1,\ldots,L_r\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ be a finite family with units $\mathrm{s}^{-1/2}$, where $r\geq0$. For the selected time-homogeneous finite GKSL model, put $\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_{a=1}^r(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\})$. With $K=-iH/\hbar-\frac12\sum_aL_a^*L_a$ and the finite branch operators of [[def-nrqmx-finite-jump-trajectories]], each no-jump operator $R(u)=e^{uK}$ is a contraction, each branch state $W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)\rho W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)^*$ is positive for $\rho\geq0$, and for every density matrix $\rho$ and $t\geq0$,

$$e^{t\mathcal L}(\rho)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\ \sum_{\mathbf a\in\{1,\ldots,r\}^n}\ \int_{0<s_1<\cdots<s_n<t}W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)\rho W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)^*\,ds_1\cdots ds_n,$$

where the $n=0$ term is $R(t)\rho R(t)^*$ and branches with $n\geq1$ are absent when $r=0$. The series converges in trace norm, uniformly on each bounded time interval; the sum of all branch weights is one. This is an ensemble representation of the finite GKSL solution, not a unique microscopic trajectory or a claim about a particular detector.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

$$\exp(x)\to+\infty\quad(x\to+\infty),\qquad \exp(x)\to0\quad(x\to-\infty),$$
and the range of $\exp$ is contained in $(0,\infty)$ and is unbounded above with infimum $0$.

derivations.claim: For $L=\sqrt{\gamma}|0\rangle\langle1|$, the no-jump generator is $K=\operatorname{diag}(0,-i\omega-\gamma/2)$. Hence $R(t)|1\rangle=e^{-(i\omega+\gamma/2)t}|1\rangle$ and $R(t)|0\rangle=|0\rangle$. For the initial state $|1\rangle\langle1|$, the no-jump branch weight is $\operatorname{Tr}(R(t)|1\rangle\langle1|R(t)^*)=e^{-\gamma t}$, equal to the excited population in [F1].

For $\gamma>0$ and a one-jump history at $s\in(0,T)$, $R(T-s)LR(s)|1\rangle=\sqrt{\gamma}\,e^{-(i\omega+\gamma/2)s}|0\rangle$, since $L|1\rangle=\sqrt{\gamma}|0\rangle$ and $R(T-s)|0\rangle=|0\rangle$. Its branch-weight density from [F2] is $\gamma e^{-\gamma s}$. Because $L|0\rangle=0$ and $R(u)|0\rangle=|0\rangle$, every branch with at least two jumps has zero weight. The normalized ensemble [F3] therefore gives $\int_0^T\gamma e^{-\gamma s}\,ds=1-e^{-\gamma T}$: the only nonzero contributions are the no-jump weight $e^{-\gamma T}$ from step 1.1 and the one-jump integral. Letting $T\to\infty$, [F4] identifies this as the real exponential and [F5] gives $e^{-\gamma T}\to0$ because $\gamma>0$; hence the first-jump density has total mass one. Each first jump leaves the normalized state $|0\rangle\langle0|$. If $\gamma=0$, then $L=0$, all positive-jump branches vanish, and the no-jump weight is one.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, an integer $r\ge1$, and an action scale
$\hbar>0$. Inner products are linear in the first argument
([[def-inner-product-space]]). Use the Fock-to-Schrödinger unitary
$\mathcal U:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^r)\to L^2(\mathbb R^r)$ of
[[lem-nrqmx-finite-mode-fock-schr-identification]]. In Schrödinger coordinates
define the self-adjoint quadratures
$$Q_j=\mathcal U^{-1}(\sqrt\hbar\,x_j)\mathcal U,\qquad P_j=\mathcal U^{-1}(-i\sqrt\hbar\,\partial_{x_j})\mathcal U,$$
where $x_j$ is the real multiplication operator on its maximal domain. Fix the
angular-frequency Fourier unitary by
$$[\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}f](k)=(2\pi)^{-r/2}\int_{\mathbb R^r}e^{-ik\cdot x}f(x)\,dx\quad(f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)),$$
and define $-i\partial_{x_j}:=\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}^{-1}M_{k_j}\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}$, where $M_{k_j}$ is multiplication by $k_j$ on its maximal domain. Their common Schwartz core satisfies
$$[Q_j,Q_k]=[P_j,P_k]=0,\qquad [Q_j,P_k]=i\hbar\delta_{jk}I.$$
Write $R=(Q_1,P_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_r)^T$ and
$J=\bigoplus_{j=1}^r\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$.
The Weyl unitary labelled by $z=(q_1,p_1,\ldots,q_r,p_r)$ is the unitary
whose grouped-coordinate formula, with $q=(q_1,\ldots,q_r)$ and
$p=(p_1,\ldots,p_r)$, is
$$[W(z)f](x)=e^{i\sqrt\hbar\,q\cdot(x+\sqrt\hbar p/2)}f(x+\sqrt\hbar p).$$
It obeys $W(z)W(z')=e^{-i\hbar z^TJz'/2}W(z+z')$ and is regular and
irreducible. By the finite-dimensional Stone–von Neumann theorem, every
nonzero irreducible regular Weyl system with this finite phase space and this
same nonzero central parameter is unitarily equivalent to it.

A density operator is a positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with
$\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$. Its quadrature second moments are finite when, for
one (equivalently every) spectral expansion
$\rho=\sum_n w_n|\psi_n\rangle\langle\psi_n|$ with $w_n>0$,
$\sum_nw_n\|R_j\psi_n\|^2<\infty$ for every $j$. For such a state define
$$d_j=\sum_nw_n\langle R_j\psi_n,\psi_n\rangle,\qquad V_{jk}=\operatorname{Re}\sum_nw_n \langle(R_j-d_jI)\psi_n,(R_k-d_kI)\psi_n\rangle.$$
These quantities are independent of the chosen orthonormal eigenbasis in
each eigenspace. The state is Gaussian when its Weyl characteristic function
has the form
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho W(z))= \exp\!\left(i z^Td-\tfrac12z^TVz\right)\quad(z\in\mathbb R^{2r}),$$
with real $d$ and real symmetric $V$. Here $R_j$ has units
$\sqrt{\mathrm{action}}$, each Weyl label has units
$1/\sqrt{\mathrm{action}}$, and $V$ has units of action. No finite particle
number truncation is used.

Let $r\ge1$, $J_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_r\\-I_r&0\end{pmatrix}$, and
$$\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)=\{S\in M_{2r}(\mathbb R):S^TJ_0S=J_0\}.$$
Every $S\in\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ is a finite product of matrices
of the following three types and their inverses:
$$U_X=\begin{pmatrix}I&X\\0&I\end{pmatrix},\quad L_Y=\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\Y&I\end{pmatrix},\quad D_A=\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\0&A^{-T}\end{pmatrix},$$
where $X,Y$ are real symmetric and $A$ is real invertible. Partial Fourier
rotations, which act by $(q_j,p_j)\mapsto(-p_j,q_j)$ on any selected set of
coordinates and fix the others, are also products of these matrices.
In addition, for every $S$ there is a product $G$ of these generators such
that the upper-left block of $SG$ is invertible.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. On $L^2(\mathbb R^r)$, for $r\ge1$ and $\hbar>0$,
define the Weyl unitaries in grouped label order $(q,p)\in\mathbb R^r\oplus
\mathbb R^r$ by
$$[W(q,p)f](x)=e^{i\sqrt\hbar\,q\cdot(x+\sqrt\hbar p/2)}f(x+\sqrt\hbar p).$$
For $J_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\-I&0\end{pmatrix}$, every
$T\in\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ has a unitary $M_T$ such that
$$M_T^*W(z)M_T=W(Tz)\quad(z\in\mathbb R^{2r}).$$
Any two such unitaries differ by a scalar of modulus one. The covariance
identity holds on all of $L^2$; the corresponding unbounded quadrature
identities hold on the common transported Schwartz domain. This is an
individual existence and phase-uniqueness result; it does not identify the
global topology or kernel of a continuously chosen implementer family.

Let $n\ge1$ and $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, with the componentwise integral and quotient conventions of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. Define
$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. Absolute convergence and representative independence are the obligations discharged by [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]. The output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class. At frequency zero the formula reads $\widehat f(0)=\int f$. No choice selection of representatives for a family of classes is part of this definition.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.
Assume countable choice. The Fourier transform is a topological automorphism of $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$, with $\mathcal F^2=R$ and $\mathcal F^{-1}=R\mathcal F$, where $Rf(x)=f(-x)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

Here $\mathfrak h^{\otimes_s n}$ is the range of the orthogonal symmetrizer in the completed $n$-fold Hilbert tensor product, with the zero-particle sector $\mathbb C\Omega$. For $\mathbf n=(n_1,\ldots,n_M)\in\mathbb N_0^M$, let $|\mathbf n\rangle$ be the normalized occupation vector. Define the finite-particle subspace $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{fin}}:=\{\psi=(\psi^{(n)})_{n\ge0}\in\mathcal F_s(\mathfrak h):\psi^{(n)}=0\text{ for all but finitely many }n\}=\operatorname{span}\{|\mathbf n\rangle:\mathbf n\in\mathbb N_0^M\}$. The mode operators are dimensionless and on $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{fin}}$ satisfy $a_j|\mathbf n\rangle=\sqrt{n_j}|\mathbf n-\mathbf e_j\rangle$ and $a_j^*|\mathbf n\rangle=\sqrt{n_j+1}|\mathbf n+\mathbf e_j\rangle$, with the first expression zero if $n_j=0$. The Fock space is infinite-dimensional for each $M\ge1$; no particle-number cutoff or tensor factorization of an individual photon into position and spin is part of this assignment.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and countable choice wherever the finite-mode Fock, quadrature, and implementability suppliers require them. These are mathematical hypotheses of the assignment, not physical postulates.

For each selected mode $j$, choose a positive angular frequency $\omega_j>0$ in seconds$^{-1}$; the assigned one-quantum energy scale is $\hbar\omega_j$ joules. **(b) Finite atom and dipole data.** Choose $d\ge1$, an atomic Hilbert space $\mathcal H_A=\mathbb C^d$, a Hermitian atomic energy matrix $H_A$ in joules, Hermitian compressed dipole matrices $D_j$ in coulomb-metres, and real mode field scales $\mathcal E_j$ in volts per metre. The matrix elements of $G_j:=\mathcal E_jD_j/\hbar$ have units seconds$^{-1}$, where $\hbar>0$ is retained in joule-seconds. The finite matrices and scales are chosen model data. If they are obtained by compressing a larger atomic model, that compression's error is a separate model input and is not bounded here.

Write $\mathcal H_{AF}:=\mathcal H_A\widehat\otimes\mathcal F_s(\mathfrak h)$ for the completed ordered Hilbert tensor product, with the atom factor first, and let $\kappa:\mathcal H_A\odot\mathcal F_s(\mathfrak h)\to\mathcal H_{AF}$ be the canonical isometric inclusion. Let $I_A$ and $I_F$ denote the identity operators on $\mathcal H_A$ and $\mathcal F_s(\mathfrak h)$. Let $\mathcal D_0:=\kappa[\mathcal H_A\odot\mathcal F_{\mathrm{fin}}]\subseteq\mathcal H_{AF}$ be the algebraic product domain. If $f_1,\ldots,f_d$ is the standard orthonormal basis of $\mathcal H_A=\mathbb C^d$, then the vectors $\kappa(f_\alpha\otimes|\mathbf n\rangle)$ form a complete orthonormal basis by the Hilbert tensor product and finite-mode Fock product-basis conclusions for this ordered pair. Hence $\mathcal D_0$ is dense in $\mathcal H_{AF}$.

The assigned dipole interaction is the linear operator $V_{\mathrm{dip}}:\mathcal D_0\to\mathcal H_{AF}$ defined on elementary tensors by $V_{\mathrm{dip}}(\kappa(\phi\otimes\psi)):=-\sum_{j=1}^{M}\mathcal E_j\kappa(D_j\phi\otimes(a_j+a_j^*)\psi)$ for $\phi\in\mathcal H_A$ and $\psi\in\mathcal F_{\mathrm{fin}}$, and extended linearly to $\mathcal D_0$. Each map $(\phi,\psi)\mapsto\kappa(D_j\phi\otimes(a_j+a_j^*)\psi)$ is bilinear, so it descends to the algebraic tensor product; $a_j,a_j^*$ preserve $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{fin}}$. Each summand has units joules. This is the declared algebraic product domain of the finite-core expression; no graph-core assertion for a closed realization is made. The assignment does not assert that an arbitrary such sum has a self-adjoint realization or generates an evolution; any dynamical use must state and justify its operator domain. The Jaynes–Cummings supplier below gives one specific self-adjoint direct-sum realization.

**(c) Mode transformations.** A finite mode-coordinate change is assigned only when its finite Bogoliubov matrices satisfy the exact hypotheses of the finite-mode implementability statement: for $U,V\in M_M(\mathbb C)$, $UU^*-VV^*=I_M$ and $UV^T=VU^T$. The resulting unitary acts on this finite-mode Fock space. The statement assumes the Axiom of Choice; this is a mathematical assumption, not a physical law. No infinite-mode implementability follows.

**(d) Detector outcome models.** A detector's outcome space $(X,\Sigma)$ and POVM $E:\Sigma\to\mathcal B(\mathcal H_{AF})$ are declared model data: each $E(B)$ is bounded and positive, $E(X)=I$, and $E$ is countably additive in the weak operator topology. For a density operator $\rho$ on $\mathcal H_{AF}$ (a positive trace-class operator of trace one), the assigned probability is $\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ under the framework's stated measurement convention. An ideal number-resolving model on the field has outcomes $\mathbf n\in\mathbb N_0^M$ and effects $I_A\otimes|\mathbf n\rangle\langle\mathbf n|$; these are bounded tensor maps and projections on $\mathcal H_{AF}$ by the tensor-map adjoint and composition rules. For ideal homodyne of mode $j$ at phase $\theta\in\mathbb R$, let $R_j(\theta)|\mathbf n\rangle=e^{i\theta n_j}|\mathbf n\rangle$ and $X_{j,\theta}:=\hbar^{-1/2}R_j(\theta)Q_jR_j(\theta)^*$, where $\mathcal U:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^M)\to L^2(\mathbb R^M)$ is the Fock-to-Schrödinger unitary and $Q_j:=\mathcal U^{-1}M_{\sqrt\hbar x_j}\mathcal U$. Here $M_{\sqrt\hbar x_j}$ multiplies by $\sqrt\hbar x_j$ on its maximal domain $\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R^M):x_jf\in L^2(\mathbb R^M)\}$. Thus $X_{j,\theta}$ is self-adjoint by unitary conjugation and on $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{fin}}$ equals $(e^{-i\theta}a_j+e^{i\theta}a_j^*)/\sqrt2$. Its spectral PVM $B\mapsto I_A\otimes\mathbf1_B(X_{j,\theta})$ is defined by the same bounded tensor maps and is the ideal homodyne POVM on the product space. These are ideal outcome assignments, not claims about a detector's optical local oscillator, efficiency, bandwidth, calibration or state update. If a state update or a finite detector environment is modeled, declare its instrument separately. The finite product-preparation/unitary/partial-trace assignment described by the finite open-system postulate is for $H_S=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_E=\mathbb C^m$ with a fixed environment state and a declared joint unitary; it may be used for a separately selected finite-dimensional subsystem but does not cover the Fock field. A reduced-dynamics model involving the Fock field must separately specify a trace-class joint preparation and joint unitary on $\mathcal H_{AF}$. The trace-class partial trace $\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal F_s(\mathfrak h)}:\mathcal S_1(\mathcal H_{AF})\to\mathcal S_1(\mathcal H_A)$ is defined for arbitrary Hilbert factors, is trace-norm contractive, and preserves positivity and trace by the mathematical partial-trace result listed below. No Fock-field reduced dynamics or reservoir limit is adopted here.

**(e) Optional approximation regimes.** A long-wavelength identification with a spatial electromagnetic mode requires a separately declared atomic extent $L$ and wave number $k_j$ and the scale regime $k_jL\ll1$; no error bound is supplied. A rotating-wave choice keeps only the excitation-exchange terms. For a two-level transition of frequency $\omega_0$ coupled to a mode of frequency $\omega$, its usual low-excitation regime is $|g|\sqrt{n+1}\ll\omega,\omega_0$ on the declared photon-number sectors; it is not uniform over the full Fock space. A Markov/GKSL approximation is another separate model choice and must state its rates, reservoir correlation time $\tau_B$, system time scale $\tau_S$, and regime $\tau_B\ll\tau_S$. None of these optional approximations is derived from this assignment or from the finite system-environment model.

**(a) Dimensions.** Write $\ell$, $\tau$, $\mu$, $\vartheta$ for the four independent dimension symbols of length, duration, mass and electric charge. A **dimension** is an element of $\mathbb Q^{4}$, written $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\vartheta^{d}$ with $a,b,c,d\in\mathbb Q$; products and inverses of dimensions are componentwise addition and negation, and the dimensionless dimension $\ell^{0}\tau^{0}\mu^{0}\vartheta^{0}$ is abbreviated $1$. The conventions assign to each quantity of the framework a dimension $[X]$, subject to $[XY]=[X][Y]$, $[X/Y]=[X][Y]^{-1}$ and $[dX/du]=[X][u]^{-1}$, with sums meaningful only between quantities of equal dimension, in which case the sum carries that dimension. For a rational power $q$, dimension powers mean $[X]^q=\ell^{qa}\tau^{qb}\mu^{qc}\vartheta^{qd}$ when $[X]=\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\vartheta^{d}$. Rational exponents include the half-integer wave-function dimensions in clause (d); the integer-exponent dimensions form the subgroup $\mathbb Z^4$. These are consistency requirements on the conventions, not laws of nature.

For extensions using temperature, adjoin an independent dimension symbol $\Theta$: the enlarged group is $\mathbb Q^4\times\mathbb Q$, written $\ell^a\tau^b\mu^c\vartheta^d\Theta^e$, with the same componentwise rules. The preceding group embeds by $e=0$, so all previously assigned dimensions are preserved. Temperature has dimension $\Theta$, the Boltzmann constant has dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}\Theta^{-1}$, and entropy in joules per kelvin has that same dimension; a dimensionless entropy remains dimensionless. This convention does not assign a temperature or an entropy to any system.

**(b) Reference units.** The **metre** (m), **second** (s), **kilogram** (kg) and **coulomb** (C) are the reference units of length, duration, mass and charge; a quantity of dimension $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\vartheta^{d}$ is expressed in the unit $\mathrm m^{a}\mathrm s^{b}\mathrm kg^{c}\mathrm C^{d}$. Coordinates of an inertial frame are read with the time coordinate $t$ in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the spatial coordinates $x_{i}$ in metres, $[x_{i}]=\ell$; slice distances of the arena are read in metres. In the temperature extension the reference unit of $\Theta$ is the kelvin (K), so the general reference unit gains a factor $\mathrm K^e$.

**(c) Defining constants of the current SI.** The framework keeps $\hbar$ explicit. In the current SI the constants $h$, $c$ and $e$ are exact defining constants, with the values $h=6{,}626\,070\,15\times10^{-34}$ J s, $c=2{,}99792458\times10^{8}$ m s$^{-1}$ and $e=1{,}602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}$ C, and $\hbar:=h/(2\pi)$. These are real scalar constants with dimensions and units $[h]=[\hbar]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ (J s), $[c]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ (m s$^{-1}$), and $[e]=\vartheta$ (C). The vacuum permeability $\mu_{0}$ is a positive real scalar that is experimentally determined in the current SI, with $[\mu_{0}]=\mu\ell\vartheta^{-2}$ (N A$^{-2}$ = H m$^{-1}$); $\varepsilon_{0}:=(\mu_{0}c^{2})^{-1}$ is a positive real scalar with $[\varepsilon_{0}]=\mu^{-1}\ell^{-3}\tau^{2}\vartheta^{2}$ (F m$^{-1}$). These are unit-convention statements of the SI, not measurements reported by this framework; $c$ enters the framework only through the separate radiation assumptions adopted on their own pages, not in the nonrelativistic spacetime of [[def-nrqm-framework-newtonian-spacetime]].

**(d) Dimensions and types of the framework's quantities.** The dimension map is fixed on the following quantities.

1. State quantities: a position wave function of a system with $d$ spatial dimensions and $r$ internal components is an almost-everywhere equivalence class in $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ with dimension $\ell^{-d/2}$, its norm $\|\psi\|$ is dimensionless, and an abstract normalized state and the density operators of the state postulate are dimensionless.
2. Probability: the outcome probability $\mu(B)$ of the observable postulate is a dimensionless number; a position density $|\psi|^{2}$ has dimension $\ell^{-d}$; a momentum wave function normalized against $\mathrm d^{d}p$ has dimension $(\mu\ell\tau^{-1})^{-d/2}$; an amplitude for a finite outcome is a dimensionless complex number, while an amplitude read against a detector coordinate carries the square-root of the inverse of the detector measure.
3. Frame parameters ([[def-nrqm-framework-galilei-transformations]]): $[b]=\tau$, $[a_{i}]=\ell$, $[v_{i}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $[R_{ij}]=1$.
4. Mechanical quantities: action $[\hbar]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$; energy and the Hamiltonian eigenvalues $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$; momentum $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$; position components $\ell$; angular momentum and spin $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$; mass $\mu$; velocity of a free spinless model $\ell\tau^{-1}$; force $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$; a real potential energy $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$.
5. Probability current: in the ordinary continuous-field regime, fix an integer $d\ge1$, an open spatial region $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and an open time interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$. A **probability current density** is a declared continuous map $j:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^d$, whose spatial components have dimension $\ell^{1-d}\tau^{-1}$ and reference unit $\mathrm m^{1-d}\mathrm s^{-1}$. At fixed time it is a spatial vector field; its signed normal component is read as probability transported per unit spatial $(d-1)$-area and time. Explicitly, for a flat face $S=\{x:x_k=a,\ a_i\le x_i\le b_i\ (i\ne k)\}\subset\Omega$, with $a_i<b_i$ and chosen normal $n=\epsilon e_k$, $\epsilon\in\{-1,1\}$, define its **signed probability flux** at $t\in I$ as $\Phi_S(t):=\epsilon\int_{\prod_{i\ne k}[a_i,b_i]}j_k(x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1},a,x_{k+1},\ldots,x_d,t)\prod_{i\ne k}dx_i$. Here $e_k$ is the $k$th coordinate unit vector and the integral uses $(d-1)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure; for $d=1$ this means $\Phi_{\{a\}}(t)=\epsilon j(a,t)$. The flux has dimension $\tau^{-1}$ and unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$; positive sign means transport in the chosen normal direction. Fluxes through curved surfaces, or currents with weaker regularity, require separately specified surface measures or traces. This fixes the quantity type and flux convention; it supplies neither a current associated to an arbitrary $L^2$ state nor a conservation or detector law. Each dynamical model supplies its current construction and balance hypotheses.
6. Electric quantities of the model parameters: charge has dimension $\vartheta$; a magnetic moment has dimension $\ell^{2}\vartheta\tau^{-1}$, equivalently $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{2}=\mathrm J\,\mathrm T^{-1}$, and a gyromagnetic parameter $\gamma$ in the relation $\boldsymbol\mu=\gamma\mathbf S$ has dimension $\mu^{-1}\vartheta$, equivalently $\mathrm s^{-1}\mathrm T^{-1}$; these quantities appear only in the model assumptions that introduce them.
7. Statistical quantities: a mean has the dimension of its outcome coordinate, a variance the square of it and a standard deviation it; a mean, variance or higher moment exists only when the corresponding moment of the outcome probability is finite, so a symbolic average is not a number unless that integrability is established. Angles and phases are dimensionless under the radian convention.
8. Quantities of later extension assumptions - radiation frequencies and energies, electric dipole moments, cross sections, temperatures and entropies - are declared with their dimensions and units by the items that introduce those assumptions, under the rules fixed here; they are not part of the present list.

**(e) Conventions only.** No numerical value of any model parameter is fixed by this item: no mass, charge, spin label, potential or measured constant is asserted, and natural-unit shorthand (for example setting $\hbar=1$ or $c=1$) is read as an abbreviation for the corresponding SI-dimensioned statement with the constant restored.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$\mathbb H:=\mathbb C$ with its standard inner product (linear in the first
argument), let $F(\mathbb C)$ be its Fock space as in
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]], let
$e_n\in F(\mathbb C)$ be the unit vector supported in coordinate $n$ (so
$(e_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is a complete orthonormal family of $F(\mathbb C)$),
let $N$ be the number operator and let $A_\pm(1)$ be the maximal creation and
annihilation operators of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-closed-adjoint-sector-domains]] for the vector
$1\in\mathbb C$. Then:

(a) *oscillator coefficients*: for every $n\in\mathbb N$,
$$A_+(1)e_n=\sqrt{n+1}\,e_{n+1},\qquad A_-(1)e_n=\sqrt n\,e_{n-1}\ (n\ge1),\qquad A_-(1)e_0=0;$$

(b) *coherent vectors*: for every $z\in\mathbb C$ the series
$$\psi_z:=e^{-|z|^2/2}\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\frac{z^n}{\sqrt{n!}}\,e_n$$
converges absolutely in $F(\mathbb C)$
([[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]]),
$\|\psi_z\|=1$, $\psi_z\in D(A_-(1))$ with
$$A_-(1)\psi_z=z\,\psi_z,$$
and for all $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$\langle\psi_z,\psi_w\rangle=e^{-(|z|^2+|w|^2)/2+z\overline w};$$

(c) *number law*: for every $n\in\mathbb N$,
$$\bigl|\langle e_n,\psi_z\rangle\bigr|^2=e^{-|z|^2}\frac{|z|^{2n}}{n!},$$
and $\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}|\langle e_n,\psi_z\rangle|^2=1$.

The numbers in (c) are squared moduli of overlaps of unit vectors; identifying
them with outcome probabilities of a number measurement requires a separately
adopted measurement postulate, and no such physical claim is made here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) with completed tensor powers
$H^{\otimes n}$, symmetric projections $P_+^{(n)}$, contraction maps
$\Psi_f^{(n)}$, Fock space $F(H)$ and core operators $S_\pm(f)$ on the
finite-particle space $F_0$ as in
[[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-creation-contraction-bounds]]. For $f\in H$
define
$$D(A_+(f)):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(H):\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}(n+1)\bigl\|P_+^{(n+1)}(f\otimes\psi_n)\bigr\|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad (A_+(f)\psi)_n:=\sqrt n\,P_+^{(n)}(f\otimes\psi_{n-1})\ (n\ge1),\ (A_+(f)\psi)_0:=0,$$
$$D(A_-(f)):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(H):\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}(n+1)\bigl\|\Psi_f^{(n)}(\psi_{n+1})\bigr\|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad (A_-(f)\psi)_n:=\sqrt{n+1}\,\Psi_f^{(n)}(\psi_{n+1}).$$
Put $D_1:=\{\psi\in F(H):\sum_n(n+1)\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$. Then:

(a) $A_+(f)$ and $A_-(f)$ are well-defined linear operators on $F(H)$ with the
displayed domains, and they are the closure and the adjoint of the core operator:
$$A_+(f)=\overline{S_+(f)}=S_-(f)^*,\qquad A_-(f)=S_+(f)^*=\overline{S_-(f)}$$
([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]],
[[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]],
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]);

(b) both $A_\pm(f)$ are closed, densely defined and satisfy
$A_+(f)^*=A_-(f)$, $A_-(f)^*=A_+(f)$; in particular $F_0\subseteq D_1\subseteq D(A_\pm(f))$;

(c) for every $\psi\in D_1$, $\|A_+(f)\psi\|\le\|f\|\,\|\psi\|_1$ and
$\|A_-(f)\psi\|\le\|f\|\,\|\psi\|_1$, where
$\|\psi\|_1^2=\sum_n(n+1)\|\psi_n\|^2$;

(d) for every $g\in H$ and $\psi\in D_1$ the identity
$$\|A_+(g)\psi\|^2=\|A_-(g)\psi\|^2+\|g\|^2\|\psi\|^2$$
holds.

No boundedness of $A_\pm(f)$ on $F(H)$, no self-adjointness of $A_\pm(f)$, and
no physical interpretation is asserted.

derivations.claim: On the finite-particle core, $[a^*a,a]=-a$ and $[a^*a,a^*]=a^*$ by [F1], while $[\sigma_+\sigma_-,\sigma_+]=\sigma_+$ and $[\sigma_+\sigma_-,\sigma_-]=-\sigma_-$. Therefore $[N_{\rm exc},\sigma_+\otimes a]=\sigma_+\otimes a-\sigma_+\otimes a=0$ and $[N_{\rm exc},\sigma_-\otimes a^*]=-\sigma_-\otimes a^*+\sigma_-\otimes a^*=0$. The free terms commute with $N_{\rm exc}$, so $[N_{\rm exc},H_{\rm core}]=0$ on the core.

The vectors $|g,0\rangle$ and $|e,n\rangle,|g,n+1\rangle$ have excitation eigenvalues $0$ and $n+1$, respectively. Applying the displayed ladder actions [F1] to each basis vector shows $H_{\rm core}|g,0\rangle=-(\hbar\omega_0/2)|g,0\rangle$, $H_{\rm core}|e,n\rangle=(\hbar\omega n+\hbar\omega_0/2)|e,n\rangle+\hbar g\sqrt{n+1}|g,n+1\rangle$, and $H_{\rm core}|g,n+1\rangle=\hbar g\sqrt{n+1}|e,n\rangle+(\hbar\omega(n+1)-\hbar\omega_0/2)|g,n+1\rangle$. The product occupation basis [F3] consists exactly of $|g,0\rangle$ and these pairs: $|e,m\rangle$ occurs in the pair indexed by $m$, while $|g,m\rangle$ with $m\ge1$ occurs in the pair indexed by $m-1$. They are mutually orthogonal and exhaust the space. Hence the displayed subspaces are invariant blocks with matrix $H_n$.

Write $H_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)I+\hbar\begin{pmatrix}\Delta/2&g\sqrt{n+1}\\g\sqrt{n+1}&-\Delta/2\end{pmatrix}$. The traceless matrix has characteristic polynomial $\lambda^2-(\Delta^2/4+g^2(n+1))$, so its eigenvalues are $\pm\frac12\sqrt{\Delta^2+4g^2(n+1)}$. Their difference gives the stated splitting.

Each block matrix and the ground-line scalar are Hermitian. Finite-support vectors are dense by [F2] and lie in the stated domain. If $y\in D(H_{\rm JC}^*)$ with adjoint value $z$, testing against vectors supported in the ground line and each individual block gives $z_g=-(\hbar\omega_0/2)y_g$ and $z_n=H_ny_n$. Since $z$ is square-summable, $\sum_n\|H_ny_n\|^2<\infty$, so $y\in D(H_{\rm JC})$ and $H_{\rm JC}^*y=H_{\rm JC}y$. Conversely, for $x,y\in D(H_{\rm JC})$, Cauchy–Schwarz makes the block inner-product series absolutely convergent, and the Hermitian block identities give $\langle H_{\rm JC}x,y\rangle=\langle x,H_{\rm JC}y\rangle$. Hence $H_{\rm JC}\subseteq H_{\rm JC}^*$ and equality holds. The direct-sum operator is self-adjoint, and its restriction to finite-support vectors is $H_{\rm core}$.

For ideal homodyne of mode $j$ at phase $\theta\in\mathbb R$, let $R_j(\theta)|\mathbf n\rangle=e^{i\theta n_j}|\mathbf n\rangle$ and $X_{j,\theta}:=\hbar^{-1/2}R_j(\theta)Q_jR_j(\theta)^*$, where $Q_j$ is the self-adjoint quadrature fixed by [[def-nrqmx-finite-mode-symplectic-data]]. supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
**(a) Dimensions.** Write $\ell$, $\tau$, $\mu$, $\vartheta$ for the four independent dimension symbols of length, duration, mass and electric charge. A **dimension** is an element of $\mathbb Q^{4}$, written $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\vartheta^{d}$ with $a,b,c,d\in\mathbb Q$; products and inverses of dimensions are componentwise addition and negation, and the dimensionless dimension $\ell^{0}\tau^{0}\mu^{0}\vartheta^{0}$ is abbreviated $1$. The conventions assign to each quantity of the framework a dimension $[X]$, subject to $[XY]=[X][Y]$, $[X/Y]=[X][Y]^{-1}$ and $[dX/du]=[X][u]^{-1}$, with sums meaningful only between quantities of equal dimension, in which case the sum carries that dimension. For a rational power $q$, dimension powers mean $[X]^q=\ell^{qa}\tau^{qb}\mu^{qc}\vartheta^{qd}$ when $[X]=\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\vartheta^{d}$. Rational exponents include the half-integer wave-function dimensions in clause (d); the integer-exponent dimensions form the subgroup $\mathbb Z^4$. These are consistency requirements on the conventions, not laws of nature.

For extensions using temperature, adjoin an independent dimension symbol $\Theta$: the enlarged group is $\mathbb Q^4\times\mathbb Q$, written $\ell^a\tau^b\mu^c\vartheta^d\Theta^e$, with the same componentwise rules. The preceding group embeds by $e=0$, so all previously assigned dimensions are preserved. Temperature has dimension $\Theta$, the Boltzmann constant has dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}\Theta^{-1}$, and entropy in joules per kelvin has that same dimension; a dimensionless entropy remains dimensionless. This convention does not assign a temperature or an entropy to any system.

**(b) Reference units.** The **metre** (m), **second** (s), **kilogram** (kg) and **coulomb** (C) are the reference units of length, duration, mass and charge; a quantity of dimension $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\vartheta^{d}$ is expressed in the unit $\mathrm m^{a}\mathrm s^{b}\mathrm kg^{c}\mathrm C^{d}$. Coordinates of an inertial frame are read with the time coordinate $t$ in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the spatial coordinates $x_{i}$ in metres, $[x_{i}]=\ell$; slice distances of the arena are read in metres. In the temperature extension the reference unit of $\Theta$ is the kelvin (K), so the general reference unit gains a factor $\mathrm K^e$.

**(c) Defining constants of the current SI.** The framework keeps $\hbar$ explicit. In the current SI the constants $h$, $c$ and $e$ are exact defining constants, with the values $h=6{,}626\,070\,15\times10^{-34}$ J s, $c=2{,}99792458\times10^{8}$ m s$^{-1}$ and $e=1{,}602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}$ C, and $\hbar:=h/(2\pi)$. These are real scalar constants with dimensions and units $[h]=[\hbar]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ (J s), $[c]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ (m s$^{-1}$), and $[e]=\vartheta$ (C). The vacuum permeability $\mu_{0}$ is a positive real scalar that is experimentally determined in the current SI, with $[\mu_{0}]=\mu\ell\vartheta^{-2}$ (N A$^{-2}$ = H m$^{-1}$); $\varepsilon_{0}:=(\mu_{0}c^{2})^{-1}$ is a positive real scalar with $[\varepsilon_{0}]=\mu^{-1}\ell^{-3}\tau^{2}\vartheta^{2}$ (F m$^{-1}$). These are unit-convention statements of the SI, not measurements reported by this framework; $c$ enters the framework only through the separate radiation assumptions adopted on their own pages, not in the nonrelativistic spacetime of [[def-nrqm-framework-newtonian-spacetime]].

**(d) Dimensions and types of the framework's quantities.** The dimension map is fixed on the following quantities.

1. State quantities: a position wave function of a system with $d$ spatial dimensions and $r$ internal components is an almost-everywhere equivalence class in $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ with dimension $\ell^{-d/2}$, its norm $\|\psi\|$ is dimensionless, and an abstract normalized state and the density operators of the state postulate are dimensionless.
2. Probability: the outcome probability $\mu(B)$ of the observable postulate is a dimensionless number; a position density $|\psi|^{2}$ has dimension $\ell^{-d}$; a momentum wave function normalized against $\mathrm d^{d}p$ has dimension $(\mu\ell\tau^{-1})^{-d/2}$; an amplitude for a finite outcome is a dimensionless complex number, while an amplitude read against a detector coordinate carries the square-root of the inverse of the detector measure.
3. Frame parameters ([[def-nrqm-framework-galilei-transformations]]): $[b]=\tau$, $[a_{i}]=\ell$, $[v_{i}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $[R_{ij}]=1$.
4. Mechanical quantities: action $[\hbar]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$; energy and the Hamiltonian eigenvalues $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$; momentum $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$; position components $\ell$; angular momentum and spin $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$; mass $\mu$; velocity of a free spinless model $\ell\tau^{-1}$; force $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$; a real potential energy $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$.
5. Probability current: in the ordinary continuous-field regime, fix an integer $d\ge1$, an open spatial region $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and an open time interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$. A **probability current density** is a declared continuous map $j:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^d$, whose spatial components have dimension $\ell^{1-d}\tau^{-1}$ and reference unit $\mathrm m^{1-d}\mathrm s^{-1}$. At fixed time it is a spatial vector field; its signed normal component is read as probability transported per unit spatial $(d-1)$-area and time. Explicitly, for a flat face $S=\{x:x_k=a,\ a_i\le x_i\le b_i\ (i\ne k)\}\subset\Omega$, with $a_i<b_i$ and chosen normal $n=\epsilon e_k$, $\epsilon\in\{-1,1\}$, define its **signed probability flux** at $t\in I$ as $\Phi_S(t):=\epsilon\int_{\prod_{i\ne k}[a_i,b_i]}j_k(x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1},a,x_{k+1},\ldots,x_d,t)\prod_{i\ne k}dx_i$. Here $e_k$ is the $k$th coordinate unit vector and the integral uses $(d-1)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure; for $d=1$ this means $\Phi_{\{a\}}(t)=\epsilon j(a,t)$. The flux has dimension $\tau^{-1}$ and unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$; positive sign means transport in the chosen normal direction. Fluxes through curved surfaces, or currents with weaker regularity, require separately specified surface measures or traces. This fixes the quantity type and flux convention; it supplies neither a current associated to an arbitrary $L^2$ state nor a conservation or detector law. Each dynamical model supplies its current construction and balance hypotheses.
6. Electric quantities of the model parameters: charge has dimension $\vartheta$; a magnetic moment has dimension $\ell^{2}\vartheta\tau^{-1}$, equivalently $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{2}=\mathrm J\,\mathrm T^{-1}$, and a gyromagnetic parameter $\gamma$ in the relation $\boldsymbol\mu=\gamma\mathbf S$ has dimension $\mu^{-1}\vartheta$, equivalently $\mathrm s^{-1}\mathrm T^{-1}$; these quantities appear only in the model assumptions that introduce them.
7. Statistical quantities: a mean has the dimension of its outcome coordinate, a variance the square of it and a standard deviation it; a mean, variance or higher moment exists only when the corresponding moment of the outcome probability is finite, so a symbolic average is not a number unless that integrability is established. Angles and phases are dimensionless under the radian convention.
8. Quantities of later extension assumptions - radiation frequencies and energies, electric dipole moments, cross sections, temperatures and entropies - are declared with their dimensions and units by the items that introduce those assumptions, under the rules fixed here; they are not part of the present list.

**(e) Conventions only.** No numerical value of any model parameter is fixed by this item: no mass, charge, spin label, potential or measured constant is asserted, and natural-unit shorthand (for example setting $\hbar=1$ or $c=1$) is read as an abbreviation for the corresponding SI-dimensioned statement with the constant restored.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$\mathbb H:=\mathbb C$ with its standard inner product (linear in the first
argument), let $F(\mathbb C)$ be its Fock space as in
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]], let
$e_n\in F(\mathbb C)$ be the unit vector supported in coordinate $n$ (so
$(e_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is a complete orthonormal family of $F(\mathbb C)$),
let $N$ be the number operator and let $A_\pm(1)$ be the maximal creation and
annihilation operators of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-closed-adjoint-sector-domains]] for the vector
$1\in\mathbb C$. Then:

(a) *oscillator coefficients*: for every $n\in\mathbb N$,
$$A_+(1)e_n=\sqrt{n+1}\,e_{n+1},\qquad A_-(1)e_n=\sqrt n\,e_{n-1}\ (n\ge1),\qquad A_-(1)e_0=0;$$

(b) *coherent vectors*: for every $z\in\mathbb C$ the series
$$\psi_z:=e^{-|z|^2/2}\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\frac{z^n}{\sqrt{n!}}\,e_n$$
converges absolutely in $F(\mathbb C)$
([[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]]),
$\|\psi_z\|=1$, $\psi_z\in D(A_-(1))$ with
$$A_-(1)\psi_z=z\,\psi_z,$$
and for all $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$\langle\psi_z,\psi_w\rangle=e^{-(|z|^2+|w|^2)/2+z\overline w};$$

(c) *number law*: for every $n\in\mathbb N$,
$$\bigl|\langle e_n,\psi_z\rangle\bigr|^2=e^{-|z|^2}\frac{|z|^{2n}}{n!},$$
and $\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}|\langle e_n,\psi_z\rangle|^2=1$.

The numbers in (c) are squared moduli of overlaps of unit vectors; identifying
them with outcome probabilities of a number measurement requires a separately
adopted measurement postulate, and no such physical claim is made here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) with completed tensor powers
$H^{\otimes n}$, symmetric projections $P_+^{(n)}$, contraction maps
$\Psi_f^{(n)}$, Fock space $F(H)$ and core operators $S_\pm(f)$ on the
finite-particle space $F_0$ as in
[[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-creation-contraction-bounds]]. For $f\in H$
define
$$D(A_+(f)):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(H):\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}(n+1)\bigl\|P_+^{(n+1)}(f\otimes\psi_n)\bigr\|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad (A_+(f)\psi)_n:=\sqrt n\,P_+^{(n)}(f\otimes\psi_{n-1})\ (n\ge1),\ (A_+(f)\psi)_0:=0,$$
$$D(A_-(f)):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(H):\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}(n+1)\bigl\|\Psi_f^{(n)}(\psi_{n+1})\bigr\|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad (A_-(f)\psi)_n:=\sqrt{n+1}\,\Psi_f^{(n)}(\psi_{n+1}).$$
Put $D_1:=\{\psi\in F(H):\sum_n(n+1)\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$. Then:

(a) $A_+(f)$ and $A_-(f)$ are well-defined linear operators on $F(H)$ with the
displayed domains, and they are the closure and the adjoint of the core operator:
$$A_+(f)=\overline{S_+(f)}=S_-(f)^*,\qquad A_-(f)=S_+(f)^*=\overline{S_-(f)}$$
([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]],
[[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]],
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]);

(b) both $A_\pm(f)$ are closed, densely defined and satisfy
$A_+(f)^*=A_-(f)$, $A_-(f)^*=A_+(f)$; in particular $F_0\subseteq D_1\subseteq D(A_\pm(f))$;

(c) for every $\psi\in D_1$, $\|A_+(f)\psi\|\le\|f\|\,\|\psi\|_1$ and
$\|A_-(f)\psi\|\le\|f\|\,\|\psi\|_1$, where
$\|\psi\|_1^2=\sum_n(n+1)\|\psi_n\|^2$;

(d) for every $g\in H$ and $\psi\in D_1$ the identity
$$\|A_+(g)\psi\|^2=\|A_-(g)\psi\|^2+\|g\|^2\|\psi\|^2$$
holds.

No boundedness of $A_\pm(f)$ on $F(H)$, no self-adjointness of $A_\pm(f)$, and
no physical interpretation is asserted.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$, write Euclidean space as $E_d=\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{d-1}$ with coordinates $x=(t,\mathbf x)$, and put $S_d=\mathcal S(E_d;\mathbb C)$ and $S_{d,n}=\mathcal S(E_d^n;\mathbb C)$ for $n\ge1$, with $S_{d,0}=\mathbb C$. For $d=1$, $\mathbb R^0$ is the one-point vector space with unit measure. A Schwinger hierarchy is a sequence $S=(S_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $S_0=1$ and each $S_n\in S_{d,n}'$; its moments on elementary tests are $\langle S_n,f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n\rangle$. The associated unital algebraic test algebra is $T_d=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}^{\rm alg}S_d^{\otimes_{\rm alg}n}$ with concatenation multiplication, unit $1\in S_{d,0}=\mathbb C$, and involution $(f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n)^*=\overline f_n\otimes\cdots\otimes\overline f_1$ and $(c1)^*=\overline c1$. The moments define $\omega_S:T_d\to\mathbb C$ by linear extension. At $d=4$ this is the same four-dimensional algebra and moment convention used by the positive-tempered-moment definition.

Ordinary moment positivity means $\omega_S(1)=1$ and $\omega_S(a^*a)\ge0$ for every $a\in T_d$. It is distinct from reflection positivity. Let $\vartheta(t,\mathbf x)=(-t,\mathbf x)$ and $E_{d,+}=\{(t,\mathbf x):t>0\}$. The positive-time polynomial algebra $T_{d,+}$ is the unital star subalgebra generated by tests in $C_c^\infty(E_{d,+};\mathbb C)$. Define the antilinear reflection $\Theta$ by $\Theta f=\overline{f\circ\vartheta}$ on degree one, $\Theta(c1)=\overline c1$, and $\Theta(ab)=\Theta(b)\Theta(a)$. Reflection positivity is $\omega_S(\Theta a\,a)\in[0,\infty)$ for every $a\in T_{d,+}$. The same formula applies to finite-site test algebras with an involution exchanging the sites.

A regulated hierarchy is a family $S^\lambda=(S^\lambda_n)_{n\ge0}$ indexed by a nonempty directed set $(\Lambda,\preceq)$, where directed means every two indices have a common upper bound. A distributional continuum limit is a hierarchy $S$ such that for every fixed $n$ and every $\Phi\in S_{d,n}$, $\langle S^\lambda_n,\Phi\rangle\to\langle S_n,\Phi\rangle$ as $\lambda$ advances in $\Lambda$. A limit contract records these pairings, the regulator family, and any additional uniform estimates; pointwise-in-$n$ convergence by itself asserts no uniform bound as $n$ varies.

For explicit comparison, define the Schwartz seminorm $P_k(\Phi)=\max_{|\alpha|,|\beta|\le k}\sup_{x\in E_d^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta\Phi(x)|$ on $S_{d,n}$. A per-order uniform continuity record is a choice, for each fixed $n$, of $r_n\in\mathbb N_0$ and $C_n\ge0$ such that $|\langle S^\lambda_n,\Phi\rangle|\le C_nP_{r_n}(\Phi)$ for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$ and $\Phi\in S_{d,n}$. A uniform-order bound is the stronger explicit condition that there exist fixed $s\in\mathbb N$ and $A,B,q>0$ with $|\langle S_n,\Phi\rangle|\le A B^n(n!)^q P_{sn}(\Phi)$ for every $n\ge1$ and $\Phi\in S_{d,n}$. This bound is recorded separately and is not inferred from distributional convergence or asserted equivalent to a corrected Osterwalder–Schrader regularity hypothesis.

For $\gamma(x)=Rx+a$ with $R\in O(d)$ and $a\in E_d$, define $(U_\gamma\Phi)(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\Phi(\gamma^{-1}x_1,\ldots,\gamma^{-1}x_n)$. Euclidean invariance means $\langle S_n,U_\gamma\Phi\rangle=\langle S_n,\Phi\rangle$ for every such $\gamma$ and $\Phi\in S_{d,n}$. Permutation symmetry means invariance of the pairing under each permutation of its $n$ argument blocks. Clustering means that for every $n,m\ge1$, $f\in S_{d,n}$ and $g\in S_{d,m}$,

$$
\langle S_{n+m},f\otimes\tau_{ae_0}g\rangle\longrightarrow \langle S_n,f\rangle\langle S_m,g\rangle\quad(a\to+\infty),
$$

where $e_0=(1,\mathbf0)$ and $(\tau_{ae_0}g)(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=g(x_1-ae_0,\ldots,x_m-ae_0)$. This contract definition asserts neither existence of a regulated limit nor any of these additional properties.

derivations.claim: All four weights are positive and sum to $(1-r)/2+(1+r)/2=1$. Symmetry of the support weights gives $\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[Y]=0$, and $X^2=Y^2=1$ at every support point, so the covariance diagonal is $(1,1)$. The equal-sign outcomes have total probability $(1-r)/2$ and product $XY=1$; the opposite-sign outcomes have total probability $(1+r)/2$ and product $XY=-1$. Therefore $\mathbb E[XY]=(1-r)/2-(1+r)/2=-r$.

The covariance matrix is $C=\begin{pmatrix}1&-r\\-r&1\end{pmatrix}$. For real $u,v$, $(u,v)C(u,v)^{\mathsf T}=(u-rv)^2+(1-r^2)v^2,$ which is strictly positive unless $(u,v)=(0,0)$ because $0<r<1$. Thus $C$ is positive definite and the probability law is ordinarily positive. Since $Y$ belongs to the declared positive-site algebra, take $F=Y$. Reflection positivity would require $\mathbb E[(\Theta F)F]=\mathbb E[XY]\ge0$, but this is $-r<0$. Hence the statement is false.

Give $\mathfrak g$ its Lie bracket $[\ ,\ ]_{\mathfrak g}$ and a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_{\mathfrak g}$ satisfying $\langle[X,Y]_{\mathfrak g},Z\rangle_{\mathfrak g}=\langle X,[Y,Z]_{\mathfrak g}\rangle_{\mathfrak g}$. Write $\Omega^p(M;\mathfrak g)=\Gamma(M,\wedge^pT^*M\otimes\mathfrak g)$ for smooth $\mathfrak g$-valued $p$-forms. Extend the Lie bracket and pairing to homogeneous simple tensors by $[X\otimes\alpha,Y\otimes\beta]=[X,Y]_{\mathfrak g}\otimes(\alpha\wedge\beta)$ and $\langle X\otimes\alpha,Y\otimes\beta\rangle=\langle X,Y\rangle_{\mathfrak g}\,\alpha\wedge\beta$, then extend bilinearly.

A connection in the chosen trivialization is a form $A\in\Omega^1(M;\mathfrak g)$. Its curvature and covariant exterior derivative are $F_A=dA+\tfrac12[A,A]$ and $D_AX=dX+[A,X]$. Define the local Chern–Simons functional and the BF functional, for $B\in\Omega^1(M;\mathfrak g)$, by

$$\operatorname{CS}(A)=\int_M\left\langle A\wedge dA+\tfrac13A\wedge[A,A]\right\rangle,\qquad \operatorname{BF}(B,A)=\int_M\langle B\wedge F_A\rangle.$$

These are integrals of smooth top forms on a compact oriented manifold. The Chern–Simons formula is the local expression in the fixed trivialization; it does not define a globally gauge-invariant exponentiated action on arbitrary nontrivial bundles without additional characteristic-class and level data. No path-integral measure, quantization, or identification with a Reshetikhin–Turaev amplitude is part of this definition.

$$\int_M d\eta=\int_{\partial M}j^*\eta.$$

derivations.claim: Differentiate the Chern–Simons integrand along $A+s\alpha$. The quadratic term contributes $\langle\alpha\wedge dA+A\wedge d\alpha\rangle$. For the cubic term, the graded bracket and invariant pairing give the cyclic identities $\langle A\wedge[\alpha,A]\rangle=\langle\alpha\wedge[A,A]\rangle$ and $\langle A\wedge[A,\alpha]\rangle=\langle\alpha\wedge[A,A]\rangle$ for degree-one $A,\alpha$. Thus the three differentiated terms in $\tfrac13\langle A\wedge[A,A]\rangle$ are equal, and their average is $\langle\alpha\wedge[A,A]\rangle$. The full unintegrated variation is $\langle\alpha\wedge dA+A\wedge d\alpha+\alpha\wedge[A,A]\rangle$.

Differentiate $F_{A+s\alpha}$ at $s=0$; bilinearity of the bracket gives $\delta F_A=D_A\alpha$. Thus the BF variation before integration by parts is $\int_M\langle\beta\wedge F_A+B\wedge D_A\alpha\rangle$.

The graded Leibniz rule gives $d\langle A\wedge\alpha\rangle=\langle dA\wedge\alpha\rangle-\langle A\wedge d\alpha\rangle$. Since a two-form commutes with a one-form under wedge, $\langle A\wedge d\alpha\rangle=\langle\alpha\wedge dA\rangle-d\langle A\wedge\alpha\rangle$. Substitute this into step 1.1, combine $2dA+[A,A]=2F_A$, and apply [F2] to obtain the stated Chern–Simons formula, including its boundary sign.

For variations compactly supported in $\operatorname{int}M$, the boundary term in step 2.1 is zero. If stationarity holds for every such $\alpha$, then $\int_M\langle\alpha\wedge F_A\rangle=0$ for every local test variation. If $F_A$ were nonzero at some point, nondegeneracy of the pairing would select an algebra element pairing nontrivially with one component; continuity preserves its sign on a smaller chart, and a nonnegative bump supported there would make the integral nonzero. Hence $F_A=0$ on $\operatorname{int}M$.

For constant tangent vectors $\alpha_1,\alpha_2$ on the affine space $\mathcal A_\Sigma$, differentiating the potential current $\theta_A(\alpha)=-\lambda\langle A\wedge\alpha\rangle$ from step 2.1 gives $D_{\alpha_1}\Theta(\alpha_2)=-\lambda\int_\Sigma\langle\alpha_1\wedge\alpha_2\rangle$ and $D_{\alpha_2}\Theta(\alpha_1)=-\lambda\int_\Sigma\langle\alpha_2\wedge\alpha_1\rangle$. The field-space exterior derivative is their difference; antisymmetry of the wedge gives $\Omega_\Sigma=-2\lambda\int_\Sigma\langle\alpha_1\wedge\alpha_2\rangle$. Its coefficients are constant, so its field-space exterior derivative is zero.

Invariance of the pairing makes $D_A$ obey the graded Leibniz rule on paired forms. Therefore $d\langle B\wedge\alpha\rangle=\langle D_AB\wedge\alpha\rangle-\langle B\wedge D_A\alpha\rangle$. As in step 2.1, the two-form $D_AB$ commutes under wedge with $\alpha$. Apply [F2] to obtain the stated BF formula. For variations supported in the interior the boundary integral vanishes. Independent compactly supported $\beta$ and $\alpha$ then test $F_A$ and $D_AB$ separately; the local nondegenerate-pairing bump argument in step 3.1 shows each must vanish.

At a flat $a$, $D_a^2\epsilon=[F_a,\epsilon]=0$, so $D_a\epsilon$ is tangent to the flat locus. For a tangent $\alpha$, $D_a\alpha=0$. Invariance of the pairing yields $d\langle\epsilon,\alpha\rangle=\langle D_a\epsilon\wedge\alpha\rangle+\langle\epsilon,D_a\alpha\rangle$. Integrating and applying [F2] on $\Sigma$ gives $\int_\Sigma\langle D_a\epsilon\wedge\alpha\rangle=\int_{\partial\Sigma}\langle\epsilon,\alpha\rangle$, which proves the gauge-contraction formula.
