lie in the type-A Soergel category $\mathrm{SBim}_n$ (for instance Rouquier
word complexes), and define the alternating class
$$\chi(C):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}(-1)^m[C^m]\ \in\ K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n),$$
the cochain indexing being translated to the chain indexing of
[[def-mapping-cone-of-a-chain-map]] by $C_m:=C^{-m}$. Then:

1. $\chi$ is a homotopy invariant: if $C\simeq D$ in $K^b$, then
   $\chi(C)=\chi(D)$, so $\chi$ is well defined on isomorphism classes of the
   homotopy category;
2. $\chi$ is multiplicative: $\chi(C\otimes_RD)=\chi(C)\chi(D)$ for the signed
   tensor totalization and more generally for every finite tensor product;
3. for every chain map $f\colon C\to D$ one has
   $\chi(\operatorname{Cone}(f))=\chi(D)-\chi(C)$, and $\chi$ is additive on
   distinguished triangles of the homotopy category, so it descends to a
   homomorphism $K_0^{\mathrm{tri}}\to K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$ on
   the triangulated Grothendieck group of the full triangulated subcategory of
   complexes with terms in $\mathrm{SBim}_n$;
4. for every signed word $\sigma=\sigma_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\cdots\sigma_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r}$,
   the iterated signed tensor totalization
   $F_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RF_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r}$ (the word
   complex $F(\sigma)$ once that notation is introduced) satisfies
   $\chi(F(\sigma))=\prod_{k=1}^r\chi(F_{i_k}^{\epsilon_k})$.

In particular the alternating class of a Rouquier complex depends only on its
homotopy class and is compatible with tensor products.

Let $t,u$ be signed words for the same braid $v$. Then the normalized map
$$\gamma_{t,u}\colon F(t)\longrightarrow F(u)$$
of [[lem-rouquier-derived-comparisons-give-unique-normalized-homotopy-maps]]
is a canonical homotopy equivalence, natural with respect to the multiplication
maps: for every other braid $v'$ with chosen words $t',u'$, the diagrams
comparing $F(t)\otimes_RF(t')$ with $F(u)\otimes_RF(u')$ commute up to the
canonical associativity isomorphisms, and $\gamma_{t,u}$ is the unique homotopy
class with the prescribed derived image $c_{t,u}$. Consequently the object
$G_v$ of [[thm-rouquier-complexes-form-a-coherent-braid-group-action]] is
independent of the chosen representative up to canonical homotopy equivalence,
and the notation $F(\beta)$ for the Rouquier complex of a braid element is well
defined up to canonical isomorphism in $K^b(R^e\text{-grmod})$; this is an
isomorphism statement in the homotopy category, not an equality of complexes.

For $n\ge2$, the **braid group** $B_n$ is the group with generators
$\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{n-1}$ and relations

$$\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i=\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\qquad(1\le i\le n-2),$$

$$\sigma_i\sigma_j=\sigma_j\sigma_i\qquad(1\le i,j\le n-1,\ |i-j|>1).$$

Equivalently,

$$B_n=\langle \sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{n-1}\mid \sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i=\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\ (1\le i\le n-2),\ \sigma_i\sigma_j=\sigma_j\sigma_i\ (1\le i,j\le n-1,\ |i-j|>1)\rangle,$$

interpreted in the sense of [[def-group-presentation]] and
[[def-relators-relations-and-finite-presentations]].

For $n=0$ and $n=1$, there are no generators, and $B_n$ is the trivial group
given by the empty presentation.

**Additive setting.** Fix an additive category $\mathcal A$
([[def-additive-category]]): every hom-set is an abelian group, finite
biproducts exist, and every object has an identity morphism. All morphisms below
are morphisms of $\mathcal A$, sums and negatives are taken in the hom-groups,
and $0$ denotes the zero morphism between the indicated objects.

**Cochain complexes.** A **cochain complex** $C^\bullet=(C^n,d^n)_{n\in\mathbb Z}$
consists of objects $C^n$ of $\mathcal A$ and morphisms $d^n:C^n\to C^{n+1}$
with
$$d^{n+1}d^n=0\qquad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
The morphisms $d^n$ are the **differentials** of $C^\bullet$. No boundedness,
finiteness or nonvanishing condition is imposed on the family of objects.

**Cochain maps.** A **cochain map** $f:C^\bullet\to D^\bullet$ is a family of
morphisms $f^n:C^n\to D^n$ with
$$f^{n+1}d^n_C=d^n_Df^n\qquad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
Identities and composites of cochain maps are cochain maps, so cochain complexes
and cochain maps form a category; this category is written
$\operatorname{Ch}^\bullet(\mathcal A)$ when the ambient category needs to be
recorded.

**Homotopies.** A **homotopy** $h:f\simeq g$ between cochain maps
$f,g:C^\bullet\to D^\bullet$ is a family of morphisms $h^n:C^n\to D^{n-1}$, one
in each degree, such that
$$f^n-g^n=d^{n-1}_Dh^n+h^{n+1}d^n_C\qquad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
Thus $h$ has degree $-1$, and the right-hand side is the $n$-th component of the
graded map
$$dh+hd:=(d^{n-1}_Dh^n+h^{n+1}d^n_C)_{n\in\mathbb Z},$$
written with $d$ on both sides. A **null
homotopy** of a cochain map $f:C^\bullet\to D^\bullet$ is a homotopy
$f\simeq0$ to the zero map with the same source and target; $D^\bullet$
need not be the zero complex. A map admitting such a homotopy is
**null-homotopic**.

**Homotopy equivalence.** A cochain map $f:C^\bullet\to D^\bullet$ is a
**homotopy equivalence** when there is a cochain map
$g:D^\bullet\to C^\bullet$ with $gf\simeq1_{C^\bullet}$ and
$fg\simeq1_{D^\bullet}$; the complexes are then **homotopy equivalent**. The maps
$f$ and $g$ are homotopy inverses of one another.

**Contractibility.** A cochain complex $C^\bullet$ is **contractible** when its
identity is null-homotopic, $1_{C^\bullet}\simeq0$: that is, when there is a
family of morphisms $h^n:C^n\to C^{n-1}$ with
$$1_{C^n}=d^{n-1}h^n+h^{n+1}d^n\qquad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
A complex is contractible exactly when it is homotopy equivalent to the zero
complex, since a homotopy equivalence onto the zero complex is a pair of
null-homotopies of the identities.

**Degreewise biproducts.** If $C^\bullet$ and $D^\bullet$ are cochain complexes,
then defining
$$(C\oplus D)^n:=C^n\oplus D^n,\qquad d^n_{C\oplus D}:=d^n_C\oplus d^n_D$$
gives a cochain complex, because
$(d^{n+1}_C\oplus d^{n+1}_D)(d^n_C\oplus d^n_D)=0\oplus0=0$. The degreewise
injections and projections are cochain maps, and the biproduct identities hold in
each degree and are therefore identities of cochain maps; hence $C\oplus D$ is a
biproduct of $C$ and $D$. Iterating, finite direct sums of cochain complexes are
formed degreewise, and finite direct sums of cochain maps and of homotopies are
formed degreewise as well. Under the reindexing below this is the additive
structure on complexes over an additive category recorded in
[[thm-the-category-of-complexes-in-an-additive-category-is-additive]].

**Dictionary with the published chain convention.** Reindex by
$C_n:=C^{-n}$ and $d_n:=d^{-n}$. Then $d_n:C_n\to C_{n-1}$ and
$$d_{n-1}d_n=d^{-(n-1)}d^{-n}=d^{-n+1}d^{-n}=0,$$
so $(C_\bullet,d_\bullet)$ is an ordinary chain complex. A cochain map $f$
becomes the chain map with components $f_n:=f^{-n}$, and a homotopy
$h:f\simeq g$ becomes the chain homotopy $s_n:=h^{-n}:C_n\to D_{n+1}$, because
substituting $n\mapsto-n$ into the displayed homotopy equation produces exactly
$$f_n-g_n=d^D_{n+1}s_n+s_{n-1}d^C_n .$$
Consequently, when $\mathcal A$ is abelian, these definitions restrict under this
dictionary to the published [[def-chain-homotopy]] and
[[def-contractible-complex]], which are stated for chain complexes in an abelian
category. Reindexing reverses the sign of the differential degree ($+1$ for
cochains, $-1$ for chains) and of the homotopy degree ($-1$ for cochains, $+1$
for chains), and introduces no further sign.

**What is not asserted.** The definitions use only zero morphisms, addition,
negatives, composition and identities. No kernel, cokernel, image, homology
object or exactness is assumed or defined, no linear structure on the hom-groups
beyond the additive one is used, and no homology object is attached to a complex
in an arbitrary additive category; contractibility is the existence of the
displayed family $h$, not the vanishing of homology.

Fix an integer $n\ge2$, let $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with $\deg x_j=2$, and let $S_n$ act on $R$ by permuting variables. Let $\mathrm{SBim}_n$ be the idempotent-complete additive monoidal category of graded $(R,R)$-Soergel bimodules generated by the unit bimodule $R$, the bimodules $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ for the adjacent transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$, internal grading shifts, finite direct sums, tensor products over $R$, and direct summands. Use the shift convention $M(1)_d=M_{d+1}$; on the split Grothendieck ring it is recorded by $v[M]=[M(1)]$. Let $K^b(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$ denote the category of bounded cochain complexes in $\mathrm{SBim}_n$ with chain maps modulo chain homotopy.

For $1\le i<n$, let $F_i=[B_i\xrightarrow{\varepsilon_i}R(1)]$ in cohomological degrees $0,1$ and $F_i^{-1}=[R(-1)\xrightarrow{\eta_i}B_i]$ in degrees $-1,0$, with the maps and grading conventions of the positive and negative Rouquier generator complexes. For a signed word $\sigma=\sigma_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\cdots\sigma_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r}$, $\epsilon_k\in\{+1,-1\}$, let $F(\sigma)=F_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_R F_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r}$, using signed tensor totalization and left-to-right bracketing; the empty word gives $R$ in degree zero. If $\beta\in B_n$ is the braid represented by $\sigma$, the **Rouquier categorified line operator** $F(\beta)$ is this complex considered up to the canonical homotopy equivalence between words representing $\beta$. Tensor product is the categorical stacking operation. The comparison maps give the unit and coherent multiplication maps $F(\beta)\otimes_R F(\gamma)\simeq F(\beta\gamma)$; equivalently, left tensoring defines the coherent braid-group action on $K^b(R\text{-grmod})$.

A **physical defect realization** is additional data. A monoidal category $\mathcal D$ here means a category with a tensor bifunctor, a unit object, associator and unit isomorphisms satisfying the pentagon and unit triangles; its objects are declared line-defect types, its morphisms are declared junction maps, and its tensor product is the chosen stacking operation. The realization is a strong monoidal functor $\mathcal R:K^b(\mathrm{SBim}_n)\to\mathcal D$, meaning a functor with natural product and unit isomorphisms satisfying those same coherence equations and assigning images to every morphism, including junction maps, in its domain. Calling $\mathcal D$ a category of defects in a particular quantum field theory also requires an independently specified physical model. The Soergel and Rouquier data alone supply neither $\mathcal D$ nor this functor.

derivations.claim: Choose a signed word $\sigma=\sigma_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\cdots\sigma_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r}$ representing $\beta$. By the word definition and multiplicativity in [F2], $\chi(F(\sigma))=\prod_{k=1}^r\chi(F_{i_k}^{\epsilon_k})$. Applying the algebra homomorphism $\Phi$ and the generator values in [F1] gives $\Phi(\chi(F(\sigma)))=v^{\sum_k\epsilon_k}T_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\cdots T_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r}$.

The exponent sum is unchanged by each defining relation: the two sides of an adjacent braid relation each have sum $3$, the two sides of a distant commutation relation each have sum $2$, and an inverse pair has sum $0$. Thus $e(\sigma)$ descends to $e(\beta)\in\mathbb Z$ and satisfies $e(\beta\gamma)=e(\beta)+e(\gamma)$. The product of the $T_i^{\epsilon_k}$ is $T_\beta$ by the specified group homomorphism, so step 1.1 gives the displayed formula independent of the chosen word.

The comparison in [F3] identifies $F(\beta\gamma)$ in the homotopy category with the signed tensor totalization $F(\beta)\otimes_R F(\gamma)$. Applying homotopy invariance and multiplicativity from [F2], then applying the algebra homomorphism $\Phi$, gives $\Phi(\chi(F(\beta\gamma)))=\Phi(\chi(F(\beta)))\Phi(\chi(F(\gamma)))$. Dividing by $v^{e(\beta\gamma)}=v^{e(\beta)}v^{e(\gamma)}$ proves multiplicativity of the normalized map.

For a positive generator the formula is $vT_i$ and for its inverse it is $v^{-1}T_i^{-1}$ by [F1]. Since $v$ is an indeterminate in the Laurent polynomial coefficient ring, these factors cannot be discarded for nonzero exponent sum. The normalized value is exactly $T_\beta$ by step 2.1.

Let $D$ be the two-term complex with $D^0=D^1=R$, differential $d^0=1_R$, and all other terms zero. The map $h^1=1_R:D^1\to D^0$ (all other $h^m=0$) satisfies the contracting-homotopy equation in [F5], so $D$ is homotopy equivalent to the zero complex. But its graded terms are $R$ in degrees $0$ and $1$, whereas the zero complex has zero terms; since $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ has $1\ne0$, the complexes are not isomorphic as graded complexes. Their Euler classes are both zero by [F2] and $[R]-[R]=0$.

Let $\Phi\colon K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)\to H_{S_n}$ be the unique
algebra isomorphism of
[[thm-split-grothendieck-group-of-the-soergel-category-is-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]
with $\Phi([B_i])=H_i=v(T_i+1)$ and $\Phi(vX)=v\,\Phi(X)$, where $H_{S_n}$ is
the Hecke algebra over $A=\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$ with $q=v^{-2}$ and standard
generators $T_i$, and let $\chi$ be the alternating class of
[[lem-euler-class-of-a-rouquier-complex-is-homotopy-invariant-and-multiplicative]].

(a) $\Phi(\chi(F_i))=H_i-v=v\,T_i$ and
$\Phi(\chi(F_i^{-1}))=H_i-v^{-1}=v^{-1}T_i^{-1}$; equivalently
$\chi(F_i(-1))$ maps to $T_i$ and $\chi(F_i^{-1}(1))$ maps to $T_i^{-1}$. In
particular $\chi(F_i)\chi(F_i^{-1})=1$, and the powers of $v$ are the exact
normalization of the library's shift convention, not an ambiguity.

(b) For every braid $\beta\in B_n$ and every signed word $\sigma$ for $\beta$,
$\Phi(\chi(F(\sigma)))=v^{e(\sigma)}T_\beta$, where
$T_\beta:=T_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\cdots T_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r}$ is the image of
$\beta$ under the standard group homomorphism $B_n\to H_{S_n}^{\times}$,
$\sigma_i\mapsto T_i$, and
$e(\sigma)=\#\{\epsilon_k=1\}-\#\{\epsilon_k=-1\}$ depends only on $\beta$.
Hence $\beta\mapsto v^{-e(\beta)}\chi(F(\beta))$, composed with $\Phi$, is that
standard homomorphism: up to the grading normalization, the Rouquier complex of
a braid decategorifies to the image of the braid in the Hecke algebra.

$$\sigma_i\sigma_j=\sigma_j\sigma_i\qquad(1\le i,j\le n-1,\ |i-j|>1).$$

Equivalently,

$$B_n=\langle \sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{n-1}\mid \sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i=\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\ (1\le i\le n-2),\ \sigma_i\sigma_j=\sigma_j\sigma_i\ (1\le i,j\le n-1,\ |i-j|>1)\rangle,$$

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
**Additive setting.** Fix an additive category $\mathcal A$
([[def-additive-category]]): every hom-set is an abelian group, finite
biproducts exist, and every object has an identity morphism. All morphisms below
are morphisms of $\mathcal A$, sums and negatives are taken in the hom-groups,
and $0$ denotes the zero morphism between the indicated objects.

**Cochain complexes.** A **cochain complex** $C^\bullet=(C^n,d^n)_{n\in\mathbb Z}$
consists of objects $C^n$ of $\mathcal A$ and morphisms $d^n:C^n\to C^{n+1}$
with
$$d^{n+1}d^n=0\qquad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
The morphisms $d^n$ are the **differentials** of $C^\bullet$. No boundedness,
finiteness or nonvanishing condition is imposed on the family of objects.

**Cochain maps.** A **cochain map** $f:C^\bullet\to D^\bullet$ is a family of
morphisms $f^n:C^n\to D^n$ with
$$f^{n+1}d^n_C=d^n_Df^n\qquad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
Identities and composites of cochain maps are cochain maps, so cochain complexes
and cochain maps form a category; this category is written
$\operatorname{Ch}^\bullet(\mathcal A)$ when the ambient category needs to be
recorded.

**Homotopies.** A **homotopy** $h:f\simeq g$ between cochain maps
$f,g:C^\bullet\to D^\bullet$ is a family of morphisms $h^n:C^n\to D^{n-1}$, one
in each degree, such that
$$f^n-g^n=d^{n-1}_Dh^n+h^{n+1}d^n_C\qquad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
Thus $h$ has degree $-1$, and the right-hand side is the $n$-th component of the
graded map
$$dh+hd:=(d^{n-1}_Dh^n+h^{n+1}d^n_C)_{n\in\mathbb Z},$$
written with $d$ on both sides. A **null
homotopy** of a cochain map $f:C^\bullet\to D^\bullet$ is a homotopy
$f\simeq0$ to the zero map with the same source and target; $D^\bullet$
need not be the zero complex. A map admitting such a homotopy is
**null-homotopic**.

**Homotopy equivalence.** A cochain map $f:C^\bullet\to D^\bullet$ is a
**homotopy equivalence** when there is a cochain map
$g:D^\bullet\to C^\bullet$ with $gf\simeq1_{C^\bullet}$ and
$fg\simeq1_{D^\bullet}$; the complexes are then **homotopy equivalent**. The maps
$f$ and $g$ are homotopy inverses of one another.

**Contractibility.** A cochain complex $C^\bullet$ is **contractible** when its
identity is null-homotopic, $1_{C^\bullet}\simeq0$: that is, when there is a
family of morphisms $h^n:C^n\to C^{n-1}$ with
$$1_{C^n}=d^{n-1}h^n+h^{n+1}d^n\qquad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
A complex is contractible exactly when it is homotopy equivalent to the zero
complex, since a homotopy equivalence onto the zero complex is a pair of
null-homotopies of the identities.

**Degreewise biproducts.** If $C^\bullet$ and $D^\bullet$ are cochain complexes,
then defining
$$(C\oplus D)^n:=C^n\oplus D^n,\qquad d^n_{C\oplus D}:=d^n_C\oplus d^n_D$$
gives a cochain complex, because
$(d^{n+1}_C\oplus d^{n+1}_D)(d^n_C\oplus d^n_D)=0\oplus0=0$. The degreewise
injections and projections are cochain maps, and the biproduct identities hold in
each degree and are therefore identities of cochain maps; hence $C\oplus D$ is a
biproduct of $C$ and $D$. Iterating, finite direct sums of cochain complexes are
formed degreewise, and finite direct sums of cochain maps and of homotopies are
formed degreewise as well. Under the reindexing below this is the additive
structure on complexes over an additive category recorded in
[[thm-the-category-of-complexes-in-an-additive-category-is-additive]].

**Dictionary with the published chain convention.** Reindex by
$C_n:=C^{-n}$ and $d_n:=d^{-n}$. Then $d_n:C_n\to C_{n-1}$ and
$$d_{n-1}d_n=d^{-(n-1)}d^{-n}=d^{-n+1}d^{-n}=0,$$
so $(C_\bullet,d_\bullet)$ is an ordinary chain complex. A cochain map $f$
becomes the chain map with components $f_n:=f^{-n}$, and a homotopy
$h:f\simeq g$ becomes the chain homotopy $s_n:=h^{-n}:C_n\to D_{n+1}$, because
substituting $n\mapsto-n$ into the displayed homotopy equation produces exactly
$$f_n-g_n=d^D_{n+1}s_n+s_{n-1}d^C_n .$$
Consequently, when $\mathcal A$ is abelian, these definitions restrict under this
dictionary to the published [[def-chain-homotopy]] and
[[def-contractible-complex]], which are stated for chain complexes in an abelian
category. Reindexing reverses the sign of the differential degree ($+1$ for
cochains, $-1$ for chains) and of the homotopy degree ($-1$ for cochains, $+1$
for chains), and introduces no further sign.

**What is not asserted.** The definitions use only zero morphisms, addition,
negatives, composition and identities. No kernel, cokernel, image, homology
object or exactness is assumed or defined, no linear structure on the hom-groups
beyond the additive one is used, and no homology object is attached to a complex
in an arbitrary additive category; contractibility is the existence of the
displayed family $h$, not the vanishing of homology.

Fix an integer $n\ge2$, let $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with $\deg x_j=2$, and let $S_n$ act on $R$ by permuting variables. Let $\mathrm{SBim}_n$ be the idempotent-complete additive monoidal category of graded $(R,R)$-Soergel bimodules generated by the unit bimodule $R$, the bimodules $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ for the adjacent transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$, internal grading shifts, finite direct sums, tensor products over $R$, and direct summands. Use the shift convention $M(1)_d=M_{d+1}$; on the split Grothendieck ring it is recorded by $v[M]=[M(1)]$. Let $K^b(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$ denote the category of bounded cochain complexes in $\mathrm{SBim}_n$ with chain maps modulo chain homotopy.

For $1\le i<n$, let $F_i=[B_i\xrightarrow{\varepsilon_i}R(1)]$ in cohomological degrees $0,1$ and $F_i^{-1}=[R(-1)\xrightarrow{\eta_i}B_i]$ in degrees $-1,0$, with the maps and grading conventions of the positive and negative Rouquier generator complexes. For a signed word $\sigma=\sigma_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\cdots\sigma_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r}$, $\epsilon_k\in\{+1,-1\}$, let $F(\sigma)=F_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_R F_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r}$, using signed tensor totalization and left-to-right bracketing; the empty word gives $R$ in degree zero. If $\beta\in B_n$ is the braid represented by $\sigma$, the **Rouquier categorified line operator** $F(\beta)$ is this complex considered up to the canonical homotopy equivalence between words representing $\beta$. Tensor product is the categorical stacking operation. The comparison maps give the unit and coherent multiplication maps $F(\beta)\otimes_R F(\gamma)\simeq F(\beta\gamma)$; equivalently, left tensoring defines the coherent braid-group action on $K^b(R\text{-grmod})$.

A **physical defect realization** is additional data. A monoidal category $\mathcal D$ here means a category with a tensor bifunctor, a unit object, associator and unit isomorphisms satisfying the pentagon and unit triangles; its objects are declared line-defect types, its morphisms are declared junction maps, and its tensor product is the chosen stacking operation. The realization is a strong monoidal functor $\mathcal R:K^b(\mathrm{SBim}_n)\to\mathcal D$, meaning a functor with natural product and unit isomorphisms satisfying those same coherence equations and assigning images to every morphism, including junction maps, in its domain. Calling $\mathcal D$ a category of defects in a particular quantum field theory also requires an independently specified physical model. The Soergel and Rouquier data alone supply neither $\mathcal D$ nor this functor.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Fix an integer dimension $d\geq1$ and a finite nonempty alphabet $A$. A configuration is a function $\sigma:\mathbb Z^d\to A$. An interaction list consists of a finite index set $\mathcal R$ and, for each $r\in\mathcal R$, a finite nonempty shape $S_r\subset\mathbb Z^d$ containing $0$ and a function $\Phi_r:A^{S_r}\to\mathbb R$. The index $r$ is part of the data: two equal shapes with different indices represent two terms and are both counted. Every translate $x+S_r$ contributes once, with value $\Phi_r((\sigma_{x+y})_{y\in S_r})$.

The range is $R=\max_{r\in\mathcal R}\operatorname{diam}_\infty(S_r)$, with $R=0$ when $\mathcal R$ is empty. For finite $\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^d$, define the free-volume energy and the energy conditioned on an exterior configuration $\eta\in A^{\Lambda^c}$ by
$$H^{\mathrm{free}}_\Lambda(\sigma)=\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}\ \sum_{x:x+S_r\subseteq\Lambda}\Phi_r(\sigma_{x+S_r}),\qquad E_\Lambda(\tau_\Lambda\mid\eta)=\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}\ \sum_{x:(x+S_r)\cap\Lambda\ne\varnothing}\Phi_r((\tau_\Lambda\eta)_{x+S_r}).$$
Here $\tau_\Lambda\in A^\Lambda$, and $\tau_\Lambda\eta\in A^{\mathbb Z^d}$ is the concatenated configuration equal to $\tau_\Lambda$ on $\Lambda$ and to $\eta$ on $\Lambda^c$.
These are finite sums: for each finite shape $S_r$, only finitely many anchors $x$ make $x+S_r$ meet $\Lambda$. Terms meeting $\Lambda$ but not contained in it appear in the conditional energy and not in the free-volume energy. The definitions are mathematical and assign no physical units; a physical model must state its units separately.

Assume Countable Choice for the product-measure extension framework of [[def-countable-choice]] and [[lem-csm-lattice-product-and-measure-compactness]]. Work in the finite-alphabet configuration space $X=A^{\mathbb Z^d}$ with its cylinder-generated Borel sigma-algebra. Let the finite-range interaction and its conditional energy be as in [[def-csm-finite-range-lattice-interaction]], and fix $\beta>0$. For a finite $\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^d$ and exterior configuration $\eta\in A^{\Lambda^c}$, put
$$Z_\Lambda^\eta=\sum_{\tau\in A^\Lambda}e^{-\beta E_\Lambda(\tau\mid\eta)},\qquad \gamma_\Lambda(f\mid\eta)=\frac{\sum_{\tau\in A^\Lambda}f(\tau\eta)e^{-\beta E_\Lambda(\tau\mid\eta)}}{Z_\Lambda^\eta}$$
for bounded measurable $f:X\to\mathbb R$. Here $\gamma_\Lambda f$ denotes the function $\eta\mapsto\gamma_\Lambda(f\mid\eta)$, composition is operator composition, and $\mu\gamma_\Lambda(f)=\int\gamma_\Lambda(f\mid\eta)\,d\mu(\eta)$. A proper kernel leaves every exterior-measurable event fixed. A specification is a family $(\gamma_\Lambda)_{\Lambda\text{ finite}}$ of proper probability kernels satisfying $\gamma_\Lambda\gamma_\Delta=\gamma_\Lambda$ whenever $\Delta\subseteq\Lambda$. A DLR state is a probability measure $\mu$ on $X$ satisfying $\mu\gamma_\Lambda=\mu$ for every finite $\Lambda$.

For the existence and uniqueness results below, a specification has **finite range** when for every finite $\Delta$ and every cylinder event $C$ the function $\eta\mapsto\gamma_\Delta(\mathbf1_C\mid\eta)$ depends on only finitely many coordinates of $\eta$. The displayed finite-range Gibbs formula has this property because only finitely many interaction terms meet $\Delta$, and a cylinder indicator depends on only finitely many additional coordinates.

The formula is the candidate Gibbs specification; [[lem-csm-lattice-specification-consistency]] establishes its positive finite normalization, measurability, properness and consistency under the stated hypotheses. The Countable Choice assumption is used for the product-measure construction, not for any finite conditional sum.

Assume the finite-alphabet product-measure convention and conditional Gibbs formula of [[def-csm-lattice-gibbs-specification]], a finite-range interaction, and $\beta>0$. For every finite $\Lambda$ and exterior $\eta$, the displayed partition $Z_\Lambda^\eta$ is finite and strictly positive, the formula $\gamma_\Lambda(\cdot\mid\eta)$ defines a measurable proper probability kernel, and the family satisfies $\gamma_\Lambda\gamma_\Delta=\gamma_\Lambda$ whenever finite $\Delta\subseteq\Lambda$.

Let $d\geq1$, let $S$ be a finite nonempty set, and put $X=S^{\mathbb Z^d}$ with the $\sigma$-algebra generated by finite-coordinate cylinders. A specification on $X$ is a family $\gamma=(\gamma_\Lambda)$ of probability kernels indexed by finite $\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^d$. It is proper when each kernel leaves every exterior-measurable event fixed, and consistent when $\gamma_\Lambda\gamma_\Delta=\gamma_\Lambda$ for all finite $\Delta\subseteq\Lambda$. For $i\in\mathbb Z^d$, write $\gamma_i(\cdot\mid\eta)$ for its one-site conditional probability vector on $S$, where $\eta\in S^{\mathbb Z^d\setminus\{i\}}$. For probability vectors $p,q$ on $S$, define their total-variation distance by $\lVert p-q\rVert_{\rm TV}:=\frac12\sum_{s\in S}|p(s)-q(s)|$. The influence coefficient of site $j$ on the conditional law at site $i$ is

$$c^\gamma_{ij}:=\begin{cases}0,&i=j,\\[2pt]\displaystyle\sup_{\substack{\eta,\eta'\in S^{\mathbb Z^d\setminus\{i\}}\\ \eta_k=\eta'_k\ \text{for every }k\notin\{i,j\}}}\lVert\gamma_i(\cdot\mid\eta)-\gamma_i(\cdot\mid\eta')\rVert_{\rm TV},&i\ne j.\end{cases}$$

The matrix $C^\gamma=(c^\gamma_{ij})_{i,j\in\mathbb Z^d}$ is the Dobrushin influence matrix of $\gamma$. Its coefficients lie in $[0,1]$; a supremum need not be attained. The Dobrushin row constant is $c_\gamma:=\sup_i\sum_j c^\gamma_{ij}$, with value $+\infty$ allowed. A common uniform finite influence radius $R$ means $c^\gamma_{ij}=0$ whenever $\lVert i-j\rVert_\infty>R$.

Assume Countable Choice, $d\geq1$, a finite nonempty alphabet $A$, and a proper, consistent finite-range specification $\gamma$ on $X=A^{\mathbb Z^d}$ with its cylinder-generated Borel $\sigma$-algebra, using [[def-csm-lattice-gibbs-specification]]. Here consistency means $\gamma_\Lambda\gamma_\Delta=\gamma_\Lambda$ for finite $\Delta\subseteq\Lambda$, properness means $\gamma_\Lambda(r_\Lambda^{-1}(D)\mid\eta)=\mathbf1_D(\eta)$ for each exterior-measurable event $D\subseteq A^{\Lambda^c}$ and $\eta\in A^{\Lambda^c}$, where $r_\Lambda:X\to A^{\Lambda^c}$ is coordinate restriction; in compositions and integrals against measures on $X$, every kernel takes the appropriate exterior restriction of the global configuration as its argument, and finite range means each $\gamma_\Delta(\mathbf1_C\mid\cdot)$ for finite $\Delta$ and cylinder event $C$ depends on only finitely many exterior coordinates. Also assume a uniform finite integer radius $R\geq0$ such that each one-site kernel $\gamma_{\{i\}}$ depends only on exterior spins $j$ with $\|i-j\|_\infty\leq R$. For each pair of sites define $c_{ij}$ as the supremum of the half-total-variation change in the one-site conditional law at $i$ when only exterior spin $j$ is changed, where half-total variation for probability vectors $p,q$ on $A$ is $\frac12\sum_{a\in A}|p(a)-q(a)|$, and set $c_{ii}=0$. If
$$c=\sup_i\sum_jc_{ij}<1,$$
then the DLR state is unique. Moreover, for a finite region $\Lambda$ and two exterior conditions $\xi,\zeta$, couple the random-scan finite-volume heat-bath chains by choosing the same uniformly random site and using a maximal coupling of its two single-site conditional laws. A stationary joint law of this pair chain exists. If the distance $\operatorname{dist}_\infty(i,\Lambda^c):=\inf_{j\notin\Lambda}\|i-j\|_\infty$ is at least $r(R+1)$ for a nonnegative integer $r$, then its disagreement probability at $i$ is at most $c^r/(1-c)$. Consequently every local conditional expectation becomes uniformly insensitive to boundary conditions as $\Lambda\uparrow\mathbb Z^d$.

Let $S$ be finite nonempty, let $H_0,M:S\to\mathbb R$, fix $\beta>0$, and set $H_t=H_0-tM$ and $Z(t)=\sum_{s\in S}e^{-\beta H_t(s)}$ for $t\in\mathbb R$. For the normalized finite Gibbs law $\gamma_t(s)=Z(t)^{-1}e^{-\beta H_t(s)}$,
$$\frac{d}{dt}\log Z(t)=\beta\,\gamma_t(M),\qquad \frac{d^2}{dt^2}\log Z(t)=\beta^2\operatorname{Var}_{\gamma_t}(M)\geq0,$$ where $\operatorname{Var}_{\gamma}(M):=\gamma(M^2)-\gamma(M)^2$.
For fixed $H:S\to\mathbb R$, the corresponding inverse-temperature identities are
$$\frac{d}{d\beta}\log Z(\beta)=-\gamma_\beta(H),\qquad \frac{d^2}{d\beta^2}\log Z(\beta)=\operatorname{Var}_{\gamma_\beta}(H)\geq0.$$
These are finite-state identities; they do not justify differentiating an infinite-volume limit.

Let $E$ be a finite nonempty set, let $H_0,M,F:E\to\mathbb R$, fix $\beta>0$, and for $t\in\mathbb R$ define $H_t(x):=H_0(x)-tM(x)$, $Z(t):=\sum_{x\in E}e^{-\beta H_t(x)}$, and $\gamma_t(x):=Z(t)^{-1}e^{-\beta H_t(x)}$. For functions $F,M:E\to\mathbb R$, define $\operatorname{Cov}_{\gamma_t}(F,M):=\sum_x\gamma_t(x)F(x)M(x)-(\sum_x\gamma_t(x)F(x))(\sum_x\gamma_t(x)M(x))$. Then $t\mapsto\sum_x\gamma_t(x)F(x)$ is differentiable on $\mathbb R$ and

$$\frac{d}{dt}\sum_{x\in E}\gamma_t(x)F(x)=\beta\operatorname{Cov}_{\gamma_t}(F,M).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\geq1$, let $S$ be a finite nonempty set, and put $X=S^{\mathbb Z^d}$ with its cylinder-generated Borel $\sigma$-algebra. Let $\gamma$ and $\widetilde\gamma$ be proper consistent finite-range specifications on $X$, each with a uniform finite one-site influence radius. Finite range means that for every finite $\Delta$ and cylinder event $A$, each function $\eta\mapsto\gamma_\Delta(\mathbf1_A\mid\eta)$ and $\eta\mapsto\widetilde\gamma_\Delta(\mathbf1_A\mid\eta)$ depends on only finitely many exterior coordinates, as in [[def-csm-lattice-gibbs-specification]]. For each $i,j\in\mathbb Z^d$, let $C_{ii}=0$ and let $C_{ij}\geq0$ dominate both Dobrushin coefficients $c^\gamma_{ij}$ and $c^{\widetilde\gamma}_{ij}$ of [[def-csm-frontier-dobrushin-matrix]]. Assume $C_{ij}=0$ whenever $\lVert i-j\rVert_\infty>R$ for some finite integer $R\geq0$ and assume

$$\sup_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z^d}C_{ij}\leq c<1.$$

For each site $i$, define the one-site conditional discrepancy

$$b_i:=\sup_{\eta\in S^{\mathbb Z^d\setminus\{i\}}}\lVert\gamma_i(\cdot\mid\eta)-\widetilde\gamma_i(\cdot\mid\eta)\rVert_{\rm TV}.$$

Write $C_\Lambda=(C_{ij})_{i,j\in\Lambda}$ and $D^\Lambda:=\sum_{n=0}^\infty C_\Lambda^n$ for finite $\Lambda$, with $C_\Lambda^0$ the identity matrix on $\Lambda$; also write $D_{ij}:=\sum_{n=0}^\infty(C^n)_{ij}$ for the infinite-lattice resolvent entries. These sums are finite entrywise, because every row sum of $C^n$ and $C_\Lambda^n$ is at most $c^n$. A cylinder function is one depending only on the spins in some finite set. For a bounded real cylinder function $f:X\to\mathbb R$, define its oscillation by $\delta_i(f):=\sup_{\sigma,\sigma':\,\sigma_k=\sigma'_k\ (k\ne i)}|f(\sigma)-f(\sigma')|$; only finitely many $\delta_i(f)$ are nonzero.

For every nonempty finite $\Lambda$ containing a finite coordinate set $K_f$ on which $f$ depends, and exterior configurations $\xi,\zeta\in S^{\Lambda^c}$, the corresponding finite-volume Gibbs distributions satisfy

$$|\gamma_\Lambda(f\mid\xi)-\widetilde\gamma_\Lambda(f\mid\zeta)|\leq\sum_{i\in\Lambda}\delta_i(f)\sum_{k\in\Lambda}D^\Lambda_{ik}\left(b_k+\sum_{j\notin\Lambda}C_{kj}\mathbf1_{\{\xi_j\ne\zeta_j\}}\right).$$

Moreover, each specification has a unique DLR state, denoted $\mu$ and $\widetilde\mu$, and every bounded real cylinder function satisfies

$$|\mu(f)-\widetilde\mu(f)|\leq\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}\delta_i(f)\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z^d}D_{ij}b_j.$$

In particular, when $\gamma=\widetilde\gamma$ the comparison bound is zero. The estimates are conditional mathematical consequences of the stated finite-spin specifications and strict row bound.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power (Integer powers $a^m$),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges (Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

derivations.claim: For each $\lambda\in I$, [F1]–[F2] give a proper consistent finite-range Ising specification. Its Dobrushin row constant is at most $c_*<1$, so [A1] and [F4] give a unique DLR state $\mu_\lambda$. A lattice translation of $\mu_\lambda$ is another DLR state for the same translation-invariant kernels; uniqueness therefore makes $\mu_\lambda$ translation invariant.

Fix finite $\Lambda$ containing distinct sites $i,j$ and an exterior configuration $\eta$, and write $\nu_{\Lambda,\lambda}:=\gamma_{\Lambda,\lambda}(\cdot\mid\eta)$. Every finite Gibbs weight is positive, so the finite-volume probabilities of $\sigma_j=\pm1$ are positive. Conditional on either value, consistency [F2] identifies the law on $\Lambda\setminus\{j\}$ with the corresponding finite-volume Gibbs kernel, with the same exterior spins away from $j$ and the spin at $j$ fixed to the selected sign. Apply the finite-volume comparison bound [F7] with the same specification and $b=0$ to these two boundary conditions. For $f=\sigma_i$, $\delta_i(f)=2$ and all other oscillations vanish; the bound is $2\sum_{k\in\Lambda\setminus\{j\}}D^{\Lambda\setminus\{j\}}_{ik}C_{kj}(\lambda)$. Each term is a sum of weights of paths from the boundary site $j$ to $i$ whose intermediate vertices avoid $j$, so it is at most $2\sum_{n\geq1}C(\lambda)^n_{ij}$.

Let $\Lambda_n=[-n,n]^d$ and let $\nu_{n,\lambda}:=\gamma_{\Lambda_n,\lambda}(\cdot\mid\eta^+)$, where $\eta^+_i=+1$ for all exterior sites. For any fixed cylinder function $g$, choose a finite coordinate set $K$ on which it depends (take any nonempty finite $K$ if $g$ is constant). By the DLR identity, $\mu_\lambda(g)=\int\gamma_{\Lambda_n,\lambda}(g\mid\eta)\,d\mu_\lambda(\eta)$ whenever $K\subseteq\Lambda_n$. The finite-volume comparison estimate [F7] with the same specification, $b=0$, and arbitrary boundary conditions bounds the difference between $\gamma_{\Lambda_n,\lambda}(g\mid\eta^+)$ and every integrand by $\sum_{i\in K}\delta_i(g)$ times the total influence-path weight from $i$ to $\Lambda_n^c$. If $R\geq1$, each such path has at least $q_n:=\lfloor\operatorname{dist}_\infty(K,\Lambda_n^c)/R\rfloor$ edges, and its total weight is at most $\sum_{k\geq q_n}c_*^k=c_*^{q_n}/(1-c_*)$ by [F9]; $q_n\to\infty$. If $R=0$, the boundary term is zero. Thus $\nu_{n,\lambda}(g)\to\mu_\lambda(g)$ locally uniformly on $I$.

For every $n\geq0$, nonnegativity and the row bound give $\sum_j C(\lambda)^{n+1}_{ij}=\sum_k C(\lambda)^n_{ik}\sum_jC_{kj}(\lambda)\leq c_*\sum_kC(\lambda)^n_{ik}$; induction from $C^0=I$ yields $\sum_jC(\lambda)^n_{ij}\leq c_*^n$. Summing the off-site bound from step 3.1 and using [F9] gives $\sum_{j\ne i}|\operatorname{Cov}(\sigma_i,\sigma_j)|\leq\sum_{n\geq1}\sum_jC(\lambda)^n_{ij}\leq c_* /(1-c_*)$. Adding the diagonal variance, at most $1$, proves the absolute covariance sum bound. If $R\geq1$ and $\lVert j-i\rVert_\infty\geq r$, then $C(\lambda)^n_{ij}=0$ for $n<\lceil r/R\rceil$, because an $n$-step path moves at most $nR$ in the $\ell^\infty$ metric. Summing the remaining row tails with [F9] proves the stated spatial-tail bound. If $R=0$, the zero diagonal and range condition make every off-site coefficient zero, so step 3.1 gives zero off-site covariance.

Step 2.1 with $g=\sigma_0$ gives $m_n\to m$ locally uniformly, while step 5.1 gives $m_n'=S_n\to S$ locally uniformly. Each $S_n$ is continuous because it is a finite sum of finite Gibbs expectations, each a finite ratio of exponentials; hence $S$ is continuous as a locally uniform limit. On any closed subinterval of $I$, [F8] applied to $G=m_n$ and derivative $S_n$ gives $m_n(\lambda)-m_n(\lambda_0)=\int_{\lambda_0}^{\lambda}S_n(u)\,du$. Passing to the locally uniform limits yields $m(\lambda)-m(\lambda_0)=\int_{\lambda_0}^{\lambda}S(u)\,du$, so $m'(\lambda)=S(\lambda)$. Since $\lambda=\beta h$, the chain rule gives $d m/dh=\beta S(\beta h)$.

For finite nonempty $\Lambda$, expand the variance of $\overline\sigma_\Lambda$ as $|\Lambda|^{-2}\sum_{i,j\in\Lambda}\operatorname{Cov}(\sigma_i,\sigma_j)$. By the uniform row bound proved in step 4.1, the sum of the absolute values in each row is at most $1/(1-c_*)$, so the variance is at most $1/((1-c_*)|\Lambda|)$. Pointwise, $\mathbf1_{\{|X-\mathbb EX|\geq\varepsilon\}}\leq |X-\mathbb EX|^2/\varepsilon^2$; taking expectations with $X=\overline\sigma_\Lambda$ proves the Chebyshev bound.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite nonempty alphabet, let $p=(p(a))_{a\in\mathcal A}$ be a probability vector with $p(a)>0$ for every $a$, and write
$$\Delta(\mathcal A):=\left\{q\in[0,1]^{\mathcal A}:\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}q(a)=1\right\}$$
with its $\ell^1$ topology. For each integer $n\geq1$, the configuration space is $\Omega_n:=\mathcal A^n$ with the full power-set $\sigma$-algebra. Its reference probability is the product law $p^{\otimes n}$, which gives the word $x^n=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ mass $\prod_{i=1}^n p(x_i)$. By [[lem-it-finite-product-law-is-iid]], this mass assignment is normalized and is a probability law; explicitly, $\sum_{x^n\in\mathcal A^n}\prod_{i=1}^np(x_i)=\prod_{i=1}^n\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}p(a)=1$. The empirical macrostate is the probability vector
$$L_n(x^n)(a):=\frac1n\#\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i=a\},\qquad a\in\mathcal A.$$
Thus $L_n$ is the empirical type defined by the finite-alphabet supplier.

For a continuous function $h:\Delta(\mathcal A)\to\mathbb R$ and a real parameter $\beta$, define the finite canonical normalizer and word law by
$$Z_{n,\beta}:=\sum_{x^n\in\Omega_n}p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))},\qquad p_{n,\beta}(x^n):=\frac{p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))}}{Z_{n,\beta}}.$$
The normalizer is finite and positive because the sum is finite and every summand is finite and positive. The canonical macrostate law is the pushforward $p_{n,\beta}\circ L_n^{-1}$.

For $q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)$, set
$$D(q\|p):=\sum_{a:q(a)>0}q(a)\ln\frac{q(a)}{p(a)},$$
omitting zero-mass terms, as in the finite relative-entropy convention. For $u\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))$, define the constrained cost, entropy, canonical variational set, and constrained variational set by
$$d(u):=\inf_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p),\qquad s(u):=-d(u),$$
$$\mathcal M_\beta:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}\bigl[D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)\bigr],\qquad \mathcal M_u:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p).$$
For $\delta>0$, the microcanonical shell event is $E_{n,\delta,u}:=\{x^n:|h(L_n(x^n))-u|<\delta\}$. Whenever $p^{\otimes n}(E_{n,\delta,u})>0$, its microcanonical shell law is the conditional probability $p^{\otimes n}(\,\cdot\mid E_{n,\delta,u})$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be finite and nonempty, let $p(a)>0$ for every $a\in\mathcal A$, and let $h:\Delta(\mathcal A)\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, where $\Delta(\mathcal A)$ is the probability simplex with its $\ell^1$ topology. Let $L_n$ be the empirical probability vector of an $n$-word drawn from $p^{\otimes n}$, and use $D(q\|p)=\sum_{a:q(a)>0}q(a)\ln(q(a)/p(a))$ with zero-mass terms omitted. For $\beta\in\mathbb R$, the canonical word law weights $x^n$ proportionally to $p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))}$.

The canonical macrostate law of $L_n$ satisfies a speed-$n$ large-deviation principle with rate
$$R_\beta(q)=D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)-m_\beta,\qquad m_\beta:=\min_{r\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}\bigl[D(r\|p)+\beta h(r)\bigr].$$
Thus its canonical equilibrium macrostate set is $\mathcal M_\beta=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}[D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)]$.

For $u\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))$, let $d(u):=\min_{h(q)=u}D(q\|p)$, $s(u):=-d(u)$, and $\mathcal M_u:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{h(q)=u}D(q\|p)$. If there is a sequence $\delta_j\downarrow0$ for which
$$\inf_{|h(q)-u|<\delta_j}D(q\|p)=\inf_{|h(q)-u|\leq\delta_j}D(q\|p)\quad\text{for every }j,$$
then the iterated microcanonical shell limit exists and is
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln p^{\otimes n}\!\left(|h(L_n)-u|<\delta_j\right)=s(u).$$
In the same iterated limit, for every open neighborhood $U$ of $\mathcal M_u$,
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}\limsup_{n\to\infty}p^{\otimes n}\!\left(L_n\notin U\mid |h(L_n)-u|<\delta_j\right)=0.$$
Finally,
$$h(\mathcal M_\beta)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{v\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))}\bigl[s(v)-\beta v\bigr],$$
and a macrostate $q$ is canonical at $\beta$ exactly when $q\in\mathcal M_{h(q)}$ and $h(q)$ maximizes $s(v)-\beta v$. Equivalently, $u$ is a canonical energy at $\beta$ exactly when $v\mapsto s(u)+\beta(v-u)$ is an upper supporting affine function for $s$ on the whole energy range. An energy with no upper supporting line for any slope is not realized by a canonical ensemble.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which

the average rate of change across the whole interval.

derivations.claim:
Write $q(+1)=(1+m)/2$ and $q(-1)=(1-m)/2$. Substituting into [F1] with $p(+1)=p(-1)=1/2$ gives
$$D(q\|p)=\frac{1+m}{2}\ln(1+m)+\frac{1-m}{2}\ln(1-m),$$
with the zero-mass endpoint term omitted. Since $q$ depends continuously on $m\in[-1,1]$ and [F8] makes $D(q\|p)$ continuous on the whole simplex, adding $\beta h(q)=-\beta Jm^2/2$ shows that $\Phi_\beta$ is continuous on $[-1,1]$; [F8] supplies the boundary limit $t\ln t\to0$ behind the convention $0\ln0=0$. The formula is even in $m$.

For $|m|<1$ define $a(m):=\operatorname{atanh}(m):=\tfrac12\ln\frac{1+m}{1-m}$. By [F3]–[F5] and direct differentiation, $$a'(m)=\frac1{1-m^2},\qquad \Phi_\beta'(m)=a(m)-\beta Jm.$$ For $0<m<1$ put $g(m):=a(m)/m$ and define $r:[0,1)\to\mathbb R$ by $r(m):=m/(1-m^2)-a(m)$. Then $g'(m)=r(m)/m^2$, $r(0)=0$, and $r'(m)=2m^2/(1-m^2)^2>0$ for $0<m<1$. The mean value theorem [F6] applies to $r$ on $[0,m]$ because $r$ is continuous there and differentiable on $(0,m)$; it gives $r(m)>0$, hence $g'(m)>0$.

The same theorem [F6] applied to $a$ on $[0,m]$ gives $g(m)=a'(c_m)$ for some $c_m\in(0,m)$; as $m\downarrow0$, $c_m\downarrow0$ and $a'(c_m)\to1$, so $\lim_{m\downarrow0}g(m)=1$. As $m\uparrow1$, $(1+m)/(1-m)\to+\infty$, and the increasing onto logarithm [F3] gives $a(m)\to+\infty$, hence $g(m)\to+\infty$. Thus $g$ is continuous, strictly increasing from limiting value $1$ to $+\infty$ on $(0,1)$.

If $\beta J\leq1$, then for $0<m<1$, $\Phi_\beta'(m)=m(g(m)-\beta J)>0$ by step 2.1. The mean value theorem [F6] on each subinterval of $[0,1]$ makes $\Phi_\beta$ strictly increasing there; continuity includes the endpoint $m=1$. Evenness then shows $\Phi_\beta(m)>\Phi_\beta(0)$ for every $m\neq0$, so $0$ is the unique global minimizer.

If $\beta J>1$, the limits in step 2.1 give $a,b$ with $0<a<b<1$, $g(a)<\beta J<g(b)$. Continuity of $g$ on $[a,b]$ and the intermediate value theorem [F7] give an $m_\beta\in(a,b)$ with $g(m_\beta)=\beta J$; strict increase of $g$ makes it unique on $(0,1)$. The derivative formula in step 1.2 is negative for $0<m<m_\beta$ and positive for $m_\beta<m<1$. By [F6], $\Phi_\beta$ strictly decreases on $[0,m_\beta]$ and strictly increases on $[m_\beta,1]$, including the endpoint by continuity. Evenness proves that the only global minimizers on $[-1,1]$ are $\pm m_\beta$; in particular the stationary point $m=0$ is not a minimizer.

The equation $g(m_\beta)=\beta J$ is $\operatorname{atanh}(m_\beta)=\beta Jm_\beta$. If $r=(1+m_\beta)/(1-m_\beta)$, then $e^{2\operatorname{atanh}(m_\beta)}=e^{\ln r}=r$ by [F3], so the stated formula for $\tanh$ gives $\tanh(\operatorname{atanh}(m_\beta))=(r-1)/(r+1)=m_\beta$. Hence $m_\beta=\tanh(\beta Jm_\beta)$. Conversely, any $m\in(0,1)$ solving this fixed-point equation yields $e^{2\beta Jm}=(1+m)/(1-m)$ by rearrangement of the stated $\tanh$ formula; applying $\ln$ and [F3] gives $g(m)=\beta J$. Strict increase of $g$ therefore proves uniqueness of the positive fixed point. By [F2], the global minimizers just classified are exactly the canonical equilibrium magnetizations.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

derivations.claim: For each $\theta$ and each $\sigma$, $H_\theta^\eta(\sigma)$ is a finite sum of finite real values. Thus every weight $e^{-H_\theta^\eta(\sigma)}$ is positive and finite by [F1, F2], and the partition denominator is a finite nonempty sum of positive finite terms. This makes $\pi_\theta^\eta$ a probability vector on the finite nonempty set $S^\Lambda$.

Fix $i\in\Lambda$ and $\sigma_{\Lambda\setminus\{i\}}$. The denominator in $q_{i,\theta}^\eta$ is likewise a finite nonempty sum of positive finite terms. Dividing the corresponding joint Gibbs masses by their sum over the possible value at site $i$ cancels the joint partition function and gives exactly the displayed ratio; summing that ratio over $s\in S$ gives one. Hence it is the conditional probability vector of site $i$ given the other spins. Since $\mathcal C$ is finite and each $C$ is finite, $N_i$ is finite. In the ratio, every potential indexed by a set $C$ not containing $i$ is the same for all values of $s$ and cancels; hence only potentials meeting $i$, and therefore only spins in $N_i$ and the fixed boundary values there, affect this conditional.

Each $H_\theta^\eta(\sigma)$ is measurable in $\theta$ because it is a finite sum of the stipulated measurable potentials. The exponential is Borel measurable by continuity [F3], so composition with these potentials preserves measurability. The finite partition and conditional denominators are positive by [F2], so $\pi_\theta^\eta(\sigma)$ and each $q_{i,\theta}^\eta$ are measurable in $\theta$. Their finite product $PL_\theta^\eta(\sigma)$ is therefore a measurable, positive finite real-valued objective. This does not assert that its sum over configurations is one.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement: Take $\Lambda=\{1,2\}$, $S=\{-1,+1\}$, and any fixed exterior boundary; the sole interaction set $\{1,2\}$ has no exterior sites, so its energy is independent of that boundary. Use parameter space $\Theta=\{0,1\}$ with its full power-set sigma-algebra, prior mass $1/2$ at each parameter, and the single potential $\Phi_{\{1,2\}}((\sigma_1,\sigma_2);J)=-J\sigma_1\sigma_2$. Use the real exponential $\exp$, put $e:=\exp(1)$, and define $\cosh J:=(\exp(J)+\exp(-J))/2$. For the hypothetical observation $(+1,+1)$, the exact joint likelihood is $\exp(J)/(4\cosh J)$, whereas the product of the two one-site Gibbs conditional probabilities is $[\exp(J)/(2\cosh J)]^2$. By pseudo-posterior I mean the probability vector obtained by multiplying this product by the prior weights and normalizing over $J\in\{0,1\}$. The exact and pseudo-posterior distributions are different.
