citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, $D=\dim H\ge1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. With composition, Hilbert adjoint, identity and the induced operator norm, $\mathcal B(H)$ is a nonzero unital complex C*-algebra in the sense of [[def-c-star-algebra]]. In particular it is complete, $\|AB\|\le\|A\|\|B\|$, $\|A^*A\|=\|A\|^2$, $\|A^*\|=\|A\|$ and $\|I\|=1$. The matrix $\|A\|^2I-A^*A$ is positive semidefinite and has a positive square root in $\mathcal B(H)$.

Every complex-linear functional $\omega:\mathcal B(H)\to\mathbb C$ that is positive, meaning $\omega(B^*B)\ge0$ for all $B$, has a unique positive semidefinite matrix $\rho$ such that $\omega(A)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)$ for all $A$. It is bounded and satisfies

$$|\omega(A)|\le\operatorname{Tr}(\rho)\|A\|\quad(A\in\mathcal B(H)),\qquad \|\omega\|=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho)=\omega(I).$$

Consequently the canonical states of [[def-state-on-a-c-star-algebra]] are exactly the trace pairings of density operators of [[def-qc-density-operator]]; for a positive functional, normalization $\omega(I)=1$ is equivalent to norm one. The result includes zero positive functionals, nonfaithful densities and $D=1$; it makes no infinite-dimensional density representation assertion.

Fix an integer dimension $d\ge1$, the countable site set $\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}^d$ of [[lem-qsm-integer-lattice-countable]], and one finite spin dimension $q\ge1$, where $q$ is a positive integer (so $q\in\mathbb N$ and $1\le q$, by [[def-natural-numbers]] and [[def-nat-order]]). For $n\in\mathbb Z$, define $|n|=n$ if $0\le n$ and $|n|=-n$ if $n<0$, using the integer order and additive inverse of [[def-int-order]] and [[def-int-operations]]. Totality and compatibility of the integer order with addition ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]) give $0\le|n|$ and $-|n|\le n\le|n|$. Adding these bounds for $m,n\in\mathbb Z$ gives $|m+n|\le|m|+|n|$. Equip $\Gamma$ with the max-coordinate metric $d_\infty(x,y)=\max_{1\le r\le d}|x_r-y_r|$; the maximum exists because the coordinate set is finite and nonempty, symmetry and separation hold coordinatewise, and the absolute-value triangle inequality gives $|x_r-z_r|\le|x_r-y_r|+|y_r-z_r|$ for every coordinate, hence the triangle inequality for $d_\infty$. A **finite region** is a finite subset $\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma$; its cardinality is $|\Lambda|$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]).

For a finite region $\Lambda$, let $S_\Lambda=\{1,\ldots,q\}^{\Lambda}$ be the set of spin configurations on $\Lambda$. Induction on $|\Lambda|$ gives $|S_\Lambda|=q^{|\Lambda|}$: the empty region has one configuration, and for $x\in\Lambda$ the restriction map $s\mapsto(s|_{\Lambda\setminus\{x\}},s(x))$ is a bijection $S_\Lambda\to S_{\Lambda\setminus\{x\}}\times\{1,\ldots,q\}$, so adjoining one site multiplies the number of configurations by $q$, according to the recursion defining natural-number powers in [[def-nat-power]]. Let $\mathcal H_\Lambda$ be the vector space of functions $f:S_\Lambda\to\mathbb C$ with inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}f(s)\overline{g(s)}$. For each $s\in S_\Lambda$, let $e_s$ be the indicator function of $\{s\}$; these vectors form an orthonormal basis. For $\Lambda=\varnothing$, $S_\Lambda$ is a singleton and $\mathcal H_\Lambda\cong\mathbb C$. The **local spin matrix algebra** is

$$\mathcal A_\Lambda:=\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)\cong M_{q^{|\Lambda|}}(\mathbb C),$$

Here $\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)$ denotes all complex-linear endomorphisms of the finite-dimensional Hilbert space; they are bounded. The algebra has composition, Hilbert adjoint, identity $I_\Lambda$, and induced operator norm

$$\|T\|:=\sup_{\|\xi\|=1}\|T\xi\|.$$

The **finite local trace** is $\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(T):=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}\langle T e_s,e_s\rangle$ in the displayed configuration basis $(e_s)$. This is the usual finite-matrix trace; basis independence and its cyclic/unitary identities are supplied by [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]].

If $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'$, restriction of configurations gives the canonical factorization $\mathcal H_{\Lambda'}\cong\mathcal H_\Lambda\otimes\mathcal H_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$, with sites ordered lexicographically. The **factor inclusion** is the unital $*$-homomorphism $\iota_{\Lambda,\Lambda'}:\mathcal A_\Lambda\to\mathcal A_{\Lambda'}$ given by $T\mapsto T\otimes I_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$. A **localization region** for $T$ is any finite $\Lambda$ for which $T\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ under these inclusions; a localization region need not be minimal.

The ordinary operator norm makes each local matrix algebra a nonzero unital complete C*-algebra, and every positive normalized complex-linear functional is uniquely a trace pairing with a density matrix, by [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]]. This includes the empty region, whose Hilbert space is $\mathbb C$. This definition does not posit an infinite-dimensional tensor-product Hilbert space.

Use the finite local matrix algebras and isometric factor inclusions of [[def-qsm-local-spin-algebras]] and [[lem-qsm-local-spin-inclusions-isometric]]. Identify $A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ with its image in every larger finite-region algebra. The directed union

$$\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}:=\bigcup_{\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma,\ |\Lambda|<\infty}\mathcal A_\Lambda$$

is the algebra of **strictly local observables**. Its norm is $\|A\|=\|A\|_{\mathcal A_\Lambda}$ for any finite localization region $\Lambda$ of $A$; isometric inclusions make this independent of the chosen region. The **quasi-local spin algebra** is the norm completion

$$\mathcal A:=\overline{\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}}^{\,\|\cdot\|}.$$

The C*-algebra structure on this completion has product and adjoint extended continuously from the finite local matrix algebras. Countable Choice is assumed for the published existence theorem for metric completions; [[lem-qsm-quasilocal-completion]] supplies the full extension argument using the finite C*-identity of [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]].

**No global Hilbert tensor product is selected.** “Quasi-local” means norm completion of the directed algebra of finite-region observables; it does not mean a chosen representation as operators on an infinite tensor-product Hilbert space. A local operator $A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ may have more than one localization region. Disjoint finite local factors commute in their common finite tensor algebra.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Cauchy-sequence completion. For the local spin system of [[def-qsm-local-spin-algebras]], the normed $*$-algebra $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and its completion $\mathcal A$ of [[def-qsm-quasilocal-spin-algebra]] are well defined; $\mathcal A$ is a unital complex C*-algebra and $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is norm dense in it. If $A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ and $B\in\mathcal A_\Delta$ for disjoint finite regions $\Lambda,\Delta$, then $AB=BA$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be the unital quasi-local spin C*-algebra of [[def-qsm-quasilocal-spin-algebra]], whose C*-structure uses Countable Choice as in [[lem-qsm-quasilocal-completion]]. An **infinite algebraic state** is a bounded complex-linear functional $\omega:\mathcal A\to\mathbb C$ satisfying $\omega(I)=1$ and $\omega(A^*A)\ge0$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$.

For each finite region $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$, the restriction $\omega|_{\mathcal A_\Lambda}$ is a finite-matrix state. By [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]], every positive normalized functional on a finite matrix algebra is represented by a unique density matrix. Define its **local density matrix** $\rho_\Lambda$ by

$$\omega(A)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda}(\rho_\Lambda A)\qquad(A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda),$$

where $\rho_\Lambda=\rho_\Lambda^*\ge0$ and $\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda}\rho_\Lambda=1$. For $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'$, put $\Delta=\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda$ and use the configuration-basis factorization $\mathcal H_{\Lambda'}\cong\mathcal H_\Lambda\otimes\mathcal H_\Delta$ of [[def-qsm-local-spin-algebras]]. If $T\in\mathcal A_{\Lambda'}$, define its **partial trace over $\Delta$**, $\operatorname{Tr}_\Delta(T)\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$, by its matrix coefficients

$$\langle \operatorname{Tr}_\Delta(T)e_s,e_{s'}\rangle:=\sum_{t\in S_\Delta}\langle T(e_s\otimes e_t),e_{s'}\otimes e_t\rangle\qquad(s,s'\in S_\Lambda),$$

where $e_s$ and $e_t$ are the configuration basis vectors of $\mathcal H_\Lambda$ and $\mathcal H_\Delta$. The finite sums depend linearly on $T$, so they define a linear map $\mathcal A_{\Lambda'}\to\mathcal A_\Lambda$ with a unique output matrix for each $T$. Expanding both configuration-basis traces gives its pairing identity

$$\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda\!\left(A\operatorname{Tr}_\Delta(T)\right)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda'}\!\left((A\otimes I_\Delta)T\right)\qquad(A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda),$$

with the common value given by

$$\sum_{s,s'\in S_\Lambda}\sum_{t\in S_\Delta}\langle A e_{s'},e_s\rangle\langle T(e_s\otimes e_t),e_{s'}\otimes e_t\rangle.$$

The pairing identity determines this matrix uniquely: if $D\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ pairs to zero with every $A$, taking the configuration-basis matrix units $A=E_{ji}$ gives $\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(E_{ji}D)=\langle D e_j,e_i\rangle=0$ for every $i,j$, so $D=0$. The local densities are **consistent** when $\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}(\rho_{\Lambda'})=\rho_\Lambda$. No density operator on a globally chosen Hilbert space is part of this definition.

This agrees with the canonical state convention of [[def-state-on-a-c-star-algebra]]: the finite restrictions have norm one by [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]], giving $|\omega(A)|\le\|A\|$ on the dense local algebra and hence on its completion; evaluation at the norm-one identity gives $\|\omega\|=1$. Conversely a canonical state has local restrictions with density matrices of trace one, since the finite norm formula and continuity on the dense local algebra imply $\|\omega\|=\omega(I)$. No global density representation is asserted.

Use the lattice $\Gamma=\mathbb Z^d$, $d\ge1$, the finite spin dimension $q\ge1$, the local matrix algebras $\mathcal A_\Lambda$, and the max-coordinate metric $d_\infty$ of [[def-qsm-local-spin-algebras]]. For finite nonempty $Z\subset\Gamma$, write $\operatorname{diam}_\infty Z=\max_{x,y\in Z}d_\infty(x,y)$; for finite nonempty $X,Y\subset\Gamma$, write $\operatorname{dist}_\infty(X,Y)=\min_{x\in X,y\in Y}d_\infty(x,y)$.

A **uniformly bounded finite-range interaction** is a family $\Phi(Z)\in\mathcal A_Z$, indexed by finite nonempty $Z\subset\Gamma$, such that $\Phi(Z)^*=\Phi(Z)$ and there are an integer $M\ge1$, a finite $R\ge0$, and $\kappa<\infty$ satisfying

$$\Phi(Z)=0\quad\text{if }|Z|>M\text{ or }\operatorname{diam}_\infty Z>R,\qquad\kappa:=\sup_{x\in\Gamma}\sum_{Z\ni x}\|\Phi(Z)\|<\infty.$$

The norm in this sum is the operator norm in the local matrix algebra $\mathcal A_Z$. If a model lists several terms with the same support, first add them in that local algebra; the resulting single operator is $\Phi(Z)$, and $\kappa$ uses its norm. Thus no multiplicity is implicit.

For a finite region $\Lambda\subset\Gamma$, define the **free-boundary finite-volume Hamiltonian** by summing only terms whose complete support lies inside $\Lambda$; terms meeting $\Lambda$ but extending outside it are omitted:

$$H_\Lambda:=\sum_{\varnothing\ne Z\subseteq\Lambda}\Phi(Z)\in\mathcal A_\Lambda.$$

It is a finite sum of self-adjoint matrices. For a fixed scale $\hbar>0$ and any finite $\Omega\supseteq\Lambda$, embed $H_\Lambda$ in $\mathcal A_\Omega$ by the canonical factor inclusion and define

$$\alpha_t^\Lambda(A):=e^{itH_\Lambda/\hbar}Ae^{-itH_\Lambda/\hbar}\qquad(A\in\mathcal A_\Omega,\ t\in\mathbb R).$$

These actions are compatible as $\Omega$ increases, because the extra tensor factors carry the identity. On $\mathcal A_\Lambda$ this is the ordinary finite matrix Heisenberg dynamics.

In physical SI bookkeeping, when $\Phi(Z)$ is interpreted as an energy, $\Phi(Z)$, $\kappa$, and $H_\Lambda$ have units J, $t$ has units s, and $\hbar$ is the adopted reduced Planck constant with units J s. The mathematics below uses only $\hbar>0$ and asserts no measured parameter value.

Assume Countable Choice and the finite-matrix C*-identity condition [A1] below. Let $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}=\bigcup_{\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^d,\ |\Lambda|<\infty}\mathcal A_\Lambda$ and let $\mathcal A$ be its norm completion as in [[def-qsm-quasilocal-spin-algebra]]. These assumptions give the conditional unital C*-algebra structure supplied by [[lem-qsm-quasilocal-completion]]. Let $\Phi$ be a uniformly bounded finite-range interaction of [[def-qsm-bounded-finite-range-interaction]].

For any increasing finite exhaustion $(\Lambda_n)_{n\ge1}$ in the convention of [[lem-qsm-boundary-dynamics-cauchy]]—that is, each $\Lambda_n$ is finite, $\Lambda_n\subseteq\Lambda_{n+1}$, and $\bigcup_{n\ge1}\Lambda_n=\mathbb Z^d$—the free-boundary finite-volume maps $\alpha_t^{\Lambda_n}$ converge in norm on every local observable, uniformly for $t$ in compact intervals. Their limit is independent of the exhaustion and extends uniquely to a strongly continuous one-parameter group $\alpha_t$ of maps $\alpha_t:\mathcal A\to\mathcal A$. Here “one-parameter group” means $\alpha_0=\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal A}$ and $\alpha_{s+t}=\alpha_s\circ\alpha_t$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$. Each $\alpha_t$ is a bijective complex-linear unital $*$-homomorphism (a $*$-automorphism), with inverse $\alpha_{-t}$. Strong continuity means $t\mapsto\alpha_t(A)$ is norm-continuous for every fixed $A\in\mathcal A$. This result does not assert that an infinite-volume Hamiltonian is an element of $\mathcal A$ or a bounded operator on a preselected infinite tensor-product Hilbert space.

Fix $d\ge1$, the site set $\Gamma=\mathbb Z^d$, its max-coordinate metric $d_\infty$, and the local spin algebras $\mathcal A_\Lambda$ of the uniformly finite-dimensional spin system. A finite interaction is a family $\Phi(Z)=\Phi(Z)^*\in\mathcal A_Z$ indexed by finite nonempty $Z\subset\Gamma$. For a finite $\Lambda\subset\Gamma$, define

$$H_\Lambda^\Phi:=\sum_{\varnothing\ne Z\subseteq\Lambda}\Phi(Z),\qquad \tau_t^{\Lambda,\Phi}(A):=e^{itH_\Lambda^\Phi/\hbar}Ae^{-itH_\Lambda^\Phi/\hbar},$$

where $\hbar>0$, $A$ is embedded in a common finite local algebra, and the finite sum is a self-adjoint matrix. When a path $\Phi_s$, $s\in[0,1]$, is used, each $\Phi_s(Z)$ is $C^1$ in matrix norm and the derivative is taken term by term.

For $r\ge0$ put $F(r)=(1+r)^{-d-1}$. The admissible weights used here are

$$F_a(r):=e^{-ar}F(r)\quad(a>0),\qquad F_\rho(r):=(1+r)^{-\rho}\quad(\rho>d).$$

For an admissible weight $G$, define the weighted interaction norm

$$\|\Phi\|_G:=\sup_{x,y\in\Gamma}\frac{1}{G(d_\infty(x,y))} \sum_{\substack{Z\subset\Gamma\ {\rm finite,\ nonempty}\\x,y\in Z}}\|\Phi(Z)\|.$$

The derivative norm of a path is

$$\|\partial\Phi\|_G:=\sup_{s\in[0,1]}\sup_{x,y\in\Gamma} \frac{1}{G(d_\infty(x,y))} \sum_{Z\ni x,y}|Z|\,\|\partial_s\Phi_s(Z)\|.$$

A finite-volume spectral band is a nonempty selected subset $\Sigma_\Lambda(s)\subseteq\sigma(H_\Lambda^{\Phi_s})$ together with the orthogonal projection onto the sum of its eigenspaces. It may be specified by an interval $I_\Lambda(s)$ with smoothly varying endpoints, in which case $\Sigma_\Lambda(s)=\sigma(H_\Lambda^{\Phi_s})\cap I_\Lambda(s)$. The band is uniformly isolated with gap $\gamma>0$ along a specified finite-volume exhaustion when

$$\operatorname{dist}\!\left(\Sigma_\Lambda(s),\sigma(H_\Lambda^{\Phi_s})\setminus\Sigma_\Lambda(s)\right)\ge\gamma$$

for every volume in that exhaustion and every $s\in[0,1]$. For spectral-flow arguments, the selected eigenvalues must also form a locally fixed spectral cluster: for each $s_0$, a contour in the resolvent set encloses exactly the selected eigenvalues for all $s$ in a neighborhood of $s_0$. In finite dimension this implies that its projection is $C^1$ when the Hamiltonian path is $C^1$. This cluster condition holds, for example, for the first $r_\Lambda$ eigenvalues counted with multiplicity when the integer $r_\Lambda$ is fixed along the path and the gap after them stays open. Uniform distance between the selected and unselected spectra alone does not prevent an interval from changing membership discontinuously. A ground band is such a band containing the lowest eigenvalue or a finite-volume cluster of lowest eigenvalues; no uniqueness is implicit.

For physical units, take interaction terms and Hamiltonians in joules, time in seconds, and $\hbar$ in joule-seconds. The path parameter $s$, lattice distance, and admissible weights are dimensionless; the interaction norm therefore has energy units and the derivative norm has energy units per dimensionless path parameter.

Let $d\ge1$, $\Gamma=\mathbb Z^d$, and $d_\infty$ be the max-coordinate metric. For $F(r)=(1+r)^{-d-1}$, $F_a(r)=e^{-ar}F(r)$ with $a>0$, and $F_\rho(r)=(1+r)^{-\rho}$ with $\rho>d$, each weight $G\in\{F_a,F_\rho\}$ is summable on $\Gamma$. Its convolution constant

$$C_G:=\sup_{x,y\in\Gamma} \frac{\sum_{z\in\Gamma}G(d_\infty(x,z))G(d_\infty(z,y))} {G(d_\infty(x,y))}$$

is finite and positive. In particular, for all $x,y\in\Gamma$,

$$\sum_{z\in\Gamma}G(d_\infty(x,z))G(d_\infty(z,y)) \le C_G\,G(d_\infty(x,y)).$$

The constant $C_{F_a}$ may be taken to be the convolution constant $C_F$ of $F$, independently of $a$.

Let $G$ be either $F_a$, $a>0$, or $F_\rho$, $\rho>d$, as in the weighted-interaction definition. Let $\Phi_u$ be a norm-continuous family of finite interactions on $\mathbb Z^d$, indexed by $u\in[0,T]$, with $M_G:=\sup_{u\in[0,T]}\|\Phi_u\|_G<\infty$. For finite $\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^d$, define $H_\Lambda(u)=\sum_{\varnothing\ne Z\subseteq\Lambda}\Phi_u(Z)$ and let $U_\Lambda(0)=I$ solve

$$\frac{d}{du}U_\Lambda(u)=-iH_\Lambda(u)U_\Lambda(u)/\hbar.$$

Set $\alpha_u^\Lambda(A)=U_\Lambda(u)^* A U_\Lambda(u)$, extended by the identity outside $\Lambda$. If $A\in\mathcal A_X$, $B\in\mathcal A_Y$ for disjoint finite nonempty $X,Y\subset\Lambda$, then

$$\|[\alpha_u^\Lambda(A),B]\|\le \frac{2\|A\|\|B\|}{C_G} \left(e^{2C_GM_Gu/\hbar}-1\right) \sum_{x\in X,\,y\in Y}G(d_\infty(x,y)).$$

The same estimate holds for the inverse path. In particular, for a constant interaction $\Phi$ evolved in physical time $t$ by $\tau_t^{\Lambda,\Phi}$, take $u=|t|$ and the constant path $\Phi_u=\Phi$ to obtain

$$\|[\tau_t^{\Lambda,\Phi}(A),B]\|\le \frac{2\|A\|\|B\|}{C_G} \left(e^{2C_G\|\Phi\|_G|t|/\hbar}-1\right) \sum_{x\in X,\,y\in Y}G(d_\infty(x,y)).$$

In physical units, $u,T,t$ are times, $M_G$ and $\|\Phi\|_G$ have energy units, and $\hbar$ has energy-times-time units; the weights and convolution constants are dimensionless, so the exponential arguments are dimensionless.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), the C*-algebra completion interface of [[lem-qsm-quasilocal-completion]], and the finite-matrix positive square-root interface of [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]]. Let $\{\rho_\Lambda\}$ be a consistent family of finite local density matrices as in [[lem-qsm-consistent-local-states]], and let $\omega$ be its extended algebraic state on the unital quasi-local algebra $\mathcal A$. Then there are a complex Hilbert space $\mathcal H_\omega$, a unital $*$-representation $\pi_\omega:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\omega)$, and a unit vector $\Omega_\omega$ cyclic for $\pi_\omega$ such that

$$\omega(A)=\langle \pi_\omega(A)\Omega_\omega,\Omega_\omega\rangle\qquad(A\in\mathcal A),$$

using the linear-first inner-product convention. Here $\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\omega)$ is the space of bounded linear operators with its operator norm, a $*$-representation is a complex-linear map preserving products, adjoints and the identity, and cyclic means that $\{\pi_\omega(A)\Omega_\omega:A\in\mathcal A\}$ is norm dense in $\mathcal H_\omega$. The theorem asserts existence of a cyclic representation, not uniqueness up to unitary equivalence.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mathcal H\ne\{0\}$ be a separable complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first argument. Let $K:D(K)\to\mathcal H$ be densely defined, self-adjoint and positive, meaning $\langle Kx,x\rangle\ge0$ for $x\in D(K)$. Let $(U_t)_{t\in\mathbb R}$ be a strongly continuous unitary group with generator $iK$: its strong derivative at zero exists exactly on $D(K)$ and equals $iKx$. The spectrum $\sigma(K)$ is the complement of the set of $z$ for which $K-z:D(K)\to\mathcal H$ has a bounded everywhere-defined inverse.

For every $x,y\in\mathcal H$ there is a finite complex Borel measure $\mu_{x,y}$ on $[0,\infty)$ such that

$$\langle U_t x,y\rangle=\int_{[0,\infty)}e^{itE}\,d\mu_{x,y}(E),\qquad |\mu_{x,y}|([0,\infty))\le\|x\|\,\|y\|.$$

The measures are sesquilinear in $(x,y)$, $\mu_x:=\mu_{x,x}$ is positive with total mass $\|x\|^2$, and every $\mu_{x,y}$ is carried by $\sigma(K)$. If $P_0$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\ker K$, then

$$\mu_{x,y}(\{0\})=\langle P_0x,y\rangle.$$

In particular, if $\sigma(K)\subseteq\{0\}\cup[g,\infty)$ with $g>0$, the measures $\mu_{(I-P_0)x,(I-P_0)y}$ are carried by $[g,\infty)$. Spectral measures and a projection-valued spectral resolution are not assumptions of this statement.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mathcal A$ be a unital complex $C^*$-algebra with a strongly continuous automorphism group $\alpha_t$. Let $\pi:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ be a contractive unital $*$-representation on a separable Hilbert space, with linear-first inner product, and let $\Omega$ be a unit vector. Suppose a strongly continuous unitary group $U_t$ implements $\pi(\alpha_t(A))=U_t\pi(A)U_t^*$, fixes $\Omega$, and has positive self-adjoint generator $iK$ satisfying

$$\ker K=\mathbb C\Omega,\qquad \sigma(K)\subseteq\{0\}\cup[g,\infty),\qquad g>0.$$

Write $\omega(A)=\langle\pi(A)\Omega,\Omega\rangle$. Let $A,B\in\mathcal A$ commute, put $f(t)=\omega([A,\alpha_t(B)])$, and suppose $|f(t)|\le L|t|$ for $|t|\le\eta$, for some finite $L$ and $\eta>0$. For every $q>0$, the scalar integral

$$I_q(A,B):=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{e^{-qt^2}}{2\pi it}\,f(t)\,dt$$

is absolutely convergent, with any value assigned to its integrand at $t=0$, and satisfies

$$\left|\omega(AB)-\omega(A)\omega(B)-I_q(A,B)\right|\le\|A\|\,\|B\|e^{-g^2/(4q)}.$$

The gap is that of this infinite- or finite-dimensional representation; no finite-volume approximating gaps are assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then every $x\in H$ has a unique decomposition

$$x=m+n,\qquad m\in M,\quad n\in M^\perp ,$$

so that $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ as a direct sum of the subspace $M$ and its orthogonal complement.

Assume Countable Choice. For a densely defined linear operator $T$ on $H$ the
adjoint $T^*$ is well defined and linear with linear domain $D(T^*)$; $T^*$ is
closed; for every $z\in\mathbb C$
$$\operatorname{ran}(T-z)^\perp=\ker(T^*-\overline z),$$
and if $S\subseteq T$ and both are densely defined, then $T^*\subseteq S^*$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue-measure interfaces. Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space, let $a<b$, and let $f:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous. Differentiation uses the underlying real structure. Then $G(t):=\int_a^t f(s)\,ds$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ and has the corresponding one-sided derivatives at $a,b$, with $G'(t)=f(t)$, and this derivative extends continuously to $[a,b]$. Consequently, if $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\varphi'$ continuous on $(a,b)$ and extendable to a continuous $X$-valued function on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b\varphi'(s)\,ds=\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)$. The Bochner integral here is the one of [[def-bochner-integrable-function]]; the identities also hold for continuous curves on $[0,\infty)$ restricted to compact subintervals.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: A cyclic representation of the spin algebra is separable. Indeed, finite tuples of the countable lattice enumerate its finite subsets, and rational real/imaginary entries form a countable dense family in each finite local matrix algebra. Countable Choice permits their countable union. Density follows, for a $D\times D$ matrix, from $\|T\|\le D\max_{i,j}|T_{ij}|$, obtained by finite Cauchy–Schwarz. The resulting countable family is dense in the completion, and its vectors $\pi(A)\Omega$ are dense in the cyclic Hilbert space by contractivity. The cyclic representation supplied by [F3] has the same state pairings as any given cyclic representation: the map $[A]\mapsto\pi(A)\Omega$ preserves $\langle[A],[B]\rangle=\omega(B^*A)$ and extends by density to a unitary. Thus the chosen cyclic ground representation is a separable realization of the actual GNS state, with no extra representation hypothesis.

We verify the advertised finite-range instance of the commutator premise. If $\Phi$ has range $R$ and per-site norm bound $\kappa$, a pair separated by more than $R$ contributes no interaction term, while for a pair of distance at most $R$ the numerator of the weighted norm is at most $\kappa$. Hence $\|\Phi\|_{F_a}\le\kappa/F_a(R)<\infty$. The uniform finite-volume bound [F2] passes to the thermodynamic limit for each local $A,B$ and fixed $t$, by norm continuity of commutators. The group is isometric, so $\|[A,\alpha_t(B)]\|=\|[\alpha_{-t}(A),B]\|$, matching exactly the supplier's time/support convention. This establishes the stated constants without replacing a general infinite-volume gap by a finite-volume gap.

The cyclic restriction in the ground-state definition preserves positive energy. Let $\mathcal L=\overline{\pi(\mathcal A)\Omega}$ in a ground representation. Covariance and $U_t\Omega=\Omega$ imply that $U_t$ and $U_{-t}$ preserve $\mathcal L$; its orthogonal projection commutes with $U_t$. For $x\in D(K)$, difference quotients show that this projection preserves $D(K)$ and commutes with $K$. The generator domain inside $\mathcal L$ is dense: the vectors $h^{-1}\int_0^hU_tx\,dt$ lie in it and tend to $x$ for $x\in\mathcal L$, as their difference quotients give $iK$ equal to $(U_hx-x)/h$. The restriction is self-adjoint because $K\pm i$ are onto, their bounded inverses preserve $\mathcal L$ by the commuting projection, and the restricted symmetric operator has both ranges onto; directly, if $y$ is in its adjoint domain, solve $(K+i)x=(K_{\mathcal L}^*+i)y$ in $\mathcal L$, and the zero kernel of $K_{\mathcal L}^*+i$ forces $x=y$. It is positive by restriction. More generally, for every $z$ in the resolvent of $K$, commutation of the projection with $K$ on its domain implies commutation with $(K-z)^{-1}$: apply $(K-z)$ and its injectivity to the two candidate images. This inverse therefore restricts to the inverse on $\mathcal L$, so $\sigma(K_{\mathcal L})\subseteq\sigma(K)$ and the spectral gap is inherited, as is a simple ground kernel. The resolvent surjectivity follows from the self-adjoint closed-range estimate exactly as in the spectral-measure helper. Thus the definition using a possibly noncyclic representation agrees with its cyclic restriction, without a Stone or spectral-existence theorem.

Let $P_0$ be the ground-kernel projection in the separable representation. A unit vector $\psi\in\ker K$ satisfies $U_t\psi=\psi$, since its orbit derivative is $iU_tK\psi=0$. Its vector state $\eta_\psi(A)=\langle\pi(A)\psi,\psi\rangle$ is a positive-energy ground state using the same representation; step 1.3 also supplies its cyclic version if desired. Uniqueness gives $\eta_\psi=\omega$. Scaling and polarization inside $\ker K$ therefore yield $P_0\pi(A)P_0=\omega(A)P_0$ for every $A$. If $\psi\in\ker K$ is orthogonal to $\Omega$, this identity implies $\langle\pi(A)\Omega,\psi\rangle=0$ for every $A$. Cyclicity forces $\psi=0$. Since the fixed vector $\Omega$ has zero orbit derivative, $\Omega\in D(K)$ and $K\Omega=0$, so we have $\ker K=\mathbb C\Omega$. The alternative hypothesis stated in the theorem supplies this directly and needs no uniqueness argument.

Put $N=\|A\|\|B\|$ and $f(t)=\omega([A,\alpha_t(B)])$. The displayed Lieb–Robinson premise, $F_a(s)\le e^{-as}$ and $d_\infty(x,y)\ge r$ give $$|f(t)|\le\frac{2N}{C}|X||Y|e^{-ar}(e^{v|t|}-1),\qquad |f(t)|\le2N.$$ The first bound is $O(t)$ at zero, including $v=0$. The local observables commute by [F1], so all time-integral hypotheses in [F4] hold. The same estimates apply to the finite-range instance justified in step 1.2.

Apply [F4] using step 2.1. For any $q,\tau>0$, split its absolutely convergent integral at $|t|=\tau$. Step 2.2 gives the short-time bound $$\frac{2N|X||Y|}{\pi C}e^{-ar}\int_0^\tau\frac{e^{vt}-1}{t}dt\le\frac{2N|X||Y|}{\pi C}e^{-ar+v\tau},$$ by [F6], because $(e^{vt}-1)/t\le ve^{vt}$ and $e^{v\tau}-1\le e^{v\tau}$, with zero left side when $v=0$. On the long-time part the trivial bound gives $$\frac{2N}{\pi}\int_\tau^\infty\frac{e^{-qt^2}}t dt=\frac N\pi\int_{q\tau^2}^\infty\frac{e^{-u}}u du\le\frac{N}{\pi q\tau^2}e^{-q\tau^2}.$$ Adding the filter error $Ne^{-g^2/(4q)}$ bounds the connected correlation. These estimates use only the supplied dynamics and its infinite-volume ground representation.

Choose $\tau=ar/(v+g/2)$ and $q=g/(2\tau)$. They are positive for $r\ge1$ and $g,a>0$, even when $v=0$. Then $$ar-v\tau=q\tau^2=\frac{g^2}{4q}=\frac{ag}{2v+g}r=\mu r,\qquad \frac1{q\tau^2}=\frac{2v+g}{agr}.$$ Substitution into step 3.1 proves the displayed bound. Zero observables give $N=0$ and require no division by $N$. The independent finite-volume band multiplicity and transport statements on this page are unchanged; this proof adds no claim that a degenerate gapped state has ordinary connected clustering. The clock conversion $g=\gamma/\hbar$ gives exactly the units in the Statement.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement requires finite nonempty disjoint supports and r≥1; step 4.1 separately permits zero observables.
Step 2.2 includes v=0, step 3.1 makes its short-time term zero, and step 4.1 treats N=0 without division.
Step 4.1 applies at r=1; step 2.1 proves the normalized ground vector spans the kernel.
Step 2.1 derives a simple kernel from uniqueness; the alternative Statement explicitly assumes it. A degenerate gap alone is not used.
Step 3.1 treats t=0 through the O(t) filter and both infinite tails; step 4.1 keeps positive q,τ when v=0.
Step 1.1 constructs a countable dense cyclic realization under CC, and steps 1.3 and 2.1 use closed-subspace projections with their CC supplier.

boundaries.reason: thm-qsmx-gapped-ground-state-clustering: the public Statement is a forward construction/estimate, not an equivalence.
thm-qsmx-gapped-ground-state-clustering: no reverse characterization is asserted; the hypotheses are sufficient conditions only.

citations.quote:
Let $Q\in\{2,3,4\}$ and let $L\geq1$ be an integer. The finite Potts-clock space is
$$\mathcal H_{Q,L}:=(\mathbb C^Q)^{\otimes L}$$
of dimension $Q^L$, with the tensor-product Hermitian inner product taken linear in its first argument and computational orthonormal basis
$$|a_1,\ldots,a_L\rangle:=|a_1\rangle\otimes\cdots\otimes|a_L\rangle,\qquad a_j\in\{0,\ldots,Q-1\}.$$
On $\mathbb C^Q$, this inner product is $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{a=0}^{Q-1}x_a\overline{y_a}$, and on elementary tensors it is $\langle u_1\otimes\cdots\otimes u_L,v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_L\rangle=\prod_{j=1}^L\langle u_j,v_j\rangle$.
For a unit vector $u$, the notation $|u\rangle\langle u|$ denotes the endomorphism $v\mapsto\langle v,u\rangle u$. On one site use the clock and shift convention
$$R_Q|a\rangle=e^{2\pi i a/Q}|a\rangle,\qquad M_Q|a\rangle=|a-1\!\!\pmod Q\rangle.$$
Set $|+\rangle:=Q^{-1/2}\sum_{a=0}^{Q-1}|a\rangle$. For $1\leq j\leq L$, let $P_j$ be $|+\rangle\langle+|$ on factor $j$ and identity on every other factor. For $1\leq j<L$, let
$$D_{j,j+1}:=\sum_{a=0}^{Q-1}|aa\rangle\langle aa|$$
act on factors $j,j+1$ and as identity on the others. The open-chain local operators are
$$e_{2j-1}:=\sqrt Q\,P_j\quad(1\leq j\leq L),\qquad e_{2j}:=\sqrt Q\,D_{j,j+1}\quad(1\leq j<L).$$
Equivalently, these are the exact clock-shift operators of the open Potts representation: $e_{2j-1}=Q^{-1/2}\sum_{r=0}^{Q-1}M_{Q,j}^{\,r}$ and $e_{2j}=Q^{-1/2}\sum_{r=0}^{Q-1}R_{Q,j}^{\,r}R_{Q,j+1}^{-r}$. Thus there are $2L-1$ operators and no bond from site $L$ back to site $1$.

For real coefficients $J_1,\ldots,J_{2L-1}$, define the weighted open-chain matrix
$$H_{Q,L}(\mathbf J):=-\sum_{i=1}^{2L-1}J_i e_i.$$
It is an endomorphism of $\mathcal H_{Q,L}$. For an endomorphism $T$ of this inner-product space, $T^*$ is its adjoint, characterized by $\langle Tv,w\rangle=\langle v,T^*w\rangle$; $T$ is self-adjoint (Hermitian) exactly when $T=T^*$. An endomorphism is normal exactly when $TT^*=T^*T$, so every self-adjoint endomorphism is normal. For a subspace $W\subseteq\mathcal H_{Q,L}$, the orthogonal projection onto $W$ sends $w+z$ to $w$ in the unique decomposition $\mathcal H_{Q,L}=W\oplus W^\perp$, with $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$. Viewed as an endomorphism, it satisfies $\Pi_W^2=\Pi_W=\Pi_W^*$; the adjoint identity follows from the orthogonality of the two summands. A self-adjoint endomorphism $A$ is positive definite if $\langle Av,v\rangle>0$ for every nonzero $v$, and is positive semidefinite exactly when $\langle Av,v\rangle\geq0$ for every $v$; these quadratic forms are real because $A=A^*$. The trace $\operatorname{tr}(T)$ of a finite-dimensional endomorphism is the basis-independent sum of diagonal entries of its matrix.

For self-adjoint $H_{Q,L}$ and real $\beta$, a scalar $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $H_{Q,L}$ when $\ker(H_{Q,L}-\lambda I)\ne\{0\}$, and this kernel is its eigenspace. Let $\Lambda(H_{Q,L})$ be the finite set of distinct eigenvalues. Every $\lambda\in\Lambda(H_{Q,L})$ is real: for a unit eigenvector $v$, $\lambda=\langle H_{Q,L}v,v\rangle=\langle v,H_{Q,L}v\rangle=\overline\lambda$. Let $\Pi_\lambda$ be the orthogonal projection onto the $\lambda$-eigenspace as defined above. A self-adjoint endomorphism is normal, and every normal endomorphism of a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space has an orthonormal eigenbasis; therefore $\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda(H_{Q,L})}\Pi_\lambda=I$. Define
$$B_\beta(H_{Q,L}):=\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda(H_{Q,L})}e^{-\beta\lambda}\Pi_\lambda,\qquad Z_\beta:=\operatorname{tr}B_\beta(H_{Q,L}),\qquad \rho_\beta:=Z_\beta^{-1}B_\beta(H_{Q,L})$$
whenever $Z_\beta>0$. Here a density matrix means a self-adjoint positive semidefinite endomorphism of trace one. The A-page Gibbs lemma establishes that the displayed $H_{Q,L}$ is self-adjoint and that $Z_\beta>0$ for every finite real $\beta$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be

the endomorphism $T$** by

derivations.claim: Each $P_j$ is an orthogonal projection because $\langle+|+\rangle=1$. Each $D_{j,j+1}$ is a sum of mutually orthogonal rank-one projections onto the computational vectors $|aa\rangle$. Hence these operators are self-adjoint; since $\sqrt Q$ and each $J_i$ are real, every $e_i$ and then $H_{Q,L}=-\sum_iJ_i e_i$ are self-adjoint.

By [F2] and [F3], $H_{Q,L}$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis. For a unit eigenvector $v$ with $H_{Q,L}v=\lambda v$, self-adjointness and the linear-first inner-product convention give $\lambda=\langle H_{Q,L}v,v\rangle=\langle v,H_{Q,L}v\rangle=\overline\lambda$, so every eigenvalue $\lambda$ is real. The distinct-eigenvalue projections $\Pi_\lambda$ are self-adjoint and sum to the identity by [F1]. Each weight $w_\lambda=e^{-\beta\lambda}$ is finite, real, and strictly positive by [F4]. Therefore $B_\beta=\sum_\lambda w_\lambda\Pi_\lambda$ is self-adjoint, and for every nonzero $v$, $\langle B_\beta v,v\rangle=\sum_\lambda w_\lambda\|\Pi_\lambda v\|^2>0$: at least one projected component is nonzero since $\sum_\lambda\Pi_\lambda=I$. Thus $B_\beta$ is positive definite.

In an orthonormal eigenbasis, [F5] gives $Z_\beta=\operatorname{tr}B_\beta=\sum_\lambda w_\lambda\dim(\operatorname{ran}\Pi_\lambda)$. The space has finite positive dimension $Q^L$, so this is a finite sum with at least one positive term; hence $Z_\beta$ is finite and strictly positive. It is a real scalar. Dividing the self-adjoint positive definite $B_\beta$ by $Z_\beta$ gives a self-adjoint positive semidefinite $\rho_\beta$, and $\operatorname{tr}\rho_\beta=Z_\beta^{-1}Z_\beta=1$.

If all $J_i=0$, then $H_{Q,L}=0$; if $\beta=0$, all spectral weights also equal $e^0$. By [F4] at $x=0$, $a:=e^0>0$ and $a=1/a$, so $a=1$. In either boundary case $B=I$, $Z=Q^L$ by [F5], and $\rho=I/Q^L$.

citations.quote:
Let $d\geq1$ and let $\mathcal H=\mathbb C^d$ with its standard complex inner product. Let $H=H^*$ on $\mathcal H$ be a Hamiltonian matrix with entries in joules, let $\hbar>0$ have units joule-seconds, and let $S_1,\ldots,S_m$ be a finite family of dimensionless Hermitian matrices, where $m\geq0$. Write the finite spectral decomposition $H=\sum_{E\in\operatorname{spec}(H)} E P_E$, where $P_E$ are pairwise orthogonal spectral projections and $\sum_E P_E=I_d$. The Bohr-frequency set is

$$\Omega_H:=\{(E'-E)/\hbar:E,E'\in\operatorname{spec}(H)\}\subset\mathbb R,$$

whose frequencies have units seconds$^{-1}$. For each $\omega\in\Omega_H$ and $1\leq a\leq m$, define the dimensionless energy-resolved coupling

$$S_a(\omega):=\sum_{\substack{E,E'\in\operatorname{spec}(H)\\E'-E=\hbar\omega}}P_E S_a P_{E'}.$$

Let $\beta\in\mathbb R$ have units joules$^{-1}$. For each $\omega\in\Omega_H$, choose a finite rate matrix $\Gamma(\omega)=(\gamma_{ab}(\omega))_{a,b=1}^m$, with entries in seconds$^{-1}$, that is positive semidefinite in the explicit sense that $\Gamma(\omega)=\Gamma(\omega)^*$ and $v^*\Gamma(\omega)v\geq0$ for every $v\in\mathbb C^m$, and require the thermal balance relation

$$\gamma_{ab}(-\omega)=e^{-\beta\hbar\omega}\gamma_{ba}(\omega).$$

Let $H_{\rm LS}=H_{\rm LS}^*$ be a Hermitian matrix with units joules satisfying $[H_{\rm LS},H]=0$. For dimensionless $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, the finite energy-resolved generator is the linear map

$$\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H+H_{\rm LS},X]+\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_H}\sum_{a,b=1}^{m}\gamma_{ab}(\omega)\left(S_b(\omega)X S_a(\omega)^*-\frac12\{S_a(\omega)^*S_b(\omega),X\}\right),$$

where $[A,B]=AB-BA$, $\{A,B\}=AB+BA$, and $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. The finite sums define a linear map with units seconds$^{-1}$. This is an adopted finite effective model specification; the definition asserts no microscopic weak-coupling convergence or physical applicability.

Let $d,e\geq1$ be integers, let $H_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb C^e$ with their standard inner products, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $M_e(\mathbb C)$ for the complex linear maps on these spaces. A matrix $X$ is **positive semidefinite**, written $X\geq0$, when it is Hermitian and $\langle Xv,v\rangle\geq0$ for every vector $v$. The finite spectral convention in [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]] gives positive matrices their orthonormal eigenbases and positive square roots.

A **positive map** is a complex-linear map $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi(X)\geq0$ whenever $X\geq0$. For each integer $r\geq1$, identify $M_r(\mathbb C)\otimes M_d(\mathbb C)$ with matrices on $\mathbb C^r\otimes\mathbb C^d$ in the ordered product basis. The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** when $\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every such $r$, where $\operatorname{id}_r$ is the identity map on $M_r(\mathbb C)$.

The map $\Phi$ is **trace-preserving** when $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{Tr}(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. A **finite quantum channel** is a complex-linear map that is both completely positive and trace-preserving, abbreviated CPTP. Unitality, $\Phi(I_d)=I_e$, is a separate condition and is not part of this definition.

This is a mathematical definition. A physical preparation, measurement, or open-system model must separately identify when one of these maps represents a physical transformation.

Fix a finite dimension $d\geq1$, a positive constant $\hbar$ in joule-seconds, a Hermitian matrix $H\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ in joules, and a finite family $L_1,\ldots,L_m\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ with units ${\rm s}^{-1/2}$, where $m\geq0$. On dimensionless matrices $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, define the **finite Gorini–Kossakowski–Sudarshan–Lindblad (GKSL) generator**

$$\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_{a=1}^{m}\left(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\}\right),$$

where $[A,B]=AB-BA$, $\{A,B\}=AB+BA$, and $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. Each summand has units ${\rm s}^{-1}$ times the units of $X$. An empty sum when $m=0$ is zero. The resulting $\mathcal L$ is a linear map on the matrix space used in the finite-channel definition [[def-qsm-dt-channel-definition]].

For a compact time interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ whose coordinate is time in seconds, continuous functions $H:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $L_a:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ with $H(t)=H(t)^*$ define the corresponding **continuous finite GKSL family** $\mathcal L_t$ by the same formula at each $t$. A propagator for this family means a family of linear maps $\Lambda(t,s)$, $s\leq t$ in $I$, satisfying $\partial_t\Lambda(t,s)=\mathcal L_t\circ\Lambda(t,s)$ and $\Lambda(s,s)=\operatorname{id}$. This definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

These are finite-dimensional mathematical definitions. They do not assert that a physical system follows this generator or that a microscopic bath has a Markovian limit.

Let $\mathcal L$ be a finite GKSL generator on $M_d(\mathbb C)$, $d\geq1$, with the units and conventions of [[def-qsm-dt-gksl-definition]]. For a bounded operator $A$ on a complex Banach space, write $e^{tA}:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}t^nA^n/n!$ for the operator-norm convergent series of [[lem-exponential-series-of-a-bounded-operator]]. Then $T_t=e^{t\mathcal L}$ is a finite channel for every $t\geq0$. The family satisfies $T_0=\operatorname{id}$, $T_{t+s}=T_t\circ T_s$, and is norm-continuous. Time is measured in seconds; no negative-time channel or physical bath limit is asserted.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

derivations.claim: For each $\omega$, positive semidefiniteness of the finite matrix $\Gamma(\omega)$ gives a finite factorization $\gamma_{ab}(\omega)=\sum_r\overline{c_{ra}(\omega)}c_{rb}(\omega)$, with $c_{ra}(\omega)$ in seconds$^{-1/2}$. Define $J_{r,\omega}:=\sum_b c_{rb}(\omega)S_b(\omega)$. Expanding yields $\sum_rJ_{r,\omega}XJ_{r,\omega}^*=\sum_{a,b}\gamma_{ab}(\omega)S_b(\omega)XS_a(\omega)^*$ and $\sum_rJ_{r,\omega}^*J_{r,\omega}=\sum_{a,b}\gamma_{ab}(\omega)S_a(\omega)^*S_b(\omega)$. Thus the displayed generator has the finite GKSL form of [F2] with Hamiltonian $H+H_{\rm LS}$ and finite jumps $J_{r,\omega}$, so [F3] gives a finite channel semigroup; [F1] states its complete-positivity and trace-preservation content.

From the spectral definition, $[H,S_a(\omega)]=-\hbar\omega S_a(\omega)$ and $S_a(\omega)^*=S_a(-\omega)$. Therefore $S_a(\omega)e^{-\beta H}=e^{-\beta\hbar\omega}e^{-\beta H}S_a(\omega)$. Every $S_a(-\omega)S_b(\omega)$ commutes with $H$ because its two energy shifts cancel, hence it commutes with each spectral projection of $H$ and with $\sigma_\beta$. Also $[H_{\rm LS},H]=0$ implies $H_{\rm LS}$ preserves every eigenspace of $H$: if $Hx=Ex$, then $H(H_{\rm LS}x)=H_{\rm LS}(Hx)=E(H_{\rm LS}x)$. Thus $H_{\rm LS}$ commutes with every spectral projection of $H$ and with $\sigma_\beta$. Finally, the exponential $e^{-\beta H}$ is positive definite with positive finite trace, making $\sigma_\beta$ a faithful density.

Fix $\omega>0$ and put $q=e^{-\beta\hbar\omega}$. The $\omega$ contribution is $\mathcal D_{\omega}(\sigma_\beta)=\sigma_\beta\sum_{a,b}\gamma_{ab}(\omega)(qS_b(\omega)S_a(-\omega)-S_a(-\omega)S_b(\omega))$, using $S_b(\omega)\sigma_\beta=q\sigma_\beta S_b(\omega)$ and commutation of the anticommutator product with $\sigma_\beta$. For the negative frequency, substitute $\gamma_{ab}(-\omega)=q\gamma_{ba}(\omega)$ and $S_a(-\omega)^*=S_a(\omega)$, then reindex $a,b$ to obtain $\mathcal D_{-\omega}(\sigma_\beta)=\sigma_\beta\sum_{a,b}\gamma_{ab}(\omega)(S_a(-\omega)S_b(\omega)-qS_b(\omega)S_a(-\omega))=-\mathcal D_{\omega}(\sigma_\beta)$. Thus every nonzero frequency pair cancels.

At $\omega=0$, the balance relation gives $\gamma_{ab}(0)=\gamma_{ba}(0)$. Each $S_a(0)$ is Hermitian and commutes with $H$, hence with $\sigma_\beta$; consequently the zero-frequency contribution is $\sigma_\beta\sum_{a,b}\gamma_{ab}(0)(S_b(0)S_a(0)-S_a(0)S_b(0))=0$, after swapping $a,b$ in the first finite sum. The Hamiltonian contribution vanishes because both $H$ and $H_{\rm LS}$ commute with $\sigma_\beta$. Together with step 2.1 this gives $\mathcal L(\sigma_\beta)=0$, and the exponential series then gives $T_t(\sigma_\beta)=\sigma_\beta$ for all $t\geq0$.

derivations.claim: Regard $B=iA$ as a complex matrix on $\mathbb C^{2N}$. Since $A^{\mathsf T}=-A$ and $A$ is real, $B^*=(-i)A^{\mathsf T}=iA=B$. By [F1], $B$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. Complex conjugation sends an eigenvector of eigenvalue $\epsilon>0$ to an eigenvector of eigenvalue $-\epsilon$, because conjugating $iAz=\epsilon z$ gives $-iA\overline z=\epsilon\overline z$. Thus nonzero eigenvalues occur in opposite pairs.

Fix a unit eigenvector $z=u+iv$ for $\epsilon>0$, with real vectors $u,v$. The vectors $z$ and $\overline z$ belong to distinct eigenspaces of the Hermitian matrix $B$, so $\langle z,\overline z\rangle=0$. Expanding this equality gives $\|u\|^2=\|v\|^2$ and $u\cdot v=0$; $\|z\|=1$ then gives $\|u\|=\|v\|=1/\sqrt2$. From $Az=-i\epsilon z$, comparison of real and imaginary parts gives $Au=\epsilon v$ and $Av=-\epsilon u$. Therefore $e_1=\sqrt2u$ and $e_2=-\sqrt2v$ are orthonormal and $Ae_1=-\epsilon e_2$, $Ae_2=\epsilon e_1$, which is the displayed block in this basis.

Choose an orthonormal basis in each positive eigenspace of $B$; [F1] supplies these finite-dimensional bases. Together with their complex conjugates, the chosen vectors are orthonormal: conjugation preserves orthonormality, and every positive eigenspace is orthogonal to every negative eigenspace of the Hermitian matrix $B$. Hence the real planes from step 2.1 are mutually orthogonal. On the zero eigenspace, $Az=0$, so the real and imaginary parts of each vector lie in the real kernel of $A$. The real and complex kernels have equal dimension because row reduction of the real matrix $A$ has the same pivots over $\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb C$; this dimension is $2N$ minus twice the total number of positive eigenvectors, hence even. Choose a real basis of $\ker A$ and successively subtract projections onto earlier vectors and normalize each nonzero residual; this gives an orthonormal real basis. Pairing consecutive vectors gives zero blocks. The resulting real orthonormal basis gives the required $O$.

Since $O$ is orthogonal, $(OAO^{\mathsf T})^{\mathsf T}(OAO^{\mathsf T})=OA^{\mathsf T}AO^{\mathsf T}=\bigoplus_{r=1}^N\epsilon_r^2I_2$. Thus the singular-value multiset from the Statement has two entries $\epsilon_r$ for each block $r$, including its two zero entries when $\epsilon_r=0$. This identifies every positive block value once per real two-plane and completes the multiplicity assertion.

derivations.claim: Choose a closed interval $I_0\subset U$ whose interior contains $\mu_0$, and for $r\in I_0$ define $f(r,x)=N(x)p(T_0/N(x),(r-q\Phi(x))/N(x))/(k_BT_0)$. The image of $I_0\times\Sigma$ in $D$ is compact, so $p_\mu$ and $p_{\mu\mu}$ are bounded and uniformly continuous there. Since $N$ is continuous and positive on compact $\Sigma$, its image has a minimum $N_{\min}>0$; also $dV_h(\Sigma)<\infty$. The one-variable mean value theorem and uniform continuity of $\partial_r f$ make the difference quotients of $f$ converge uniformly in $x$ to $\partial_r f=p_\mu(T_0/N,(r-q\Phi)/N)/(k_BT_0)$. For these quotients $q_h$, the estimate $|\int_\Sigma q_h\,dV_h-\int_\Sigma\partial_r f\,dV_h|\le dV_h(\Sigma)\sup_x|q_h(x)-\partial_r f(r,x)|$ tends to zero. Thus differentiation passes through the finite-volume integral and yields $\partial_{\mu_0}W_{\rm hs}=\int_\Sigma p_\mu/(k_BT_0)\,dV_h$.

Applying the same uniform difference-quotient argument to $\partial_r f$, whose derivative is $\partial_r^2 f=p_{\mu\mu}(T_0/N,(r-q\Phi)/N)/(N k_BT_0)$, gives $\partial_{\mu_0}^2W_{\rm hs}=\int_\Sigma p_{\mu\mu}/(N k_BT_0)\,dV_h$. The factors $N$ cancel once in the first derivative, while the second derivative retains the positive factor $1/N$.

By [A1], each integrand value in the second formula is nonnegative because $N(x)>0$, $k_B>0$, and $T_0>0$. By [F3], the Riemannian volume density is positive, so its integral is nonnegative and therefore $\chi_{\rm hs}\ge0$.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power (Integer powers $a^m$),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges (Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Let

$$f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_n(x-c)^n$$

have radius $R$. For every $x$ with $|x-c|<R$, the function $f$ is differentiable at $x$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$f'(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\iota(n+1)a_{n+1}(x-c)^n.$$

The differentiated series has the same radius $R$.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
(Interior, closure, boundary and exterior of a subset of $\mathbb{R}$, The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)), neighbourhoods are those of
The $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood and the punctured $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood of a point of $\mathbb{R}$ and limit points those of Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$ defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by At a limit point of the domain a function has at most one limit applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$ leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
(The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of The limit at $c$ depends only on the restriction of $f$ to a punctured neighbourhood of $c$, and passes to any subset of the domain having $c$ as a limit point carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

The function induced by an inner product satisfies, for all vectors $u,v$ and scalars $\lambda$,

$$\lVert v\rVert\ge0,\qquad \lVert v\rVert=0\Longleftrightarrow v=0,$$

$$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert,\qquad \lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert.$$

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

Its radius is therefore at least $1$, and [F6] gives $P'(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}x^{n-1}=1/(1-x)$. The difference quotient for $\log$ in [F4], with increment $-h$, gives $\frac{d}{dx}[-\log(1-x)]=1/(1-x)$. Since both functions vanish at $0$ by [F3], [F7] applied to their difference yields $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}x^n/n=-\log(1-x)$ for every $|x|<1$.

For any endomorphisms $S,T$, [F9] then gives $\|STx\|\le\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|Tx\|\le\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|x\|$ for every vector $x$. Taking the supremum over unit $x$ proves $\|ST\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}$.

Hence $q:=\|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}<1$ by [F1]. Choose $r$ with $q<r<1$. By [F8], every entry of $A(t)-A_0$ tends to zero as $t\to t_0$. Since there are finitely many entries, $M(t):=\max_{i,j}|(A(t)-A_0)_{ij}|\to0$, and the matrix bound in step 1.2 gives $\|A(t)-A_0\|_{\mathrm{op}}\to0$, so choose a neighborhood where $\|A(t)-A_0\|_{\mathrm{op}}/c<(r-q)/2$. For every unit vector $x$, the inner-product norm triangle inequality [F11] and [F9] give $\|B_tx\|\le\|Bx\|+\|(A(t)-A_0)x\|/c\le q+\|A(t)-A_0\|_{\mathrm{op}}/c<r$; taking the supremum proves $\|B_t\|_{\mathrm{op}}<r$. For such $t$, the scalar identity in step 1.1 applied to each eigenvalue of $B_t$, the product law [F10], and spectral calculus [F1] give $\log A(t)=(\log c)I_H-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}B_t^n/n$, with convergence in operator norm because repeated application of step 1.2 gives $\|B_t^n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|B_t\|_{\mathrm{op}}^n<r^n$ and $\sum r^n/n\le\sum r^n<\infty$.

For $t$ sufficiently near $t_0$, put $E:=A(t)-A_0$, $Z:=-E/c$, and $z:=\|Z\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. Then $B_t=B+Z$. The supremum definition gives $z=\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}/c$, so $z\to0$ as $t\to t_0$; shrink the neighborhood so that $q+z\le r$. Distributivity writes $(B+Z)^n=B^n+S_n+R_n$, where $S_n:=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}B^j ZB^{n-1-j}$ contains the terms with exactly one $Z$, and $R_n$ contains all terms with at least two $Z$ factors. The submultiplicative bound in step 1.2 gives $\|S_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le nq^{n-1}z$. For $R_n$, each word with exactly $k$ factors $Z$ has norm at most $q^{n-k}z^k$, and there are $\binom nk$ such words, so $\|R_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\sum_{k=2}^n\binom nkq^{n-k}z^k\le\binom n2z^2(q+z)^{n-2}\le\binom n2z^2r^{n-2}$. The middle bound follows from $\binom nk\le\binom n2\binom{n-2}{k-2}$ for $k\ge2$.

Substituting the series of step 2.1 into $G(A):=\operatorname{tr}(A\log A)$, and using step 3.1, yields
$$G(A_0+E)-G(A_0)=(\log c)\operatorname{tr}E-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\operatorname{tr}(EB^n)+\operatorname{tr}(A_0S_n)}{n}+R(E),$$
where $|R(E)|\le C\|E\|^2$ for a constant $C$ independent of sufficiently small $E$. Indeed, the omitted terms are $\operatorname{tr}(A_0R_n)$, $\operatorname{tr}(ES_n)$, and $\operatorname{tr}(ER_n)$; for each orthonormal basis vector $e_i$, the $i$th coordinate of $Te_i$ is $\langle Te_i,e_i\rangle$ and [F12] gives its magnitude at most $\|Te_i\|\|e_i\|=\|Te_i\|\le\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ by [F9], since $\|e_i\|=1$, so [F2] gives $|\operatorname{tr}T|\le d\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ with $d=\dim H$, and the bounds in step 3.1 make their series after division by $n$ bounded by constants times $z^2\sum_{n\ge2}nr^{n-2}$, $z^2\sum_{n\ge1}q^{n-1}$, and $z^3\sum_{n\ge2}nr^{n-2}$, respectively. Each geometric derivative sum is finite by [F5]–[F6], and step 3.1 gives $z=\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}/c$.

The linear matrix-log term read from the series in steps 2.1 and 3.1 is
$$L(E):=\frac1c\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1n\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}B^jEB^{n-1-j}.$$
Its series converges in operator norm because the $n$th summand has norm at most $q^{n-1}\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}/c$. The remainder in the logarithm series is bounded by $\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\binom n2 z^2r^{n-2}/n=(z^2/2)\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}(n-1)r^{n-2}=O(\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2)$, so $L(E)$ is the full first-order term of $\log(A_0+E)$. In an orthonormal eigenbasis of $A_0$, write $A_0e_i=\lambda_i e_i$ and $b_i:=1-\lambda_i/c$. Then
$$L(E)_{ik}=\frac{E_{ik}}c\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1n\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}b_i^jb_k^{n-1-j}.$$
If $b_i\ne b_k$, the inner sum is $(b_i^n-b_k^n)/(b_i-b_k)$, so its coefficient is
$\frac1c\frac{\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(b_i^n-b_k^n)/n}{b_i-b_k}=\frac{\log(1-b_k)-\log(1-b_i)}{c(b_i-b_k)}=\frac{\log\lambda_i-\log\lambda_k}{\lambda_i-\lambda_k},$
where step 1.1 evaluates the series and [F10] gives $\log\lambda_j=\log c+\log(1-b_j)$, while $\lambda_i-\lambda_k=c(b_k-b_i)$. If $b_i=b_k$, the coefficient is $c^{-1}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}b_i^{n-1}=1/(c(1-b_i))=1/\lambda_i=\log'(\lambda_i)$ by [F4] and [F5]. Defining $\log^{[1]}(x,y):=(\log x-\log y)/(x-y)$ for $x\ne y$ and $\log^{[1]}(x,x):=1/x$, we have $L(E)_{ik}=\log^{[1]}(\lambda_i,\lambda_k)E_{ik}$: this is the divided-difference derivative of the matrix logarithm.

In a fixed basis, [F2] gives $\operatorname{tr}(XY)=\sum_{i,j}X_{ij}Y_{ji}=\sum_{i,j}Y_{ji}X_{ij}=\operatorname{tr}(YX)$, so trace is cyclic. Since $A_0$ commutes with $B$ and $Z=-E/c$, cycling each term gives $\operatorname{tr}(A_0S_n)=-(n/c)\operatorname{tr}(A_0B^{n-1}E)$. Thus the $A_0S_n$ terms in step 4.1 sum to $\operatorname{tr}(A_0L(E))$. In the eigenbasis used in step 4.2, $L(E)_{ii}=E_{ii}/\lambda_i$, so $\operatorname{tr}(A_0L(E))=\sum_i\lambda_iL(E)_{ii}=\operatorname{tr}E$. The remaining linear terms in step 4.1 are $\operatorname{tr}(E\log A_0)$ by the spectral series in step 2.1. Therefore $G(A_0+E)-G(A_0)=\operatorname{tr}(E(\log A_0+I_H))+O(\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2)$.

By [F8], for $h\to0$ the path increment is $E=A(t_0+h)-A_0=hA'(t_0)+o(h)$ entrywise. The finite-coordinate bound in step 2.1 gives $\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(|h|)$. Dividing the expansion in step 5.1 by $h$ makes its $O(\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2)$ remainder tend to $0$ and its linear term tend to $\operatorname{tr}(A'(t_0)(\log A(t_0)+I_H))$. This is the stated derivative.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power (Integer powers $a^m$),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges (Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
(Interior, closure, boundary and exterior of a subset of $\mathbb{R}$, The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.
supplier_excerpts.relevant_hypotheses_and_conventions: [[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]]: a continuous function on an interval with zero derivative at every interior point is constant on that interval.
